RATHER THAN OVER THE COLUMN.** The sub-project opened with two candidate fixes
and a rule that at most one could land. The first candidate was `:92`,
`matches = re.finditer(pattern, reply.body)`, whose twin `app/shared/tasks/pages.py:97`
guards the identical scan with `if post.body:` and whose column, `PostReply.body`
(`app/models.py:2901`), is nullable. **The nullable column is what made it look
like a defect and it is not evidence of one.** The reachability question was
settled by enumerating what can put a reply in front of the function:
`send_reply` is called only from `app/shared/tasks/notes.py:59` and `:72`;
`task_selector('make_reply'|'edit_reply')` appears at exactly three sites,
`app/shared/reply.py:194`, `:232` and `app/post/routes.py:928`; all three write
`body` through `piefed_markdown_to_lemmy_markdown` (`app/utils.py:1233-1237`);
and that function, **executed rather than read**, raises
`TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'NoneType'` on `None`
before any commit -- byte-identical to the crash `:92` would produce. So the bad
state dies in the writer. The writers that **can** store a `None` body
(`app/activitypub/util.py:3020`, `:2639`, `app/community/util.py:272`) are all
inbound and dispatch no task; they are **D311**. `:92` is therefore **D310**,
registered as latent and left unguarded, and the private gate landed instead.
**Three method points, each of which cost something when it was skipped
somewhere in this campaign:** enumerate call sites of the **task**, not of the
function, because the Celery indirection hides them in both directions;
**execute** the suspected raiser rather than arguing about it; and when a brief
names two writers, check whether the set is closed -- this one named two, the
implementer found three dispatchers, and the review found a **third**
`None`-capable writer the report had asserted away by writing "the TWO writers
that CAN store a `None` body".

**THE STATED REASON FOR DECLINING THE `:92` GUARD DID NOT SURVIVE REVIEW, AND
THE DECISION DID. THE WRONG REASON IS IN A COMMITTED COMMIT MESSAGE.** The
controller's brief and the implementer's report both rejected a `:92` guard as
"untestable defence whose mutants nobody can kill". **That is false and the
review showed why**: `PostReply.body` is nullable, the probe test seeds `None`
at model level, so an `if False:` mutant would be killed by the existing
mention-notification tests and an `if True:` mutant by the probe -- exactly the
way the private gate's own mutants are killed by a directly seeded
`private=True`. The distinction between "reachable by a supported model-level
write" and "reachable only by a value no writer can produce" does not survive
either, because the model-level write is available in both cases. **The decision
stands on the OTHER reason that was given**: the twin-matching shape requires
wrapping `:91-116` in `if reply.body:` and re-indenting ~26 lines, which shifts
`:120`, `:129`, `:143`, `:175`, `:185`, `:187`, `:203`, `:217` and `:225` -- every
line six later tasks cite -- by one. That is the hazard sub-project 19 paid two
fix rounds for. **A third shape existed and was argued down rather than ignored**:
`re.finditer(pattern, reply.body or '')` is one line in place and shifts nothing,
so it defeats the line-number objection entirely -- and it was refused because
its only advantage is cheapness, which is irrelevant once the guard itself is
unwarranted. **Recorded because a correct decision reached through a wrong
argument is the failure mode a green suite cannot detect**, and because the
wrong argument is now permanent in `00c2ff5e`'s message.

**THE PRIVATE-GATE ASYMMETRY, RECORDED ONCE, WITH THE ENUMERATION CORRECTED
FROM THE DESIGN'S.** `Community.private` (`app/models.py:611`) is
`db.Column(db.Boolean, default=False)` commented **"only members can view. no
federation."** The design and the briefs said ten senders in `app/shared/tasks/`
gate federation on `local_only`, that `app/shared/tasks/pages.py:153` was the
only one that also tested `private`, and that nine omitted it. **Re-derived at
this commit against every `local_only` read in `app/shared/tasks/`, the counts
are different and the criterion is what makes them different.** Taking "a guard
whose purpose is to suppress federation, keyed on `Community.local_only`" as the
criterion, there are **twelve** such functions, not ten:
`send_post` (`pages.py:153`) and `send_reply` (`notes.py:143`) test `private`;
`send_answer` (`notes.py:248`), `add_object` (`adds.py:63`), `ban_person`
(`blocks.py:104`), `delete_object` (`deletes.py:127` and `:130`),
`report_object` (`flags.py:57`), `edit_community` (`groups.py:59`), `send_vote`
(`likes.py:60`), `lock_object` (`locks.py:89`), `move_object` (`pages.py:398`)
and `remove_object` (`removes.py:63`) do not. **The two the earlier count missed
are `delete_object` and `move_object`**, and they were missed for different
reasons worth naming: `delete_object` splits its gate across two `if`s
(`:127` for non-posts, `:130` for posts with no followers) so it does not match
the one-line shape the others share, and `move_object` sits in `pages.py`
below `send_post`, in the half of that file the previous sub-project declared out
of scope -- **an out-of-scope declaration is not a reason for a site to be absent
from a cross-file enumeration**, and this one made a twelve-site family look like
a ten-site one. `pages.py:270` and `:333` are deliberately **not** in the list:
they are `if not community.local_only:` *inside* `send_post`, downstream of the
`return` at `:154` (`:153` is the `if`, and sub-project 19's own correction #3
above makes a point of that distinction), and their false arms -- the arcs
`(270, 310)` and `(333, 339)` -- are unreachable for that reason. **They carry
no D-number at all**; they are recorded in the committed comment block at
`tests/test_shared_tasks_send_post.py:1341-1355`, with a second statement of the
`:333` half at `:1801-1806`. **A draft of this sentence said "the unreachable
arms D303 records", which is false, and it is corrected here rather than
quietly**: D303 is the redundant `page['name']` statement at `pages.py:209-210`,
corroborated by `:312`'s false arm, and this very section's closing paragraph
says exactly that -- so the claim would have made this file contradict itself
sixty lines apart. Its origin is instructive: D300's cell carries the looser
pointer "see D303/**the unreachability section**", and the draft dropped the
disjunct that carried the truth and hardened the half that did not. **That is
the D292/D286 class this register warns about** -- a label taken from a nearby
citation instead of from the entry itself -- and it was caught in review rather
than by the writer. **The severity is
LATENT and the reason is that the flag's writers couple it**: `Community.private`
is written at exactly **three** statements, all in `app/community/routes.py` and
none anywhere else in the repository -- `:122` (`private=private`) on the create
path, and `:1234` (`True`) and `:1237` (`False`) on the edit path. **Only two of
the three can write `True`**, `:122` and `:1234`, and each is reached only
through an `if form.private.data:` block that sets `form.local_only.data = True`
first -- `:103-104` on create (with the local `private = True` at `:107`) and
`:1230-1231` on edit. `:1237` writes `False` and so cannot produce the uncoupled
state at all. **The count was written as "exactly two places" and that was an
enumeration claim that was wrong**; the argument it supports is unaffected,
which is precisely why a wrong enumeration inside a correct argument survives
being read. Nothing at the model or
the database level enforces that coupling, so the uncoupled state
(`private=True, local_only=False`) is settable by a test, by a migration, by a
shell, or by any future writer that forgets. **That is why the gate is worth
closing and why closing it fixes nothing today**, and it is stated once here
rather than once per site. Registered as **D309**.

**THE REDUNDANT `online()` CONJUNCT IS A FOURTH INSTANCE OF D302 AND TOOK NO NEW
NUMBER.** `:217` is
`if instance.inbox and instance.online() and not user.has_blocked_instance(instance.id) and not instance_banned(instance.domain):`,
over rows from `community.following_instances()` at `:216`.
`Community.following_instances` (`app/models.py:842-851`) filters
`Instance.dormant == False` at `:849` -- under `if not include_dormant:`, and the
call takes the default -- and `Instance.id != 1, Instance.gone_forever == False`
at `:850`; `Instance.online()` (`app/models.py:118-119`) is exactly
`return not (self.dormant or self.gone_forever)`. Both of its disjuncts are
pinned False by the query, so the conjunct is True for every row the loop can
see. **The establisher was VERIFIED against the tree rather than inherited from
the sibling entry**, which is the discipline sub-project 19's own withdrawn
fifth unreachability claim was retired for. It is appended to **D302** with a
marked note rather than given a number of its own; the reasoning for that choice
is in D302's cell and in this section's closing paragraph.

**AND IT IS THE INSTANCE THAT SHOWS WHAT "ZERO MISSING ARMS" DOES NOT MEAN.**
At `send_post:295` the same conjunct was invisible in the residual and only
mutation exposed it. Here the residual was **already zero missing arms** -- and
the conjunct is still dead. For a redundant conjunct there is no arm to miss,
because coverage.py records an arc at the `if` level and not per conjunct
(fact 87), so **a clean residual is exactly what an unreachable conjunct looks
like**. A slice that reads zero missing arms as "both arms of everything run"
will conclude the opposite of the truth. The question that found this one was
"why does a four-conjunct guard show no missing arc at all", and it is a better
question than "what is still red".

**THE TWO UNREACHABLE STATEMENTS ARE UNREACHABLE *BY INPUT*, AND THE
QUALIFICATION IS RESTATED HERE BECAUSE THE COMMITTED COMMENT BLOCK STATES THE
WEAKER FORM.** `:100-101` is the bare `except: pass` on the local arm of the
mention scan. `:95` has already established that the mention's host half equals
`SERVER_NAME`, so the name reaching `search_for_user` (`app/user/utils.py:85-158`)
at `:99` carries no `@` and no scheme, `search_for_user` takes its local branch,
and that branch's miss path returns `None` rather than raising. **No input
reaches a `raise`, so no test can reach the handler by choosing a mention.**
That is not the same as "these lines can never run": the handler is **bare** --
`except:`, not `except Exception:` -- and the guarded call is a database query,
so a `SQLAlchemyError` from a dropped connection lands in `:100-101` and is
swallowed exactly as a `raise` would be. Sub-project 19 made that distinction
explicitly for the identical shape at `send_post:107-108` and it is the
difference between "coverage will never mark these lines" (true, and the reason
no test chases them) and "these lines are dead" (false, and a claim that would
justify deleting them). **The committed block at
`tests/test_shared_tasks_send_reply.py:1500-1532` argues the callee correctly but
is headed "TWO UNREACHABLE ITEMS" and does not carry the qualification.** It is
not wrong -- it says "cannot raise for a bare local name", which is the
input-scoped claim -- but it is weaker than what sub-project 19 established, and
the register states the stronger form so the two do not drift. **This is the
SECOND instance of the shape, in a second module**, so fact 75's cause 4(c) now
has a pattern rather than a one-off.

**THE TEST HARNESS WAS REWRITTEN IN THE MIDDLE OF THIS SUB-PROJECT, AT THE
USER'S DIRECTION, AND IT CHANGED WHAT A COVERAGE RUN COSTS.** Commit `ec98595c`
replaced `db_session`'s per-test `TRUNCATE` of ~90 tables with a `DELETE` sweep
under `SET LOCAL session_replication_role = replica` plus a `setval` reset of
the public schema's sequences (`tests/conftest.py:119-133`, executed at `:191`).
Measured on identical fresh stacks over the same 629-test subset: **124.5ms mean
teardown / 55.13s to 5.2ms / 16.18s**, with no drift across a full run (first
hundred tests 6.5ms, last hundred 5.8ms). `run_tests.sh`'s `pg_class` staleness
reset was **removed**, because it existed only to restart `test-db` once
TRUNCATE's relfilenode churn had accumulated and there is no churn left to
detect. **A full `--cov=app --cov-branch` run now takes 228.46s where it
previously hit the 600s `session_timeout`**, which is the difference between
this sub-project's measurement task succeeding and its predecessor's needing a
retry. **A published figure was disproved in the process and is corrected in
`tests/README.md` rather than quietly dropped**: the claim that a single
TRUNCATE cost "about 0.05ms against a fresh database", degrading ~2500x to
124ms, is false. Truncating 90 tables on a genuinely fresh database measures
**76ms**; the degradation was real but second-order, and the base cost always
dominated. The 0.05ms figure was almost certainly measured against **one** empty
table rather than ninety. **A ratio is only as good as its denominator, and this
one had been quoted for a week.**

**A WRONG `--cov` TARGET FAILS SILENTLY AND GREEN, AND IT COST A FULL SUITE
RUN.** `pytest-cov`'s `--cov` takes a **module** path, not a file path.
`--cov=app/shared/tasks/notes.py` emits `CoverageWarning: Module
app/shared/tasks/notes.py was never imported (module-not-imported)` and
`CoverageWarning: No data was collected (no-data-collected)`, writes **no** JSON
at all, and **pytest exits 0**. A 257.23s full-suite run was spent that way
before the warnings were read. The dotted form `--cov=app.shared.tasks.notes`
works; `--cov=app` is what the spec documents and what this campaign uses,
because one run serves every module. **Re-measured for the final review rather
than carried forward**: `pytest ... -k targets_data_uses
--cov=app/shared/tasks/notes.py --cov-branch --cov-report=json:/tmp/badcov.json`
printed both warnings and `1 passed`, exited **0**, and left no
`/tmp/badcov.json`. It is carried into `tests/README.md` as fact 117.

**AND THE SENTENCE THAT ORIGINALLY FOLLOWED IT WAS FALSE, WHICH IS THE MORE
IMPORTANT FINDING OF THE TWO.** This paragraph used to end "this is the same
failure mode the campaign already guards against for `session_timeout` -- a
green exit code over a run that produced nothing -- ... never trust the exit
code." **A session timeout exits 1.** `pytest.ini:26-27` had said so all along
("Checked BETWEEN tests, so the run stops at the first test to start after the
budget is spent, **and exits non-zero**"), three lines above the `:28` this
campaign kept citing. Measured 2026-09-06, four commands, recorded in full as
`tests/README.md` fact 118: pytest inside the container exits **1** on a
`session_timeout=1` run; `./run_tests.sh` propagates that **1**; a control with
no matching test propagates **5**; and only the **pipeline** loses it --
`./run_tests.sh ... | tail -1` gives `$?` of 0 while `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is 1.
**Every campaign run pipes pytest through `grep` or `tail`, and `$?` after a
pipeline is the LAST element's status.** The observation was real; the
attribution was wrong, and the wrong attribution is the dangerous part, because
"never trust the exit code" tells an agent to ignore a genuine failure. The
corrected rule is: **do not pipe, or read `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` -- and keep
checking the test count and the report mtime as well, because those catch the
`--cov` case above, where the exit code really is 0 and really is
uninformative.** Two traps, two detectors, and conflating them is what put a
false claim into a harness reference, two designs and two plans at once.
**FOUR AGREEING CITATIONS OF AN UNMEASURED CLAIM ARE ONE CLAIM.** Fact 88's
"a correction that disagrees with N agreeing prior citations needs N-fold
verification" has a converse this campaign had not written down: N agreeing
copies of something nobody ever measured carry the weight of the single
measurement behind them, which here was zero. The tie-breaker was a five-second
experiment that no one had run in five sub-projects.

**A CITATION SWEEP SCOPED BY SUBJECT MISSED FORTY-EIGHT CITATIONS. THE TRIGGER
FOR A SWEEP IS "WHICH FILE'S LINE NUMBERS MOVED", NOT "WHAT DID THE CHANGE TALK
ABOUT".** `ec98595c` moved `tests/conftest.py` from 770 lines to 804 -- two
insertions, `_teardown_sql` and an expanded teardown comment -- so every
citation of a line at or past the first insertion point was off by 20 or 34.
The controller's Ruling 6 scoped the follow-up sweep to "`tests/README.md`'s
harness prose, which `ec98595c` invalidated", and enumerated the sites by what
they **said**: TRUNCATE, the staleness reset, the 0.05ms figure. **That axis is
wrong, and the register records it rather than the ruling's own stated cost.**
Scoping by subject caught every paragraph that talked about truncating and
missed every citation that merely **pointed into** the file: 48 across 11 files,
four of them in the sub-project's own new test file and four more in the very
README the ruling scoped. The right first command is `grep -rn 'conftest\.py:'`
across the tree, not a grep for the concept. **The ledger recorded Ruling 6's
cost as "a larger diff that mixes two subjects". That was not the cost.** The
cost was a scope narrow enough to look complete while leaving the largest
citation breakage this campaign has produced in one commit untouched -- and it
looked complete precisely because everything inside the chosen axis really had
been swept. **Two secondary shapes fell out of the repair, both worth keeping.**
First, `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_reply.py` cited **one** fact -- that
`http_mock` is built with `assert_all_called=True` -- **three different ways**
(`:287-295`, `:294`, `:283`), all correct before the shift and none after; the
repair collapses them to one wording, because *one fact stated three ways is one
fact that cannot be swept*. Second, the fix itself re-broke what it had just
mended: adding the superuser note to `tests/conftest.py`'s teardown comment
shifted the file again by 15 lines, invalidating every number the same round had
just written. **Edit the cited file FIRST, then re-derive the citations** --
the order is not a stylistic preference, it is the difference between one sweep
and two.

**NOTHING RECLAIMS RELATION SPACE ANY MORE, AND THE ODOMETER THAT WOULD HAVE
DETECTED IT WENT IN THE SAME COMMIT.** `DELETE FROM t` with no `WHERE` scans the
relation's page **high-water mark**, not its live rows. `TRUNCATE` reset every
relation to zero blocks after every test; `DELETE` never shrinks one, `VACUUM`
truncates only trailing all-empty pages, the data lives in tmpfs that survives
every run short of `--down`, and `ec98595c` removed the `pg_class` probe that
was the only automatic signal the test database had degraded. **Steady state is
genuinely fine and the measurement supports it** -- ordinary tests insert tens
of rows, and the teardown does not drift across a full run (6.5ms to 5.8ms).
**The unbounded part is a ratchet with an outlier trigger**: one test seeding
tens of thousands of rows extends those relations and their indexes permanently
for the life of the container, and every later teardown in that run and in every
later run on the same stack seq-scans the extended pages -- reproducing exactly
the evenly-spread, `--durations`-invisible slowdown `ec98595c` was written to
eliminate, with the difference that the 2026-08-31 investigation had an odometer
pointing at the cause and this arrangement has none. **Documented rather than
engineered away**, in `tests/README.md`'s teardown section, as a named risk with
its trigger, its symptom, a one-line check (`select
pg_database_size('pyfedi_test');`) and its remedy (`./run_tests.sh --down`,
which reclaims because the volume is tmpfs). **That remedy is a stated exception
to this file's own "`--down` is not for speed" advice**, which was written about
the TRUNCATE arrangement and is now true only in the ordinary case. **A change
that removes a cost and its detector in one commit should say so at the time**;
this one is being said afterwards, by a review.

**"DO NOT MODIFY ANYTHING UNDER `app/`" WAS READ AS FORBIDDING TEMPORARY
MUTATIONS, AND A TASK SHIPPED WITH ITS DISCRIMINATION UNMEASURED.** Task 5
reported: "No mutation testing was performed against `app/` since the task
forbids modifying anything under `app/`, even temporarily -- discrimination was
verified by manual argument instead." That is a reasonable reading of the
sentence and the wrong outcome; the constraint means do not **land** changes
under `app/`. The review ran the six mutations the task had skipped and all six
were killed by assertion, so the manual argument happened to be right -- **and
the reviewer said what that was worth**: "an unlucky version of this same
mistake could have produced a surviving mutant with nothing to catch it."
**The corrected wording, now standing guidance for this campaign, is that a
mutation is permitted and expected provided it is a targeted single-line edit,
restored with `git checkout -- app/`, and followed by asserting BOTH an empty
`git diff -- app/` AND the file's line count.** A prohibition on landing changes
and a prohibition on making them are one word apart and produce different work.

**AN INSTRUCTION TO PORT TEXT DOES NOT EXTEND TO KNOWINGLY PRESERVING AN
ERROR.** Task 1 was told to carry a brief's module-docstring text verbatim. The
brief cited the twin's amendment block as `app/shared/tasks/pages.py:309-330`;
it is `:309-332`. The implementer caught it, used the corrected extent in the
helper it was writing, and left the wrong number standing in the docstring
because the instruction said verbatim -- **reporting it instead of fixing it**.
The review ruled that the tree wins over a brief's prose and the disagreement
goes in the report, and the fix round found the sharper form of the point: the
two omitted lines, `:331` `note['inReplyTo'] = None` and `:332`
`create['object'] = note`, **are the aliasing the block is cited for**. So
`:309-330` would have pointed a reader at the half of the block that does not
demonstrate the claim -- a wrong number that undermines the point it is cited
for, not merely an off-by-two.

### 1. Three items registered, one of them partially fixed -- D309-D311

| # | function | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D309 | the `local_only` federation gates across `app/shared/tasks/` -- thirteen functions, of which `send_post` (`app/shared/tasks/pages.py:153`), `send_reply` (`app/shared/tasks/notes.py:143`), `send_answer` (`app/shared/tasks/notes.py:248`) and `move_object` (`app/shared/tasks/pages.py:398`), and now `add_object` (`app/shared/tasks/adds.py:63`), `remove_object` (`app/shared/tasks/removes.py:63`) and `report_object` (`app/shared/tasks/flags.py:57`), plus `lock_object` (`app/shared/tasks/locks.py:89`) and `send_vote` (`app/shared/tasks/likes.py:60`) added by sub-project 25, and `ban_person` (`app/shared/tasks/blocks.py:104`) and `edit_community` (`app/shared/tasks/groups.py:59`) added by sub-project 26, and now `delete_object` (`app/shared/tasks/deletes.py:118`), closed by sub-project 27, and `vote_for_poll` (`app/shared/tasks/likes.py:183`), a thirteenth, pre-existing site this round's final review found omitted from every prior enumeration, test `Community.private` -- **thirteen for thirteen** | **Fixed -- `Community.private` means "no federation" and, as of sub-project 27, all thirteen federation gates test it.** `app/models.py:611` is `private = db.Column(db.Boolean, default=False)` commented "only members can view. no federation." **THE COUNT WAS TEN, THEN NINE, THEN EIGHT, THEN SIX, THEN FIVE, THEN THREE, THEN ONE, AND IS NOW ZERO, updated in place each time rather than left claiming a number that has stopped being true**: sub-project 21 landed the `private` conjunct at `notes.py:248`, so `send_answer` left this list; sub-project 22 landed it at `pages.py:398`, so `move_object` left it; sub-project 23 landed it at **both** `adds.py:63` and `removes.py:63` in one commit, so `add_object` and `remove_object` left it together -- **that was the first time this list lost two entries at once, and the reason is that the two sites are the same site in two files**, `diff` of the two guards reporting them byte-identical since the two modules differ only by name substitutions; and **sub-project 24 landed it at `flags.py:57`** (commit `038f2180`), so `report_object` left it too. The three omitting sites, re-derived against the tree at sub-project 25's commit rather than copied forward, **counting by FILE and not by line**: `deletes.py` contributes two guards (`:127`, `:130`) and counts once, which is why "five sites, six lines" was correct before this round and "three sites, four lines" is correct now. The three: `ban_person` (`blocks.py:104`), `delete_object` (`deletes.py:127`, `:130`) and `edit_community` (`groups.py:59`). **AND AT A NINTH AND TENTH SITE BY SUB-PROJECT 26**, `app/shared/tasks/blocks.py:104` (commit `1d099e71`) and `app/shared/tasks/groups.py:59` (commit `16604e72`), a two-conjunct edit -- both `private` and `online()` at once, not the one-conjunct shape the eight sites before it took -- a ninth and tenth time, in an eighth and ninth file, which stayed at **190** and **149 lines** respectively. **Ten of the twelve gates have now been fixed by the same convention on seven consecutive sub-projects, across nine files.** **THIS CELL PREVIOUSLY SAID `delete_object` OMITTED BOTH `private` AND `online()` AND CALLED IT THE FAMILY'S WIDEST REMAINING GAP. ### 1. Two items registered, neither fixed -- D312-D313

| # | function | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D312 | `send_answer` (`app/shared/tasks/notes.py:242-310`) never calls `patch_db_session`, where `make_reply` (`:58`) and `edit_reply` (`:71`) both wrap their callee in it | **Not fixed -- the MECHANISM is measured and REAL, and the CONSEQUENCE was looked for and NOT reproduced. The entry is written at that strength deliberately.** `send_answer` opens its own session at `:243` with `get_task_session()` (`app/utils.py:3673-3675`, `Session(bind=db.engine)`) and uses it directly. `make_reply` and `edit_reply` open theirs at `:56` and `:69` and then enter `with patch_db_session(session):` (`app/utils.py:3679`) before calling `send_reply`, which -- when there is no request context -- makes `db.session` *become* the task session for the duration. So anything `send_answer` reaches that reads `db.session` gets the **request-scoped** session rather than the task session it just opened. **Exactly TWO such reads exist, and they were enumerated by executing the function, not by reading it**: `Community.following_instances()` (`app/models.py:843`, `db.session.query(Instance)`) called at `:299`, and `User.has_blocked_instance()` (`app/models.py:1470`, `db.session.query(InstanceBlock)`) called at `:300`. Everything else is accounted for: `:245` and `:246` and the relationship loads off those rows are on the task session, and `instance_banned` (`app/utils.py:2336`) and `post_request` (`app/activitypub/signature.py:98`) each open **their own** `get_task_session()` and are unaffected either way. **Why it is registered rather than dismissed, stated as reading-level and not measured:** a Celery worker pushes one app context at import (`celery_worker_docker.py:5-6`) and never pops it, so `app/request_hooks.py:179-183`'s `db.session.remove()` never fires and `db.session` is a single process-wide session; the transaction `send_answer` opens on it is never committed, rolled back or closed, because its own `finally` at `:309` closes only the task session, at `:310`. **That `rollback`/`close` pair is now ASSERTED and not merely reached**: sub-project 21's final-review fix wave ported Task 8's `_recording_task_session` (a genuine `Session` with only those two methods wrapped, patched onto the **notes** module because `app/shared/tasks/notes.py:10` imports `get_task_session` into that namespace) into `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_answer.py` and made `test_a_missing_post_reply_rolls_back_and_re_raises` assert the recorded order `['rollback', 'close']`, with a happy-path control asserting `['close']` alone. Verified by mutation: `sed -i '307s/session.rollback()/pass/'` left all 16 pre-fix tests green and is a **SOLE assertion-kill** of the strengthened test (**M9** in that file's record). **Why it is NOT registered as a defect:** both sessions are bound to the same engine and read the same committed rows, so no wrong answer was produced or could be produced from the states this campaign can reach. It is a plumbing asymmetry between four sibling senders in one module, not a bug | not fixed, registered only; **mechanism measured, consequence not reproduced** | **measured by execution, in six probes, and the negative results are reported alongside the positive ones.** The harness's `db.session` is `autoflush=False` (`app/__init__.py:81`, fact 64), so every probe row was flushed **explicitly** and never committed -- visible to `db.session`'s own transaction and invisible to any other session, which is what makes the two sessions distinguishable at all. **(A)** an `InstanceBlock` flushed-not-committed into `db.session` makes `send_answer` **skip** the follower: delivery count **0**, where a task-session read would have been blind to the row and delivered. **(B)** a `CommunityMember` flushed-not-committed into `db.session` makes `send_answer` **deliver** to that follower: count **1**, where a task-session read would have seen no follower and delivered nothing. **(C)** the contrast that makes A and B mean what they say: inside `with patch_db_session(task_session):`, the same flushed-not-committed membership gives `following_instances()` **0** rows. **(D) and (E)** the consequence hunt, both NEGATIVE: after `send_answer` returns, `db.session.identity_map` is **empty**, and it is equally empty after a `send_reply` run under `patch_db_session` -- SQLAlchemy's identity map holds weak references, so the cached-stale-object consequence a reader would assume does not occur, and this cell does not claim it. **(F)** a per-session census of one local-community `send_answer` with one follower, taken with a `do_orm_execute` listener keyed on session identity: **7 ORM executions -- 2 on the task session** (`:245` `User`, `:246` `PostReply`), **2 on `db.session`** (the `SELECT DISTINCT instance ...` and the `instance_block` lookup), **3 on further independent task sessions** opened by `instance_banned` and `post_request`. The probes were scratch instrumentation, deleted after measurement in the same way a mutation is reverted; they are specified above precisely enough to be re-run, and nothing in this cell rests on reading the code alone except the worker-lifetime paragraph, which says so |
| D313 | `object=` at `app/shared/tasks/notes.py:282` and `:285` shadows the builtin inside `send_answer` | **Not fixed -- reading-level, and it is registered for the MISREADING rather than for the shadowing.** `:282` is `object=undo` and `:285` is `object=lock`; the local is read at `:294` as the Announce's `'object'` value. Two separate things are wrong with it and only the second matters. (1) The name shadows the builtin `object` for the rest of the function -- harmless here, because `object` the builtin is referenced nowhere in the module (the only other occurrences of the token are the dict **keys** `'object'` at `:44`, `:192`, `:211`, `:258`, `:272` and `:294`, and the docstring note at `:47`). (2) **The unspaced `=` makes an assignment statement read as a keyword argument.** `object=undo` sits indented inside an `if`/`else` immediately above a dict literal full of `key: value` pairs, and the eye that has just read `'object': lock` at `:272` is primed to read it as one. That is the cost, and it is a reading cost, not a runtime one | not fixed, registered only; reading-level | **measured to the extent it can be: the repo's linter does not flag it, and that was run rather than assumed.** `ruff check app/shared/tasks/notes.py` reports "All checks passed!" -- `ruff.toml` selects `["E4", "E7", "E9", "F"]`, which excludes both `flake8-builtins` (`A001`, builtin shadowing) and pycodestyle's `E225` (missing whitespace around operator), so neither half of this is caught today and no lint change is proposed as part of a coverage slice. Not fixed for one stated reason: `app/shared/tasks/notes.py` had to end this sub-project at **310 lines with no diff**, since nine of its own tasks' committed citations point into the file, and renaming a local is a change no test can discriminate -- there is no observable difference to assert on. A later slice that touches this function should rename it to `announced` or `inner` in passing |

That cell closed with "A fifth such site belongs in this cell, not in a new
number", generalising from four sites to *every* caller of
`Community.following_instances()` that re-checks `instance.online()`. This

the site**: a register entry that states the *establisher* rather than the

**The detection method did not change either, and that is the reinforcement.**
`send_answer`'s residual was at **zero missing arms** before the conjunct was
found, just as `send_reply`'s was. coverage.py records a branch arc at the `if`
level and not per conjunct, so a redundant conjunct appears in no residual at
all. **A clean residual is what an unreachable conjunct looks like** -- twice
now, in two functions, found both times by asking why a four-conjunct guard
showed no missing arc, and neither time by mutation or by the percentage. The
unreachability argument, its establisher and the ternary reconciliation are
written out at the end of `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_answer.py`.

...).one()` raising `NoResultFound` against `session.query(...).get(...)`

evidence about the tests until the substitution is confirmed to have changed the
program: *survivor*, *equivalent mutant* and **no-op substitution** are three
different results and only the first two say anything about coverage (120). A
task function that opens `get_task_session()` **without** `patch_db_session`

finding, because the second session is the *test's own* (121). An activity
builder that mutates its dicts with `del` before delivery cannot be asserted
through a recorder holding the dict, because the recorder reads it in its
post-`del` state -- assert on the serialized bytes (122). And when a test's proof
depends on which row an unordered query returns first, assert the order
explicitly, which is the case fact 90 does not cover: fact 90 says avoid the
dependence, and 123 says what to do when the discriminating case requires it
(123).

### 1. Two items registered, neither fixed -- D314-D315

Why this is registered rather than dropped as a non-finding: D312 records a real mechanism -- an unpatched function's reads split across two sessions, and in a test the second one is the test's own (fact 121) -- and a reader who wants to know how far that mechanism reaches currently has no number to reach for, which is precisely the vacuum the design filled with a guess. **Not promoted to a defect**: the consequence was looked for in sub-project 21 and not reproduced, and nothing here re-opens that; both sessions bind to the same engine and read the same committed rows. ### 3. Corrections landed, not deleted

**One stale citation inside the register itself, in a cell this round was

**Two disputed counts withdrawn from committed prose and replaced with a
structural argument.** `TaskError`'s docstring in `app/utils.py` justified its
end-of-file placement with "358 `utils.py:NNN` citations in tracked files, 135 of
them at or after `:3673`". **As of `2a63f063^`, the commit the class was appended
in**, the 135 reproduces exactly -- and the anchor is not decoration: at
`dce6eee2` the same sweep gives 136, and at `78fa9fe9` it gives 141, because each
of those commits cites `app/utils.py` lines above `:3673` in the course of
describing this very argument. **The 358 does not reproduce at any commit**, and
neither does the design's companion figure of "96 `pages.py:NNN` citations": the
same sweeps give **322** occurrences for `utils.py` at `2a63f063^` -- 324 if only
the `*.po` glob is excluded and **844** if the whole `.po` family is counted --
and 82, 113, 35 or 41 for `pages.py` at the design's own commit depending on the
prefix and the `.po` question. A reviewer's independent sweep gave a fourth set
again. **The `.po` family is the main reason independent sweeps diverge**, because
those files carry auto-generated `#: app/utils.py:NNN` gettext source references
that a human "citation" count means to exclude; **and the obvious exclusion glob
`app/translations/**/*.po` is itself incomplete**, missing
`app/translations/lt/LC_MESSAGES/messages.po.original`, which carries the same
references and accounts for the 322-versus-324 gap. Naming that file is what makes
the sweep reproducible instead of "off by a couple again".

**Replaced with the argument that needs no count -- ANCHORED TO A COMMIT, because
the un-anchored form of it was falsified inside this same round.** As of
`2a63f063^`, the commit the class was appended in, the file's last line was
`:5798` and the highest `app/utils.py` line cited anywhere in the tracked tree was
`:5743`. **The sweep rule is SPLIT and saying only "count the endpoint" does not
reproduce the figures**: take the ENDPOINT for the maximum, because
`app/utils.py:5736-5743` reaches 5743 and a naive `:NNN` regex stops at 5736;
but take the START for the at-or-after `:3673` test, because exactly one
citation straddles that boundary -- `app/utils.py:3663-3673`, in D60's cell at
`:2799` -- and endpoint-counting it gives 136 rather than 135. Endpoints
everywhere yields 136 and `:5743`, starts everywhere yields 135 and `:5736`,
and only the split reading yields both published figures. A range BEGINS at a
line and REACHES another; the rule follows the meaning rather than the regex. Appending below
`:5798` therefore could not move a cited line however many there were, and
citations written *after* the append point into the appended region by
construction and cannot be shifted by it either. **The `.po` family does not
change the maximum** -- its own highest cited line is `:4484` -- so the argument
is stable under exactly the question that makes the counts diverge.

**THE UN-ANCHORED FORM DID NOT SURVIVE ITS OWN REGISTER ENTRY, AND THAT IS
RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY REPAIRED.** Commit `71d96f82` wrote "the highest
`app/utils.py` line cited anywhere in the tree is `:5743`" in the present tense.
Commit `dce6eee2` -- the register commit two below it -- then cited
`app/utils.py:5801` in D315's cell, so at `dce6eee2` the same sweep gives **323**
occurrences, **136** at or after `:3673`, and a maximum of **`:5801`**. For a
few hours this file contradicted itself: one paragraph said the maximum was
`:5743` and another cited `:5801`. **A claim about citation counts is falsifiable
by the commit that makes it**, which is a sharper version of the problem the
replacement argument existed to solve; the fix is not a better number but an
as-of clause, applied here, in the class's docstring and in `tests/README.md`
fact 125.

**One committed mutation record corrected in place, with the old wording named,
because it contradicted this round's own new fact.** The summary line at the end
of `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_post.py` read "1 no-op substitution found in the
brief's own M5 sed literal". Fact 126, written by this round and partly from that
record, reserves **no-op substitution** for the applies-cleanly-but-changes-
nothing case (fact 120's, and sub-project 21's M4) and classifies M5 as the
**does-not-parse** case: M5's `sed` exited with ``unknown option to `s'`` and
never applied anything, so the right check is the command's stderr and not a diff
of the file. The M5 *entry* was always right; only the summary was wrong, and a
later round grepping the record for prior art would have applied the wrong check.
Corrected with the old wording quoted, in the same convention as D304's `:256`. The docstring's "first narrow raise among eleven
sites" is corrected in the same edit, to the measured 69-in-9-files population.
Comment-only; commit `71d96f82`; no line above the class moved. Carried into
`tests/README.md` as fact 125.

**One claim about a register entry corrected rather than inherited.** This
round's design, plan and briefs all said "D312 names nine other unpatched task
functions". D312 names no such nine. Registered as D314 above with the measured

**The withdrawn figures were then discharged at their ORIGIN as well as at their

Normalising all eight of those hunks makes the two files **byte-identical**. **THE NORMALISATION IS HUNK-DIRECTED, NOT A BLIND `remove`->`add` REWRITE, AND AN EARLIER DRAFT OF THIS CELL SAID OTHERWISE.** Two of the eight hunks defeat a blind rewrite. `unsticky_post` -> `sticky_post` is the deletion of an `un` PREFIX, not a substitution of the token `remove`; and `:22` -- `For Announce, remove @context from inner object` -- contains the English word `remove` **identically in both files**, so rewriting it changes a line that never differed. Normalising **all eight** hunks -- with the `22!` address and the prefix rule -- yields byte identity. (c) **Coverage**: both measure 51 statements / 10 branches, both at 0 missing and 0 partial, and both execute the same ten arcs. (d) **Behaviour**: ten mutations were applied to each file separately -- **20 runs** -- and every pair came back with the same kill count, the same kill type and mirrored test names. (e) **Dead code**: they share the dead `post_request` import at `:2`, which is **D316**. **THE BEHAVIOURAL HALF IS WHAT MAKES THIS AN ENTRY RATHER THAN AN OBSERVATION.** A textual diff says the files look alike; 20 mutation runs say they *behave* alike under perturbation, and that is the claim a future reader needs. It also produces the round's operational rule: **a kill/survive asymmetry between the twins is a defect in the TESTS, not in the code** -- identical files cannot legitimately produce different kill sets, so an asymmetry means one twin's test is observing something the other's is not. Noting an absence of false positives is not noting a presence of true positives. ### 2. One earlier finding closed at a fourth and fifth site, and one entry extended in place -- D309, D302

**D309 is closed at a fourth AND a fifth of its twelve sites, in two files, in a
single commit, and its count is corrected in place from eight to six.**
`add_object`'s gate at `app/shared/tasks/adds.py:63` and `remove_object`'s at
`app/shared/tasks/removes.py:63` now both read `if community.local_only or

`notes.py:248` and sub-project 22 at `pages.py:398`. `diff` of the two new lines
reports them **byte-identical**. The six remaining omitting sites were
**re-derived at this commit** rather than copied forward, by the method
sub-project 21 established and sub-project 22 repeated: reading every `local_only`
occurrence in `app/shared/tasks/` and attributing each to its enclosing function
by `ast`. All six line numbers are unchanged from sub-project 20's original
enumeration, and the denominator was re-confirmed at the same time -- **six** gates
now test `private`, **six** do not, still twelve.

**TWO SITES IN ONE COMMIT IS STILL ONE PRODUCTION CHANGE, AND THE READING IS
WRITTEN DOWN BECAUSE THE NEXT ROUND WITH A TWIN WILL NEED IT.** The campaign's
rule is one production change per sub-project. The twins are the same file under
two names (**D318**), so guarding one and not the other would not have been a
smaller change -- it would have been this sub-project's **first structural
divergence**, breaking the very invariant its whole one-file-for-two-modules test
design rests on. The rule was therefore read as counting *changes*, not *files*.
**And the pair still had to be measured as two**, which is the check no
single-module round has ever needed: reverting `adds.py:63` alone fails exactly
one test, the adds one, with the removes twin passing, and reverting
`removes.py:63` alone fails exactly the removes one. Had reverting either failed
both, the two guards would have been indistinguishable and the pair would have
counted as one measurement wearing two names.

**D302 gains a SEVENTH and an EIGHTH site and again took no new number.**
`app/shared/tasks/adds.py:97` and `app/shared/tasks/removes.py:97` are
character-for-character the guard at `pages.py:295`, `notes.py:217`,
`notes.py:300` and `pages.py:432`, over the same `Community.following_instances()`
call with the same default `include_dormant=False`; `app/models.py:849` and `:850`
have already pinned `Instance.dormant == False` and `Instance.gone_forever ==
False` in SQL, and `Instance.online()` (`app/models.py:118-119`) is exactly
`not (self.dormant or self.gone_forever)`. Appended in place per the precedent
sub-projects 20, 21 and 22 set, **after verifying that the cell named exactly six
sites before this one** -- the verification the brief demanded rather than the
count it supplied.

**WHAT SITES SEVEN AND EIGHT ADD IS THE LIMITING CASE OF THE CELL'S OWN CLAIM.**
Sub-project 20 wrote there that "a clean residual is what a redundant conjunct
looks like". Every site since has been in a module with *some* residual left. These
two are in modules with **none**: 100.0000%, zero missing statements, zero partial
branches. The residual is not clean but empty, and the dead conjunct is still
there. **So "100% on both figures" and "every conjunct has been observed both
ways" are different claims, and the first does not imply the second.** A reader who
takes a perfect coverage figure as proof that every condition has been exercised
gets this wrong, and the twins are the cheapest possible counterexample.

**AND THE CONTROL WAS NOT RUN, FOR THE PROOF-RATHER-THAN-BUDGET REASON `:432`'s
SENTENCE ALREADY GIVES.** Dropping `online()` from `:97` is an equivalent mutant
by construction: `:96`'s query has filtered both columns it reads, so the conjunct
is True for every row either loop can yield and the mutant computes the same
function for every reachable input. A green run would be fact 120's second class
and would add nothing the SQL does not already say. **The LIVE conjunct in the
same `if` IS measured, on both twins**: M8 drops `instance.inbox and ` from `:97`
and is a double assertion-kill in each file, 2 failed / 33 passed, identical
counts. A live conjunct killing two tests beside a dead one that cannot be killed
at all is what makes the redundancy legible without a mutation of its own.

### 3. Corrections landed, not deleted

**ONE STALE SENTENCE INSIDE D309, CAUGHT BY THE SECOND CITATION PASS AND FIXED BY
STATING THE INVARIANT.** D309's evidence column ended "No test drives the
uncoupled state through any of the nine". It was written when nine sites were
open, and it survived **two** later corrections of the count above it -- to eight
by sub-project 22, and to six here -- because both rounds grepped for the sentence
they were editing rather than for the **value** they were correcting. It now reads
"any of the twelve gates". **It is replaced with the invariant rather than
re-pointed at six**, because the claim was never about the open subset: no test
drives the uncoupled state through a *fixed* gate either, and a number that has
already drifted twice will drift again. This is fact 100's second pass earning its
keep on the register itself, and the failure it caught is the one sub-project 22's
own section warned about in the paragraph immediately above it.

**ONE CLAIM IN THE TEST FILE'S OWN HEADER CORRECTED, IN THE ROUND THAT REGISTERED
THE CLAIM.** `tests/test_shared_tasks_add_remove.py`'s module docstring said the
twins were identical "after normalising names" except for "one docstring word".
Measuring it for **D318** showed that short of the truth in **both** directions:
two *string literals* also differ (`'Add'`/`'Remove'` and the
`/activities/add/`-vs-`/activities/remove/` path segment), and once the docstring
word is normalised along with everything else the two files are **byte-identical**,
so there is no residual difference at all. The header now carries the eight-hunk
enumeration and the byte-identity result. **The correction is worth its paragraph
because of where the error came from**: the claim was written by reading the diff
and summarising it, and the summary lost two hunks. Registering the equivalence is
what forced it to be counted. **THE SAME CLAIM WAS DISCHARGED AT ITS ORIGIN AS
WELL AS AT ITS RESTATEMENT**, because the test file's header is a restatement: the
sentence came from this sub-project's design
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-07-coverage-add-remove-23-design.md:30-31`) and
plan (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-07-coverage-add-remove-23.md:70-72`), and
both now carry a dated annotation appended after their last original line, in
D275's two-way-pointer form and exactly as sub-project 22 discharged its withdrawn
figures. **Briefs are derived from the plan**, so correcting only the artefact
leaves the carrier open; appending rather than rewriting keeps the original wording
intact as evidence and moves no line, so every citation into either document still
resolves.

**ONE FLAKE FOUND ON A CLEAN TREE, AND THE RULING THAT FIXED IT SUPERSEDES AN
EARLIER ONE.** Task 7's review reproduced, with **zero** mutation applied,
`test_one_instance_is_skipped_while_another_receives_the_add` and its removes twin
failing on a first run and passing on an immediate re-run. The cause is the one the
tests themselves named: `Community.following_instances()` (`app/models.py:842-851`)
ends in an unordered `.distinct().all()`, so which follower comes back first is a
property of the query plan. The explicit order assertion those tests carried --
sub-project 22's Ruling 3, carried forward into this plan -- **was working exactly
as designed**; what it revealed is that the design was hopeful. **The fix
(`3359cb53`) CONTROLS the sequence instead of observing it**, patching
`following_instances` for the duration of the call so the skipped instance is first
every run. The reasoning that decides it: the subject of those two tests is the
loop's continue-past-a-skip behaviour, and the query's ordering is incidental to
that subject; testing the loop against a known input every time is strictly more
discriminating than observing an order and hoping it is the useful one.
**This supersedes sub-project 22's Ruling 3 for this shape, and the split is
precise**: that ruling was right to reject the production change -- the delivery
loop never relied on any order, so an `ORDER BY` would be an unmotivated
production change hung off a test artefact -- and wrong about what asserting an
incidental order buys. It buys a loud failure, not a reliable test, and a test that
fails loudly at random is still a test that fails at random. Carried into
`tests/README.md` as fact **131**, which amends fact 123 rather than replacing it.

**AND THE DEFLAKE WAS PROVED LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN COINCIDENTALLY GREEN.** A
`monkeypatch.setattr` that silently fails to intercept leaves the tests green for
the wrong reason and merely hides the flake. Before committing, each stub lambda
was temporarily made to **raise**, both tests were confirmed to fail with the
injected error -- proving `object.community` is the same identity-mapped object as
`s.community`, so the patch really does intercept the call the loop makes -- and
the file was reverted and byte-diffed back. Five consecutive clean runs followed,
plus a sixth after the commit. **The count matters: one green run is what let the
flake through in the first place.** Carried into `tests/README.md` as fact **132**.

### 4. Two floors ADDED rather than raised, and each proved to bite

`coverage_floors.ini` had **no** entry for either twin. Both were added at
**100**, appended after `app/shared/tasks/notes.py` in the file's existing
ordering, which the file's own history shows is order-of-first-addition rather
than alphabetical or numerical. **This is the campaign's first sub-project to ADD
floors rather than raise them, and the first to set any floor at 100 for a module
that has branches** -- `app/request_hooks.py` and `app/instance/util.py` are at
100 already, and a 100 floor on a branch-carrying module is a strictly stronger
commitment, because `percent_covered` is a blended statement+branch figure and a
single missed arm now breaks the build.

**A FLOOR THAT HAS NEVER BEEN OBSERVED TO FAIL IS A RATCHET TOOTH NOBODY HAS
CHECKED IS ENGAGED, AND THE USUAL DEMONSTRATION DOES NOT WORK AT 100.**
Sub-projects 18-22 proved a new floor bites by copying `coverage_floors.ini` and
raising the copied entry above the measured figure. At 100 there is no headroom,
so the demonstration was inverted: **hold the floors file fixed and regress the
REPORT.** Four runs, all against `tests/check_coverage_floors.py`:

- **Control.** The real report against the real floors: exit **0**, `All 10 module
  floors met.` (it was 8 before this change).
- **The bite.** A scratch copy of the report in which `adds.py` loses **one branch
  arc** (10 covered branches -> 9, blended 61 units -> 60, **98.36%**) and
  `removes.py` loses **two statements** (51 -> 49, **96.72%**), against the real
  floors: exit **1**, with `app/shared/tasks/adds.py: 98.36% is below its floor of
  100.00%` and `app/shared/tasks/removes.py: 96.72% is below its floor of 100.00%`.
  A single dropped arm is the smallest regression either module can suffer, and it
  is caught.
- **The isolation, which is what makes the bite attributable.** The **same**
  regressed report against a floors copy identical but for the two new lines: exit
  **0**, `All 8 module floors met.` Same report, same checker, floors differing
  only in the two added entries; one run fails naming them and the other passes.
  **That is the strongest available demonstration, and the reason is NOT module
  attribution** -- a raised scratch floor names its module in the failure line
  too, so it isolates just as well, and an earlier draft of this paragraph drew
  that contrast one notch too sharply. **The real advantage is that the inversion
  exercises the COMMITTED value.** Raising a floor to 101 proves the checker
  responds to *some* floor on that module; it never touches the 100 that the
  ratchet will actually enforce, because the number under test is fabricated for
  the test. Regressing the report instead holds the committed 100 fixed and varies
  exactly one thing -- the presence of these two lines -- so what is shown to bite
  is the value that will be there tomorrow.
- **The vanish path.** A report with both twins deleted from `files`, against the
  real floors: exit **1**, both reported at `0.00%`. A floored module that
  disappears from the report -- a rename, an import failure, a wrong `--cov`
  target -- is a violation and not a pass, and the two new entries inherit that
  property like every other.

All four scratch artefacts were written under the session scratchpad; neither
`coverage_floors.ini` nor `scratch_full_cov.json` was modified by any of them, and
the final in-tree check is the control run above.

**Four shapes carried forward into `tests/README.md` as new facts 129-132.** A
factory that leaves BOTH columns a ternary selects between at `None` makes the

and D322 the per-domain exception handler's shared leak on both legs, registered
and not fixed. **Two of the four are production defects, both fixed; two are

**D309** (sub-project 20's section), whose omitting-site count drops from six to
five with `flags.py:57` as its sixth fixed site; **D314** (sub-project 22's

**Eight facts carried forward into `tests/README.md` as new facts 133-140.**
`CACHE_TYPE=NullCache` under test means every `@cache.memoize` is inert, so a
decorated function queries the database on every call and there is no stale
cache to design a defence against (133). `respx` cannot observe `Response.close()`,
because a mocked response may already report `is_closed == True` before `close()`
runs, so proving a close requires a recording double whose `close()` appends to a
real list (134). A name imported by value (`from time import sleep`) must be
patched in the importing module's own namespace, not the origin module's (135).
`app/activitypub/signature.py:100-101`'s `@context` reinjection is top-level
only, which makes "no nested `@context`" a meaningful assertion for an
Announce-wrapped activity and a vacuous one for an unwrapped activity like
`flags.py`'s Flag, where the reinjection lands on the object itself (136). The
coverage JSON written by `--cov-report=json:<path>` lands inside the test-runner
container, not on the host bind mount, and must be retrieved with `podman cp`
(137). A surviving mutation is information about the test, not proof the mutant
is defective -- the fix is a real externally-observable discriminator, and the
failure mode on the other side is a test rewritten until it asserts the
implementation rather than the behaviour it is supposed to prove (138). Four
distinct documentation-rot mechanisms shipped in this sub-project alone, none of
them caught by a sweep that only checks that a cited line resolves: a stale
ordinal (a docstring's shape claim rotting while its line number stays correct),
a reused figure (one pair's distance copied into a sentence about a different
pair), a self-invalidated citation (a citation broken by the same commit that
wrote it, which verifying-before-editing cannot catch), and prose attached to a
deleted line surviving the deletion (an `xfail` docstring still arguing against
a fix landing in the very commit that made it) (139). A docstring should state
what its test CANNOT prove -- whether a discrimination depends on an unordered
scan happening to return rows in a particular order (and, if so, whether the
degradation on the other side is lax or flaky), or whether a specific reordering
of a guard's disjuncts would reopen a crash without failing the test that
guards it (140).

The final whole-branch review of sub-project 24 read the closed module pair
once more, end to end, rather than task by task. **No production code changed
in this round**: `git diff --numstat` against `app/` for the whole round is
empty, and every change below is to a spec, this findings register, or a test

### 1. D323 -- the ban-warning miscounts LEGS as INSTANCES

| # | function | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D323 | `check_user_application`'s ban-warning text, `app/shared/tasks/users.py:47,73,81-82` | **Not fixed, registered only.** `num_banned` is incremented once for the IP leg (`:47`) and once for the email leg (`:73`) of THE SAME domain, and the persisted text (`:81-82`) is `f"{num_banned} instances have banned this account."` -- it names `num_banned` "instances" when it is actually a count of LEGS. A single domain that reports the applicant banned on both its IP check and its email check produces "2 instances have banned this account." for exactly ONE banning instance. **MEASURED, not inferred: the miscount itself is certain** -- read directly from `:47`, `:73` and `:81-82`, and reproduced by `test_both_legs_banned_counts_twice` and `test_the_warning_update_binds_its_parameters` (both single-domain, both-legs-banned scenarios, both asserting the literal string). **INFERRED, and said so rather than asserted as fact: the operational consequence.** The string reaches a human -- `app/templates/admin/approve_registrations.html:42` renders `registration.warning` verbatim as the `title` of a tooltip icon on the admin registration-approval screen -- so an admin reading "2 instances have banned this account." on a single-instance case is shown a doubled number. Whether any admin actually over-weights that number when deciding to approve or reject an application was NOT observed in this review; it is a plausible reading of what the tooltip is for, not a measured outcome. **This is the round D323 was owed to, and the reason is D319, not a coincidence of scheduling**: before D319's fix (this sub-project, commit `f5e6fa0b`), `:81-82`'s write always raised `TypeError` and the `warning` column was NEVER populated for any applicant -- the miscounted string could not reach the template because it could never reach the database. D319's fix is what made this string admin-visible for the first time, which is what makes the miscount worth a number now rather than earlier. **Not fixed, deliberately**: correcting the string (e.g. counting `set()`-deduplicated banning domains rather than legs, or splitting the message into a per-leg breakdown) would be a fourth production change, and this sub-project's rule was exactly three one-line changes, all already spent on D309, D319 and D320. | not fixed, registered only | read from source at this commit: `app/shared/tasks/users.py:47` (`num_banned += 1`, IP leg), `:73` (`num_banned += 1`, email leg, same domain, same iteration of the `for domain in ...` loop), `:81-82` (the f-string); `app/templates/admin/approve_registrations.html:42`, which renders `{{ registration.warning }}` as a `title` attribute on an `fe-warning` icon, confirmed by reading the template directly rather than assumed from the column's name. Pinned (as current, not correct, behaviour) by `test_both_legs_banned_counts_twice` (`tests/test_shared_tasks_users.py:523`) and `test_the_warning_update_binds_its_parameters` (`:595`), both docstring-annotated by this review to say the asserted string is the module's own miscount and to cite this entry; no test in the suite asserts a CORRECT (per-instance rather than per-leg) count, because no such code path exists to test |

### 2. D321's proposed remedy would have been a functional regression -- corrected in place, not appended as a footnote

D321's cell, above, originally proposed fixing `flags.py:73` by routing it
through `community.following_instances()`. **That remedy is wrong and has been
rewritten in the cell itself** rather than left standing beside a correction,
because a wrong remedy sitting uncorrected in a register cell is exactly the
kind of trap a future reader re-derives instead of re-checking.
`Community.following_instances()` (`app/models.py:842-851`) joins
`CommunityMember` and filters on `CommunityMember.community_id == self.id`
(`:843-845`), so it returns only instances with a MEMBER of that community.
`report_object`'s `instance_ids`, however, is built by its two callers
(`app/shared/post.py:909`, `app/shared/reply.py:381`) to deliberately include
the reported user's HOME instance whenever that user is remote -- with no
membership check of any kind, because a user can be reported for a post in a
community their own instance has never joined. Routing `:73` through
`following_instances()` would silently stop delivering Flags to such a
reported user's home instance, which is a real, proven behaviour change, in
exchange for closing a gap (dormant/gone-forever delivery) whose real-world
impact was never shown. The corrected remedy, now in D321's own cell: add
`Instance.dormant == False` and `Instance.gone_forever == False` directly to
`:73`'s existing filter, changing nothing about which instance ids are
selected.

- **Two mis-cited `except` arms in `tests/test_shared_tasks_users.py` are

### 4. A self-inflicted citation shift, caught before it could rot

Editing the docstrings inside `tests/test_shared_tasks_flags.py` (D324's fix)
and `tests/test_shared_tasks_users.py` (D323's pins) to correct their own
prose ADDED LINES, which shifted every line number below each edit point in
each file. This is fact 139's "self-invalidated citation" mechanism, caught
this time before it shipped rather than after: every citation in this register
and in `tests/README.md` that pointed into either file past an edit point was
re-derived against the post-edit tree by locating the cited `def` with `grep -n`
rather than by arithmetic on the old number, because the shift is NOT uniform
-- `tests/test_shared_tasks_flags.py`'s single edit (inside
`_recording_task_session`, `:308`) added a constant 8 lines to everything
below it (D317's cell and its sub-project-24 prose, the Ruling-3 citation, and
`tests/README.md` facts 136 and 140 all moved by exactly +8), but
`tests/test_shared_tasks_users.py` was edited at two separate docstrings (inside
`test_both_legs_banned_counts_twice`, then inside
`test_the_warning_update_binds_its_parameters`), so the shift is +13 lines
below the first and before the second (D319's citation of
`test_the_warning_update_binds_its_parameters`'s own `def` line, and D322's
citations of `test_a_failing_domain_does_not_stop_the_next_one`) and +19 lines
below the second (D320's and D322's citations into
`test_both_responses_are_closed`, and `tests/README.md` fact 134) -- a single
"+N" applied uniformly across that file would have re-broken exactly the
citations it was trying to fix. Nothing before an edit point moved, and
citations into files this review did not edit were left alone.

### 1. Three new numbers, one fixed and two not -- D325-D327

| # | function | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D325 | `vote_for_poll`'s missing federation gate, `app/shared/tasks/likes.py:181-184` | **Fixed in this sub-project, commit `ecf02ded`.** Every other AP sender in `app/shared/tasks/` gates on the target community's `local_only`, `private` and `instance.online()` state before putting anything on the wire -- that is what D309's whole family is *about*. `vote_for_poll` never did any of the three: its only guard, pre-fix, was `if post:`, so a poll vote cast in a private or local-only community, or one whose target instance was dormant or gone, was serialized and handed to `send_post_request` regardless. **This is not a D309 omission -- those cells describe a guard that exists and is missing one conjunct. This is the guard's total absence**, and the two families must stay distinct so a later reader does not fold this into D309's count. Fixed by inserting `community = post.community` and the same three-disjunct guard (`community.local_only or community.private or not community.instance.online()`) used everywhere else in the file, in the same order (private checked before `online()` so a private community with no instance row short-circuits before dereferencing `None`), returning before any payload is built. **THIS INSERTION ALSO ADDS A NEW, UNREGISTERED SURFACE, AT LOW LIKELIHOOD RATHER THAN ZERO.** `Community.instance_id` is a nullable FK (`app/models.py:575`), and `app/activitypub/util.py:789` guards `community.instance_id and community.instance.online()` -- checking the FK before dereferencing -- precisely because a `None` `instance_id` makes `community.instance` `None` and `None.online()` raise `AttributeError`. `vote_for_poll`'s new guard at `likes.py:183` dereferences `community.instance.online()` with no such `community.instance_id` check, so a poll vote on a community with no instance row, which the pre-fix code (guarded only by `if post:`) federated successfully, now raises. **The two `private` conjuncts inserted alongside it do not add this risk** -- `send_vote`'s own `community.instance.online()` at `:60` and `vote_for_poll`'s at `:183` are new call sites, but every other production dereference of `.instance` this file and its siblings already guard the same way `refresh_community_profile_task` does, so this is a genuinely new carrier, not a repeat of an already-registered one. Likelihood is low because every community-creation path in this codebase sets `instance_id` (local communities to the local `Instance` row, remote ones on first fetch), so a `None` `instance_id` in production would itself be a pre-existing data anomaly -- but it is a real behaviour change this round did not name, and is recorded here at that strength rather than either promoted to a blocking defect or left silent. The insertion is three lines, growing `likes.py` from 236 to 239 -- the only one of this round's three production changes that adds lines rather than editing in place. **The consequence needed no inference**: the fixing commit's own message names both the private-community leak and the wasted failed-delivery attempt against an offline instance as the two concrete harms the missing gate produced | fixed | Six tests cover the change, three pinning paths that already worked and three pinning the new gate's three disjuncts, each failing independently before the fix with a real `ActivityPubLog` row written and a real request attempted: `test_a_poll_vote_announces_to_a_following_instance` (`tests/test_shared_tasks_likes.py:639`) and `test_a_remote_poll_vote_is_sent_bare` (`:660`) are the pre-existing-behaviour controls; `test_a_poll_vote_in_a_private_community_federates_nowhere` (`:699`), `test_a_poll_vote_in_a_local_only_community_federates_nowhere` (`:728`) and `test_a_poll_vote_to_an_offline_instance_federates_nowhere` (`:748`) each assert zero `ActivityPubLog` rows and are separated into three tests specifically because the three disjuncts fail independently and one shared test could not say which one had actually fired |
| D326 | two bare `except:` clauses in `likes.py`, one closing `send_vote` at `:168`, one closing `vote_for_poll` at `:235` | **Not a defect and not fixed. Registered as a distinct family from D315, which the register must say explicitly so a later reader does not merge the two.** D315 is about what a handler *raises* -- the house idiom of `raise Exception('...')` losing a caller's ability to distinguish one failure from another. D326 is about what a handler *catches*: a bare `except:` (no exception class named) catches `BaseException`, not merely `Exception`, so it also intercepts `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` -- signals a process is meant to receive, not code the handler was written to guard -- and routes both into the same `session.rollback(); raise` path as any ordinary failure. **Why it is not promoted to a defect**: both clauses re-raise unconditionally after rolling back, so the exception still propagates to the caller and Celery still sees the task fail; nothing is swallowed. The cost is purely that a deliberate interrupt is momentarily treated as a database-transaction failure rather than a shutdown signal, and no test in this campaign demonstrates a consequence from that. Registered so the shape is on record rather than rediscovered the next time a bare `except:` is read as equivalent to `except Exception:` | not a defect; registered only, at 2 sites in 1 file | `test_a_failure_inside_send_vote_rolls_back_and_re_raises` (`tests/test_shared_tasks_likes.py:915`) reaches `:168`'s bare except naturally -- a missing post makes `:59`'s `object.community` raise `AttributeError` -- and asserts the full `['rollback', 'close', 'rollback', 'close']` sequence across both of `send_vote`'s live sessions; `test_a_database_failure_in_vote_for_poll_rolls_back_and_re_raises` (`:844`) reaches `:235`'s bare except by monkeypatching `get_task_session` to hand back a session whose `execute` raises `RuntimeError`, verified by traceback to fire at `:179`'s very first lookup, and asserts `['rollback', 'close']`. Neither test raises `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit` specifically -- that half of the claim is read from the `except:` syntax itself (a bare clause is `BaseException`-wide by Python's own exception-hierarchy rule), not measured by a test that injects one |
| D327 | `ActivityBatch.source_type` and `source_id` are written by nobody and read by nobody | **Not a defect and not fixed -- registered because it is a documented, unimplemented lookup path rather than a live gap, and the register must say what "not implemented" actually costs here.** `app/models.py:4337`'s column comment describes an undo-by-`source_id` lookup: "look it up by source_id and delete it from this table (before the batch is sent). If not found, federate the undo." Both writers that construct an `ActivityBatch` row omit both columns -- `likes.py:142` (`session.add(ActivityBatch(instance_id=..., community_id=..., payload=...))`) and `app/activitypub/routes.py:1992` (the same three keyword arguments, no more) -- and the one reader, `app/cli.py:1132`'s batch-flush cron job, filters only by `instance_id` and `community_id` before sending every pending row and deleting all of them by `id`; no code anywhere in the repository queries `ActivityBatch` by `source_id`. **The consequence is benign, and the entry says so rather than inflating it**: the comment's own documented fallback -- "if not found, federate the undo" -- is what happens on EVERY row, since the lookup it fell back from was never built. A vote followed immediately by its own undo, both queued for the same `piefed`/`pylova` peer before the batch flushes, is not deduplicated into a no-op; both payloads are queued, both are sent in the same Announce batch, and the peer ends up in the correct final state regardless, just without the efficiency the columns were added to enable. **A dead optimisation, not a live defect** -- the design in the model's own comment was never finished on the write side | not a defect; registered only, at 2 writers and 1 reader, none touching either column | read from source at this commit: `app/models.py:4337` (the column comment), `likes.py:142` and `app/activitypub/routes.py:1992` (both writer call sites, `ast`-confirmed as the only two `ActivityBatch(` constructor calls in `app/`), and `app/cli.py:1125-1138` (the sole reader, confirmed by the same walk to filter only on `instance_id`/`community_id` and never reference `source_id` or `source_type`). No test in this campaign drives an ActivityBatch row through a source_id-keyed lookup, because no such lookup exists to drive |

**Facts 141-145 carried into `tests/README.md`.**
`Community.following_instances()` joins `CommunityMember` and filters
`Instance.id != 1`, so a recipient fixture needs a member on a non-local
instance, not merely an `Instance` row (141). A redundant conjunct can be
invisible to branch coverage -- `coverage.py` does not decompose a
conjunction -- and still visible to mutation testing, which is fact 138's
stated exception rather than its contradiction (142). `likes.py` resolves
`redis_client` by importing it inside the function, so assert on what was
published, not merely that `publish` ran (143). An ordering arrangement in a
skip test was measured this round, across four runs of the same mutation,
and the measurement is stated at its bounded, environment-scoped strength
rather than promoted to a general proof (144). A mutation loop must restore
production code before any point where it might stop and report, not only
at the end of a batch -- this round's own process nearly left a mutated file
unwatched between its last run and its restore (145).

### 1. Three new numbers, one fixed and two not -- D328-D330

| # | function | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D328 | `ban_person`'s fallback send to the banned user's own instance, `app/shared/tasks/blocks.py:189-190` | **Fixed in this sub-project, commit `ef0583d6`.** Every other recipient in `ban_person`'s local-community loop is guarded by `instance.inbox and instance.online()` (`:187`); the fallback send at `:189-190`, which exists specifically to reach the banned user's OWN instance when `community.following_instances()` (`:185`) excludes it -- the comment at `:189` states why: that method excludes an instance whose only follower was the person just banned, who has just lost membership -- carried NO guard at all pre-fix, reading only `if user.instance_id not in sent_to:`. **BOTH FAILURE MODES ARE REAL AND DISTINCT, NOT ONE DEFECT DESCRIBED TWICE.** A null `instance_id` (nullable FK, same column D325's and D331's cells discuss) makes the ORM relationship `user.instance` resolve to `None`, so `user.instance.inbox` raises `AttributeError` before any request is attempted -- a crash, not a failed send. A non-null `instance_id` pointing at an instance with `inbox IS NULL` does not crash: `send_post_request` is still called with `uri=None`, which reaches `post_request`'s own `if uri is None or uri == '':` (`app/activitypub/signature.py:109`) and writes an `ActivityPubLog` row with `result='failure'`, `exception_message='empty uri'` (`:110-111`) -- a row with no request ever attempted, indistinguishable from a real transport failure to anything that isn't reading the row's own text. A dormant or gone-forever instance (online() False) is a third case the guard also now excludes, silently. **The fix preserves the fallback's reason for existing rather than removing it**: the new guard is `user.instance_id not in sent_to and user.instance and user.instance.inbox and user.instance.online()`, adding the same three conjuncts every other recipient in the function already carries, so an instance whose only follower was the banned user still gets told (the fallback's whole purpose), just no longer while unguarded against the same three failure classes the rest of the function was already immune to | fixed | `test_the_banned_users_own_instance_is_told_even_when_not_a_follower` (`tests/test_shared_tasks_blocks.py:479`) is the happy-path control the other three must not regress; `test_a_banned_user_with_no_instance_row_does_not_crash` (`:508`), `test_a_banned_users_instance_without_an_inbox_is_not_posted_to` (`:528`) and `test_a_banned_users_offline_instance_is_not_posted_to` (`:554`) each pin one of the three failure classes; the middle and third both assert an `ActivityPubLog` count rather than a delivered-inbox set, but for different reasons. The middle one's home instance has `inbox = None`, so the send never reaches respx at all -- it takes `signature.py:109`'s `empty uri` arm before any request is attempted, and a row count is simply the only observable of that. The third is the one D330/fact 148's reason actually describes: its home instance carries `inbox = OTHER_INBOX` with no route registered, so an unguarded send here would not itself fail the suite as an unmatched request |

The early return existed to suppress the follower fan-out on a moderated delete -- a deliberate choice -- but suppressed the notification cleanup as an incidental side effect of sitting above both. Moderated removals are exactly the case where a stale notification (pointing at content a moderator just removed) matters most, so the asymmetry ran backwards from what the two paths' own rationale would want. Fixed by folding the condition into the fan-out's own guard, `if is_post and followers and not reason:` at `:206`, so nothing below it returns early any more and the cleanup at `:219-226` always runs. **The same coupling this fix removed for `reason` was re-created for `private` two commits later, by D309's own closure at `:133`.** `:133`'s `return` sits above the `:219-226` cleanup too, so a post deleted in a `private` community now federates nothing (D309's fix, correct) and also no longer clears its own notifications (a new, undocumented side effect of where the guard had to go -- `:133` is the guard's only unconditional statement, so `private` could not join `:127` or `:130` instead). It is reachable: `:127` needs `not is_post` (false for a post) and `:130` needs no followers to trip, so a post delete by an author WITH followers passes both and reaches `:133`.
