### 1. `response` unbound in both identity blocks' `finally` guards -- the reachable twin of sub-project 32's own fix, now observed rather than predicted -- D383

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D383 | `monitor_healthy_instances`' Lemmy/PieFed block, `app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:640` (`response = get_request(...)`, inside the `try` at `:639`) and `:694`'s `finally: if response is not None:` (pre-fix `if response:`); the MBIN block's identical shape at `:706`/`:737` | **Fixed, observed failing pre-fix, and the reachable twin of D375 (sub-project 32).** `get_request` raises rather than returning a synthetic response, so a transport failure inside `:639`/`:705`'s `try` left `response` unbound; the `finally`'s `if response:` then raised `UnboundLocalError` before the `except Exception` at `:690`/`:733` -- which had already run -- could help, and the error escaped to the task-level handler at `:742`, rolling back and re-raising, ending the sweep for every remaining instance. Task 1's probe reproduced this against unmodified code before any fix existed, verbatim: `PROBE: task raised UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'response' where it is not associated with a value` and `PROBE: failures=2 dormant=False`. The unpatched raise itself is `respx.models.AllMockedAssertionError` (an `AssertionError` subclass, not an `httpx.HTTPError`), so it escapes all five of `get_request`'s specific `except` clauses (`app/utils.py:146-183`) immediately, with none of their retry-sleep paths triggered -- the crash is fast as well as loud. **There is a second effect this entry records that the crash framing alone misses: on a LATER iteration of the same sweep, Python function scope means `response` is not unbound at all -- it still holds the previous instance's value from the prior loop pass.** So instead of raising, the `finally` closes the PREVIOUS instance's response and leaks the current one, silently, with no error and no log line. Only the FIRST instance in a sweep to reach an unpatched raise crashes the whole task; every later one corrupts resource cleanup instead. Fixed exactly as D375 was: `response = None` seeded before each `try` (`:638`, `:704`), both `finally` guards changed from truthiness to `is not None` (`:694`, `:737`), matching sub-project 32's own idiom for `node`/`nodeinfo` rather than the surrounding code's weaker local one. This is what makes an unpatched test in this file the OPPOSITE failure shape from the harness trap sub-projects 31 and 32 both trained on: `get_request_instance`'s bare `except:` (D380, `app/utils.py:192`) swallows silently and redirects to a synthetic 500, but `get_request` (`app/utils.py:131-185`) always raises on failure, so before this fix a forgotten patch killed the task outright rather than quietly passing for the wrong reason -- the friendlier of the two failure modes | fixed (observed failing pre-fix via the verbatim `UnboundLocalError`); the later-iteration wrong-response-closed effect is registered as part of the same finding, not a separate one | `task-1-report.md` (the verbatim probe transcript, the failure-increment derivation); `task-1-review.md` finding 6-7 (the `AllMockedAssertionError` chain, the `get_request`/`get_request_instance` asymmetry); `task-2-report.md` (the pre-change failure transcript at (then) `:689`, the citation sweep); `task-2-review.md`; `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-09-coverage-maintenance-c2-33-design.md` ("There is a second effect on later iterations..."); `app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:638-640,690,694,704-706,733,737,742` read at this commit; `app/utils.py:131-185,189-196` read at this commit; D375 (sub-project 32) for the twin fix and its own upgrade-by-accident; D380 for the contrasting swallow |

### 2. The admin-role removal loop mutated its own result set mid-iteration -- fixed on its own terms, but the gate that authorised it could not have failed -- D384

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D384 | `monitor_healthy_instances`' Lemmy admin-role removal, pre-fix `for instance_admin in session.query(InstanceRole).filter_by(instance_id=instance.id): if instance_admin.user.profile_id() not in admin_profile_ids: session.query(InstanceRole).filter(...).delete()` -- a live query object consumed by a `for` loop while `.delete()` issues further queries against the SAME table inside that loop body | **Fixed on its own terms; the record states the real reason rather than the one first offered for it.** Draining the query into a `stale_roles` list comprehension (`app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:659-663`) before issuing any `.delete()` (`:664-669`) is correct independent of any ordering question: mutating a result set while a cursor is still iterating it, and desynchronizing the session's identity map from the database mid-loop, are defects on their own terms. **But the gate that authorised the change was vacuous, and this round's review caught it rather than letting a plausible-looking demonstration stand.** The gate's own design compared the set of rows the removal loop would act on before and after the change, seeded with both a surviving and a departing admin. Two independent facts make that comparison unable to fail regardless of the fixture: (1) the fixture's surviving admin's `InstanceRole` row was seeded and COMMITTED before the task ran, so `instance.user_is_admin(user.id)` was already `True` and `:656`'s `session.add` never fired during the probe -- there was no pending add in flight for the two orderings to disagree about; and (2) even with a genuinely pending add, the risk cannot exist on this codebase at all: `get_task_session()` (`app/utils.py:3673-3675`) returns a bare `Session(bind=db.engine)`, carrying SQLAlchemy's library-default `autoflush=True`, while `db.session` is pinned to `autoflush=False` (`app/__init__.py:81`) -- so a pending `session.add` is flushed to the database the moment the removal query next executes (`:661`), whether that query is consumed directly by a `for` loop or drained into a list first; both issue the identical SELECT at the identical program point and cannot diverge. This was confirmed by direct reasoning, by an isolated sandbox reproduction of a bare `Session`'s `autoflush=True` behaviour, AND empirically on this codebase: a fix round reverted the drain-before-delete change in place, under a NEW fixture built with a genuinely pending `session.add` (an admin arriving while a different, already-committed admin departs in the same sweep), reran the full suite, and it still passed 10/10 -- proving old and new orderings are indistinguishable by measurement, not only by argument. The new fixture also closed a real, independent gap the vacuous gate had been masking: nothing in the suite previously exercised the create arm's `session.add` (`:656`) firing in the SAME sweep as the removal loop's `.delete()` for the SAME instance; `test_an_admin_arrives_while_another_leaves_in_the_same_sweep` now does, proven by a mutation on `:656` that fails both it and the pre-existing add-only test | fixed (correct on mutate-while-iterate / identity-map-desync grounds); the ordering justification the commit message first offered is retracted and replaced with equivalence by construction (autoflush), not equivalence by observation on one fixture -- see facts 203-204 | `task-5-report.md` (the Step 1 gate's before/after row sets, both `{(2, 2)}`; the autoflush investigation; the reverted-fix empirical re-run at 10/10; the new combined-sweep test and its mutation proof); `task-5-review.md` (the two-part argument that the gate could not have failed, and the isolated `autoflush=True` reproduction); `progress.md` ("Ruling 11", "Ruling 12", "Ruling 13"); `app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:656,659-669` read at this commit; `app/utils.py:3673-3675`, `app/__init__.py:81` read at this commit |

### 5. `User.profile_id()` does not lowercase where `Community.profile_id()` does -- latent, not live -- D387

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D387 | `User.profile_id()` (`app/models.py:1454-1456`, returns `self.ap_profile_id` as-is when set) against `Community.profile_id()` (`app/models.py:787-789`, always calls `.lower()` on its return value) -- both are compared against a `.lower()`-appended `admin_profile_ids` list at `:662`'s removal predicate | **Latent, not live, and the round's own tests verify why.** `:662`'s `instance_admin.user.profile_id() not in admin_profile_ids` compares an UN-lowercased `User.profile_id()` against a list every entry of which was explicitly lowercased at `:648` (`admin_profile_ids.append(profile_id.lower())`). If a remote instance ever returned an admin actor id with mixed case, the removal predicate would compare a mixed-case value against an all-lowercase list, never match, and the stale role would never be removed. **It is safe today because `ap_profile_id` is stored PRE-LOWERCASED at actor-creation time** -- `app/activitypub/util.py:1233`: `ap_profile_id=activity_json['id'].lower()` -- so both sides of the comparison are lowercase because the SOURCE STRING was, not because anything normalises case at comparison time. **What would make it unsafe: any code path that sets `ap_profile_id` without lowercasing it first**, or a future refactor of `User.profile_id()` that stops returning the stored `ap_profile_id` verbatim (its own fallback branch, `f"{SERVER_URL}/u/{self.user_name.lower()}"`, IS already lowercased, so only the `ap_profile_id`-set branch is exposed). Task 4's two new tests use all-lowercase literals throughout their fixtures and do not mask the asymmetry -- they simply do not exercise it, honestly reported as such rather than claimed as coverage of it | correct in current production behaviour (given the creation-time invariant); registered as a latent asymmetry, not fixed | `task-4-report.md` ("`profile_id` lowercasing asymmetry — what I checked"); `task-4-review.md` ("`profile_id` lowercase asymmetry", independently confirmed); `app/models.py:787-789,1454-1456` read at this commit; `app/activitypub/util.py:1233` read at this commit; `app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:648,662` read at this commit |

### 6. `user_is_admin`'s role-specific check lets a non-admin `InstanceRole` row collide with a new admin insert -- latent, not live -- D388

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D388 | `monitor_healthy_instances:650`'s guard, `if user and not instance.user_is_admin(user.id):`, gating `:656`'s `session.add(new_instance_role)`; `Instance.user_is_admin` (`app/models.py:121-123`) returns `role and role.role == 'admin'`, checking the STORED ROLE VALUE specifically rather than merely whether an `InstanceRole` row exists for `(instance_id, user_id)` | **Latent, not live.** `InstanceRole.role` (`app/models.py:169`) is a free-text `db.Column(db.String(50), default='admin')`, not an enum, so a row could in principle hold any string. If a row for `(instance.id, user.id)` existed with `role` set to anything OTHER than `'admin'`, `:650`'s `user_is_admin(user.id)` would return `False` even though a row already occupies that composite primary key (`app/models.py:167-168`), so `:650`'s guard would be true and `:656`'s `session.add(new_instance_role)` would attempt to insert a SECOND row for the identical `(instance_id, user_id)` pair -- a composite-PK collision, raised on the next autoflush (the removal loop's own query at `:661`) and caught by `:690`'s `except`, incrementing `failures` rather than persisting anything. **It is safe today because every `InstanceRole(...)` construction in the codebase passes `role='admin'` literally** -- confirmed by a full-repository search: `app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:651` and `:718` (this module's own two sites) and `app/activitypub/util.py:2173`, all three literal `role='admin'`, and the column's own default is `'admin'` too. No code path currently writes any other value. **What would make it unsafe: a future admin-role variant (a moderator role, say) written to the same `InstanceRole` table with a different `role` string** -- `user_is_admin`'s specific `== 'admin'` check, rather than a plain existence check, would then let this guard's `not instance.user_is_admin(...)` go true for a user who already holds a non-admin row, and the resulting insert would collide on the composite key exactly as described. Task 3's mutation-testing traced the identical composite-PK collision mechanism for a different mutation of this same guard (dropping its second conjunct entirely), confirming the collision-and-swallow consequence by direct observation rather than only by reading the schema | correct in current production behaviour (given that no code path writes a non-'admin' role today); registered as a latent guard/schema mismatch, not fixed | `app/models.py:121-123,166-169` read at this commit; `app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:650-656` read at this commit; `grep -rn "InstanceRole(" app/` (three call sites, all literal `role='admin'`); `task-3-report.md` and `task-3-review.md` (`test_an_existing_admin_is_not_added_twice`'s independent trace of the composite-PK collision mechanism at the guard's other conjunct) |

**Facts 198-205 carried into `tests/README.md`.** Task 1's probe established
that an unpatched `get_request` crashes the whole task rather than being
silently swallowed, the opposite of what sub-projects 31 and 32 found for
`refresh_instance_chooser` and `get_request_instance` -- and DC1 then changed
that state, so the fact records both (198). An instance's `software` value
decides which blocks a test enters, and a test that sets it for one reason
enters them for all reasons (199). `_quiet_http_half` neutralises the fetch
and discovery blocks so an identity-phase test observes only the identity
phases, and the 404 it installs still contributes exactly two of `failures`'s
increments (200). Patching `cache.delete_memoized` mutates the shared `Cache`
object every module imports, not a name local to the module under test, and
under `NullCache` an invalidation has nothing to invalidate, so the oracle

coverage.py records as a single arc pair (202). `get_task_session()` carries
SQLAlchemy's default `autoflush=True` where `db.session` is pinned to
`autoflush=False`, so reasoning about pending-write visibility inside a
Celery task differs from the same reasoning in a request (203). A gate that
cannot fail is as uninformative as a test that cannot fail -- a fixture
unable to distinguish the orderings it exists to compare authorised a change
for the wrong reason, even though the change itself was right (204). A
working-tree scanner and a mutation-testing task collide on every round that
mutates production, clustering on exactly the guards worth mutating, and the
mitigation is to treat HEAD, not the tree, as the artifact during a probe
window (205).

### 2. The Group A harness facts -- this round's most reusable output -- D393

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D393 | `tests/test_shared_post_interactions.py` (the harness), `app/shared/post.py` Group A, `tests/conftest.py` | **Not a defect -- six harness facts, three of which disproved the spec that predicted them.** (a) **There is no `user=` escape hatch in Group A.** Several `app/shared/` functions take a `user=` parameter that lets a test bypass `current_user` and the request entirely -- `edit_post` (`app/shared/post.py:250`) is one. **No function in Group A has that parameter**, so every Group A test must arrange either a real bearer token (SRC_API) or a real request context with a logged-in `current_user` (SRC_WEB). (b) **`redis_double` DOES reach a function-body `from app import redis_client`, and is actively harmful there.** `tests/conftest.py:459-465` warns that its `redis_double` fixture may not reach `from app import redis_client` written inside a function body; `mark_post_read:1126` is such a site, and the probe showed the fixture DOES reach it -- the opposite of the warning's implication. But `:1127`'s `redis_client.lock(...)` releases via `EVALSHA`, which fakeredis does not implement, so every path through `mark_post_read` dies on `redis.exceptions.ResponseError: unknown command 'evalsha'` under the fixture and passes without it, bound to the compose stack's real Redis. **No test in this file requests `redis_double`.** `delete_post:765` has the same function-body import shape and Group C inherits this answer. (c) **The WEB arms return a Flask `Response`, never a `str`.** `render_template` at `app/shared/post.py:23` is `app.utils.render_template`, not Flask's: `app/utils.py:74` is annotated `-> Response` and `:86` wraps the rendered string in `make_response` before adding cache and `Link` headers. Assert `result.status_code == 200` and `result.get_data(as_text=True)`; `isinstance(result, str)` is always False and a test written that way cannot fail for the right reason. (d) **`community.private` is the federation lever; `community.local_only` is a trap.** `community.private=True` stops `app/shared/tasks/likes.py`'s eager body after its row lookups and before any outbound request, so `block_outbound_http` never fires -- verified by probe. `local_only` looks like the same lever and is not: `can_downvote` reads it at `app/utils.py:2448` (`if community.local_only and not user.is_local():`), so setting it silently changes which permission arm a vote test takes. (e) **Celery is eager** (`tests/conftest.py:105-110`), so `task_selector` runs real task bodies inline rather than enqueueing -- which is what makes PC2's "did this federate?" observation possible at all. (f) **`_seed()` must seed LOCAL users.** `authorise_api_user` rejects any user with `ap_id is not None` with `Exception('incorrect_login')` at `app/utils.py:3628-3629`, and `tests/factories.py`'s `make_user` defaults to non-local, so every SRC_API test fails before reaching the function under test unless the seed passes `local=True` | registered; binding on Groups B through E, which share the same module and the same two source arms | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-1-report.md` (probes A-E); `tests/test_shared_post_interactions.py`'s module docstring, which carries these facts in-tree; `tests/conftest.py:105-110,459-465`; `app/utils.py:74,86,2448,3628-3629`; `app/shared/post.py:23,250,765,1126-1127`; `app/shared/tasks/likes.py` |

### 3. The spec's "The SRC_API arms need a request context too" section was false, and the mechanism that falsified it -- D394

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D394 | `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34-design.md`, the section headed "The SRC_API arms need a request context too", which the spec itself called "the fact most likely to be missed" | **The spec's central harness claim was FALSE, and Task 1's very first probe disproved it.** The claim: `vote_for_post:50` and `vote_for_poll:1152` both read `if user.banned or user_ip_banned():` after the source fork, `user_ip_banned` (`app/utils.py:2311-2314`) calls `ip_address`, `app/utils.py:2308` binds that to `app/__init__.py`'s `get_ip_address`, and `get_ip_address` reads `request` -- therefore "there is no context-free path through either function" and an SRC_API test without a request context "fails inside `user_ip_banned`, not at the assertion". **The chain is correct up to the last step and the conclusion does not follow.** `get_ip_address` wraps its whole body in `try: ... except RuntimeError: ip = ''` (`app/__init__.py:68-77`), catching exactly the "working outside of request context" error; `user_ip_banned` then sees a falsy `current_ip_address`, falls off the end, and returns `None`. **SRC_API tests need no request context**, and a test carrying one it does not need teaches the next round the wrong harness. What actually blocks an SRC_API test is entirely different -- see D393(f) and D395. The spec has been **corrected in place with a marked CORRECTION block rather than silently rewritten**, because later rounds read it and a spec that quietly changes its mind is indistinguishable from one that was always right. **The transferable part: a "there is no path that avoids X" claim built by following a call chain is only as strong as the exception handling at the chain's far end, and this one was built without opening the last file.** Group B's and Group C's functions read the same `user_ip_banned` | corrected on the record (spec section rewritten with a CORRECTION marker); no production change follows | `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34-design.md` (the corrected section); `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-1-report.md` (probes D/E); `progress.md` Rulings 9 and 10; `app/__init__.py:68-77`, `app/utils.py:2308,2311-2314`, `app/shared/post.py:50,1152` read at `7cad3211` |

### 4. `authorise_api_user` pre-empts every Group A function's own ban check on the SRC_API arm -- D395

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D395 | `app/utils.py:3628-3629` (`if user.ap_id is not None or user.verified is False or user.banned is True or user.deleted is True: raise Exception('incorrect_login')`) against the internal ban gates at `app/shared/post.py:50` (`vote_for_post`) and `:1152` (`vote_for_poll`) | **Structural, not a defect -- and it collided with THREE separately-designed tests before it was recognised as one finding rather than three coincidences.** On SRC_API, the called function's first act is `authorise_api_user(auth, ...)`, which rejects a banned bearer token **before the function body runs at all**. So a Group A function's own `if user.banned or ...` check is UNREACHABLE through SRC_API for any input whatsoever. On SRC_WEB the check is reachable in principle but pre-empted in practice for the ordinary directions: `can_upvote` (`app/utils.py:2480-2482`) and `can_downvote` (`:2436-2438`) both return `False` for `user.banned`, so `vote_for_post:43-44`'s compound gate fires first for `'upvote'` and `'downvote'`. **`vote_for_post:50`'s `user.banned` disjunct is therefore reachable only via SRC_WEB with a `vote_direction` outside `{'upvote','downvote'}`** -- see D408. **Scope, stated precisely because the campaign's own rule is that an equivalence argument must say what it quantifies over:** the pre-emption was **VERIFIED by test redesign for `vote_for_post` and `vote_for_poll`**, the only two Group A functions with an internal ban gate to collide with. It is **INFERRED, not verified, for the other three Group A functions that call `authorise_api_user`** (`bookmark_post`, `remove_bookmark_post`, `subscribe_post`): the pre-emption certainly happens there too, since it is a property of `authorise_api_user` rather than of the caller, but it has no observable consequence in those three because they have no internal ban gate for it to shadow. Groups B and C have the same shape and should expect the same collision wherever a function combines a bearer-token arm with its own ban check | registered; production behaviour is correct (the outer check is strictly stronger), the finding is about what a test can reach | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-6-report.md` and `task-8-report.md` (the two redesigns); `task-6-review.md` and `task-8-review.md` (both sharpened the claim independently); `progress.md` Ruling 28; `app/utils.py:2436-2438,2480-2482,3628-3629` and `app/shared/post.py:43-44,50,1152` read at `7cad3211` |

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D396 | `vote_for_poll`, pre-fix: `Poll.query.get_or_404(post_id)` followed directly by the mode fork, with **no check that any `choice_id` in `votes` belongs to this poll**. Post-fix: `app/shared/post.py:1159-1167` | **Fixed, observed failing pre-fix.** A caller could pass a `choice_id` belonging to a different poll entirely; `Poll.vote_for_choice` (`app/models.py:3794-3803`) would then write a `PollChoiceVote` row whose `choice_id` points at another post's choice while its `post_id` is this poll's, and increment that other poll's `PollChoice.num_votes`. Fixed by building `poll_choice_ids` from `PollChoice.filter_by(post_id=post_id)` (`:1159-1160`), computing `foreign` (`:1161`), and then **raising for SRC_API (`:1163-1164`) but silently filtering for SRC_WEB (`:1165`)** -- the asymmetry is deliberate: the API has a caller that can report an error, the web route (`app/post/routes.py:643`) has none. **MY SPEC WAS WRONG ABOUT WHERE THE `None` DEREFERENCE MANIFESTS, and this is the durable half of the entry.** The spec and the task brief both predicted `AttributeError` on `.choice_text` in the `task_selector` argument. The observed failure is **`'NoneType' object has no attribute 'num_votes'`, raised inside `Poll.vote_for_choice` at `app/models.py:3800-3801`** (`choice = PollChoice.query.get(choice_id)` then `choice.num_votes += 1`). Cause: `:1173` calls `poll.vote_for_choice(votes[0], ...)` and that call is fully evaluated **before** the `task_selector(...)` call whose argument contains `.choice_text`, so the dereference happens one call earlier than predicted. The defect and the fix are unaffected; the prediction about the observable was wrong, and a later round reading the spec rather than this entry would go looking at the wrong line. **The first form of the fix introduced the exact failure it existed to prevent**, caught by review rather than by any test: a single-mode SRC_WEB vote whose only choice is foreign filtered `votes` to `[]`, `:1169`'s length check was then true but `:1170`'s raise is SRC_API-only with no `else` and no `return`, control fell through, and `:1173` indexed `votes[0]` on an empty list -- an unhandled `IndexError` and a 500 on a route with no error handling. Closed by `if not votes: return` at `:1166-1167`, placed **inside** `if foreign:`. **Task 9's safety demonstration, worth reusing:** the gate for the filter was exact SET EQUALITY on the recorded `PollChoiceVote` rows, not a count and not a "the foreign one is absent" assertion -- chosen because set equality fails for a too-PERMISSIVE filter AND for a too-AGGRESSIVE one, where either weaker oracle passes for one of the two | fixed (observed failing pre-fix twice: once for the original defect, once for the `IndexError` the first fix introduced) | commits `ecb7b1f7` and `e47cd5fe`; `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-9-report.md` (the verbatim `num_votes` failure, the discrepancy with the spec's prediction); `task-9-review.md` (Critical C1, dispatched on Opus for the data-integrity stakes); `progress.md` Task 9 block; `app/shared/post.py:1158-1175` and `app/models.py:3794-3803` read at `7cad3211`; `app/post/routes.py:642-643` read at `7cad3211` |

| D398 | `app/shared/post.py:1159-1165` (PC1's membership filter) and `:1181-1183` (PC2's call-site duplicate check) | **Architectural, found by the mutation pass, and the round's most important structural finding.** Adding `PollChoiceVote.post_id == post_id` to PC2's duplicate check SURVIVED every mutation -- i.e. scoping the check on `post_id` is equivalent to not scoping it. **It is equivalent ONLY BECAUSE PC1 exists**, and the argument needs all four steps: (1) `vote_for_choice` is the only thing that ever constructs a `PollChoiceVote` (`app/models.py:3798`, the sole constructor, always `post_id=self.post_id`), and all four of its production callers pass a `choice_id` drawn from the post being processed; (4) therefore any row matching `(user_id, choice_id)` for a choice of this poll was written with `post_id == post_id`, the added conjunct is satisfied whenever the other two are, and the predicate selects the same rows. **Step 3 is the load-bearing one.** Before PC1, a foreign `choice_id` could reach the loop, a pre-existing vote row for it would carry a DIFFERENT `post_id`, the `post_id`-scoped predicate would report `already_voted == False` while `vote_for_choice`'s own unscoped check found the row and no-opped -- federating a phantom vote, which is exactly the defect PC2 fixed. **So weakening or removing PC1's membership filter would silently make PC2's call-site check wrong again, and nothing at either site says so.** Neither the spec, the plan, the two implementers nor the two reviewers noticed the coupling while the two changes were being made a task apart; only the mutation pass surfaced it, and only because a surviving mutant demanded an argument for why it survived. **The general shape: a survivor's equivalence argument is where hidden coupling between two changes becomes visible, because it is the only place anyone is forced to write down the premise the other change supplies** | registered; both changes are correct as they stand, the coupling is a constraint on future edits | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-11-report.md` section 5 ("Not a hole: N8"); `task-11-review.md` (upheld on independent verification; the reviewer audited all three `vote_for_choice` callers to confirm a premise the report had left unstated); `app/shared/post.py:1158-1165,1180-1187` and `app/models.py:3781,3794-3803` read at `7cad3211` |

### 16. `app/post/routes.py:280`'s precedence bug: a post with no cross-posts is never marked read -- D407

### 17. A `vote_direction` outside `{'upvote','downvote'}` bypasses every permission gate on both arms -- and `Post.vote`'s reversal is not purely vote-removal -- D408

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D408 | `app/shared/post.py:35`, `:37` and `:43-44` -- all three permission gates in `vote_for_post` -- each of which tests `vote_direction == 'upvote'` or `vote_direction == 'downvote'` before consulting `can_upvote`/`can_downvote` | **Registered, NOT fixed; a real gate weakness, live but bounded.** Every permission gate in `vote_for_post` is direction-specific, so a `vote_direction` that is neither `'upvote'` nor `'downvote'` matches none of them and reaches `:50` with no permission check performed at all. **This is a real production value, not a hypothetical:** `app/api/alpha/utils/post.py:1391-1397` sets `direction = 'reversal'` whenever `score` is neither `1` nor `-1`, and `app/post/routes.py:539-540,544` takes `vote_direction` from an **unvalidated URL path segment**. So a bot account, or a user banned from the community, can reverse a vote it could not have cast -- and `:50`'s own `user.banned` disjunct is the ONLY gate such a call meets (which is also the only way that disjunct is reachable at all: see D395). **Bounded by what `Post.vote` actually does with a reversal, and the campaign's earlier statement of that was wrong.** `app/models.py:2732-2741`: a reversal with no existing vote returns `None` immediately, and a reversal of a zero-effect vote likewise; a reversal WITH an existing vote rewrites `vote_direction` to match that vote's own effect (`:2734-2737`) and falls through to `:2742`'s assert. **That fall-through is where "reversal is just vote-removal" breaks:** at `:2744-2752`, if `emoji` is non-null then `existing_vote.emoji` is overwritten IN PLACE, the reaction cache is refreshed, and the function returns `None` **without deleting the vote** -- and because `:2734-2737` has already forced `vote_direction` to agree with the existing vote's sign, `:2746`'s condition is ALWAYS satisfied for a reversal carrying an emoji. So a reversal is vote-removal only when `emoji` is null; with an emoji it is an in-place emoji edit on a vote the caller may have had no permission to cast. Both API and web callers can supply an emoji (`app/api/alpha/utils/post.py:1390`; `app/post/routes.py:540`'s `/<emoji>` route variant). **Registered rather than fixed because this round's approved production scope was three named changes and this is a fourth**; the mutation pass confirms the gates are otherwise discriminated -- `test_a_web_reversal_bypasses_the_upvote_gate_for_a_blocked_user` pins the bypass itself, and it is what kills the `vote_direction == 'upvote' -> True` mutant (D412) | registered, NOT fixed; **live, not latent**; the reversal semantics are corrected here against the round's own earlier statement of them | `app/shared/post.py:35,37,43-44,50` read at `7cad3211`; `app/models.py:2725-2752` read at `7cad3211`; `app/api/alpha/utils/post.py:1390-1399` and `app/post/routes.py:539-549` read at `7cad3211`; `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-5-report.md` and `task-6-report.md`; `progress.md` Rulings 21, 22, 23 and the Task 5 deferred minor; `app/utils.py:2436-2438,2480-2482` (the `can_*` implication that makes the gate weakness observable only off the two normal directions) |

### 18. The mutation pass: 60 mutations, two holes, and three survivor classes rather than two -- D409

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D409 | `app/shared/post.py` Group A, all of it; the pass ran on Opus over the 1187-line tree, applying one mutation at a time and asserting `git diff -- app/` empty and `wc -l` = 1187 after each | **Not a defect -- the round's verification result, and the classification scheme is the reusable part.** **60 mutations: 53 killed, 7 survived with a recorded argument apiece, 2 holes found and closed** with three new tests; the file went 55 -> 58 tests, every count taken from pytest's own `--collect-only` output. **Hole 1:** dedenting PC1's `if not votes: return` out of `if foreign:` -- making it unconditional -- survived all 55 tests, so PC1's guard PLACEMENT was unobservable. ### 19. The masking finding: `:1161`'s cast is masked by `:1165`'s, and no single-site mutation can show it -- D410

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D410 | `app/shared/post.py:1161` (`foreign = [choice_id for choice_id in votes if int(choice_id) not in poll_choice_ids]`) and `:1165` (`votes = [choice_id for choice_id in votes if int(choice_id) in poll_choice_ids]`) | **Registered as a CONDITIONAL RULE, and it is a limit of single-site mutation as a technique rather than of this pass.** Dropping `:1161`'s `int()` alone SURVIVES: with string input, `'5' not in {5}` is true, so `foreign` fills with every choice and `:1162` opens -- but `:1163`'s raise is SRC_API-only and the API schema never delivers a string, and `:1165`'s intact cast then re-filters `votes` and **reconstructs the identical list**, so `:1166` is false and the loop records exactly what it would have. The only consequence of wrongly entering `:1162` is `:1164`'s raise, which SRC_API cannot reach with a non-int. Dropping `:1165`'s cast alone KILLS (it was Hole 2: a web vote naming two valid choices and one foreign one loses ALL THREE silently, because the web arm has no raise). **Dropping BOTH together is a live defect that dropping EITHER alone is not, and no single-site mutation can detect that.** The rule, to be applied by anyone editing this function: **never remove the two casts in one change** -- `:1161`'s cast becomes load-bearing the moment `:1165`'s is removed, or the moment `app/api/alpha/schema.py:1745` stops coercing. This is the exact mirror of D398's PC1/PC2 coupling, one level down: there a fix's equivalence depended on another fix's premise, here a cast's redundancy depends on another cast's presence. **The general lesson for every remaining round: a mutation pass that applies one change at a time is blind to a defect that requires two, and the places where that blindness bites are precisely the places where two sites enforce the same invariant redundantly.** A docstring in the test file briefly claimed dropping `:1161` ALONE produced the double-mutation's behaviour and had to be corrected -- see D412's second half for how that was caught | registered as a conditional rule on future edits; no production change | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-11-report.md` sections 10.3-10.5 and 12.1-12.2; `task-11-review.md` re-review (verified the masking argument step by step, including that `app/api/alpha/schema.py:1745` makes non-ints unreachable at `:1164`'s raise); `progress.md` Ruling 36; `app/shared/post.py:1161-1167` read at `7cad3211` |

### 20. The int-versus-string harness gap: API and web callers of a shared function routinely disagree about type -- D411

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D411 | `app/post/routes.py:642` against `app/api/alpha/schema.py:1745`, and every test call site in `tests/test_shared_post_interactions.py` | **A harness fact for Groups B through E, and the round's cheapest reusable check.** `vote_for_poll`'s two production callers hand it different Python types for the same argument. The API deserializes through marshmallow -- `choice_id = fields.List(fields.Integer(), ...)` -- so `"5"` arrives as `5` and `"abc"` is rejected before the handler runs. The web route reads `request.form` raw: `app/post/routes.py:642` is a single ternary whose single-mode half applies `int(...)` and whose multiple-mode half is `request.form.getlist('poll_choice[]')`, **a list of STRINGS**. All 18 test call sites in the file passed ints, so the entire suite exercised only the API's type on both arms. **The gap produced a genuine hole** (`:1165`, D410) that coverage could not see and that only mutation found. **The instructive part is that the file KNEW and reasoned its way to the wrong conclusion:** `test_multiple_mode_records_every_choice`'s docstring already said the real caller sends strings, cited the cast as the reason it exists, and then concluded "the cast is exercised either way" -- **true of EXECUTION and false of OBSERVATION.** The line was covered, the reasoning was written down, and nothing downstream could tell whether the cast had run. The docstring has been amended in place. **The rule: where a shared-layer function is called by both the API and the web route, read the route that BUILDS the argument and confirm at least one test supplies that type.** A suite that seeds through the ORM gets ints for free and will silently test only one caller's type on both arms | registered; one docstring corrected, two tests added (one of which pins the real caller's type on the ordinary path and kills no mutant today, kept deliberately and labelled as such) | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-11-report.md` section 10.7; `progress.md` Rulings 34 and 35, and the re-review's decision that the "a test that cannot fail is a defect" rule does not bind here because the test fails under the C1+C2 double mutation, under a dialect change, and under type-strictness in `vote_for_choice`; `app/post/routes.py:642` and `app/api/alpha/schema.py:1745` read at `7cad3211` |

### 21. Two equivalence claims refuted by mutation, one of them confirmed by a reviewer first -- D412

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Dropping the `not` SWAPS the arms, so a post WITH flair takes the `flair_list = []` branch and returns empty. An existing test in the file already killed it. **Refutation 2:** Task 5 claimed `vote_direction == 'upvote' -> True` at `:43` is equivalent because `can_downvote` implies `can_upvote` -- an implication that genuinely holds, verified pointwise against `app/utils.py:2436-2491`. But it is only true for calls where `vote_direction == 'downvote'`, and `vote_direction` is not restricted to two values (D408). With `'reversal'` and a bot user the mutant diverges observably; a test was required and written, and the mutant DIED. **The lesson, in one line: an equivalence argument must quantify over the inputs that REACH the site, not over the one input the test happens to use -- and a reviewer who checks only the ARGUMENT inherits its blind spot.** The second half is the part this campaign had not written down before: review is not an independent sample when it re-checks the reasoning rather than the input space. **A third instance of the same shape appeared inside the mutation pass itself** and is recorded here because it shows the failure surviving even under mutation discipline: a test docstring claimed a single-site mutation produced behaviour that was actually the double mutation's, while **section 10.3 of the same report recorded `C1 SURVIVED (58 passed)` four sections above it** -- if the docstring's claim were true, that very test would have killed C1. The evidence and the claim sat in one document, disagreeing, and neither the implementer nor the first reviewer caught it, because both checked the claim's reasoning rather than the claim against the number | registered; both refuted claims corrected in the test file's docstrings, and the mutants that refuted them are now killed by tests | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-10-coverage-post-a-34/task-11-report.md` section 4 (Predictions 1 and 3) and sections 10.3, 12.1; `task-1-review.md` (the confirmation that was wrong); `progress.md` Task 1 harness facts, Rulings 21-22, 36; `app/shared/post.py:35,43,1133-1143` and `app/utils.py:2436-2491` read at `7cad3211` |

|---|---|---|---|---|

### 23. The commit-trailer failure is a pattern with a cause, and warnings do not address it -- D414

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D414 | The `Co-Authored-By:` trailer on implementer commits, across sub-projects 33 and 34 | **Registered as a PATTERN, not as three incidents, because the third occurrence is what identified the cause.** Three commits in two rounds shipped `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5` where the campaign's literal constant is `Claude Opus 5` -- sub-project 33's Task 4, sub-project 34's Task 4, and sub-project 34's Task 6. The third occurred **despite a dispatch that explicitly named the second as a failure to avoid**, which is what rules out carelessness. **The cause: the implementer runs on Sonnet, reads `Co-Authored-By:` as a field ASSERTING ITS OWN IDENTITY, and writes what it believes to be true. It is being accurate, not careless -- which is exactly why a louder warning fails.** The countermeasure that worked was rewording rather than emphasis: state that the string is a **literal constant and not a self-description**, and say outright "you are running on Sonnet and the trailer still says Opus 5." No further occurrence after that rewording landed, across Tasks 7 through 11. A secondary process note: a wrong trailer is one metadata line with zero reviewable logic, and the campaign's established handling is that the implementer amends it as part of a fix round it is already doing, or the controller amends it directly when no other finding exists -- spending a full fix-and-re-review cycle on it is waste this campaign has paid for twice | registered as a process finding; the rewording is the durable countermeasure | `progress.md` Rulings 19, 20, 24, 25; commits `34f0c91d` (amended from `69565e24`) and `10a03763` (amended from `b0bc2f0a`); sub-project 33's Task 4 |

### 25. `vote_for_poll`'s single-mode branch coerces nothing, while every other choice-id site in the function coerces -- D415

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D415 | `app/shared/post.py:1173` (`poll.vote_for_choice(votes[0], user.id)`) and `:1175` (`choice_text=PollChoice.query.get(votes[0]).choice_text`), against `:1161`, `:1165`, `:1183`, `:1184` and `:1187`, which all wrap the choice id in `int()` | **Registered, deliberately not fixed -- pre-existing, correct today, and outside the round's approved production scope. It was decided TWICE and recorded only in the workspace, which is what this entry exists to undo.** The single-mode branch passes `votes[0]` to `Poll.vote_for_choice` and to `PollChoice.query.get()` with **no `int()` coercion at all**, while the multiple-mode branch coerces at every one of its three sites and PC1's filter coerces at both of its two. **It is correct today** because `app/post/routes.py:642` normalizes single mode to a bare `int` before calling (D400/D411) and `app/api/alpha/schema.py:1745`'s `fields.List(fields.Integer())` makes the API arm's elements ints, so no string choice id reaches `:1173` from either production caller. The contract that makes it safe is unwritten. **Three things sharpen it, and none of them was recorded anywhere durable before this entry.** (1) **PC1 keeps the uncast path REACHABLE rather than closing it.** `:1165` rebuilds `votes` by *filtering* on `int(choice_id) in poll_choice_ids` but emitting the **ORIGINAL** element, not the cast one -- so a string id that survives the membership filter arrives at `:1173` still a string. ### 1. Group B's harness facts, and the append-not-insert rule for a widely-cited file -- D416

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D416 | `tests/factories.py:1183-1234`, `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py:83-140`, `app/models.py:716-722,778-779`, `app/utils.py:3564-3582` | **Not a defect -- five harness facts Groups C, D and E should extend rather than re-derive.** (a) **The Group A harness was consolidated into `tests/factories.py` and is now public:** `seed_post_context(*, private=True, community_name='interactions')` at `:1187`, `web_ctx(app, user, query_string='')` at `:1217` and `bearer(user)` at `:1228`. They were **appended to the end of the file, with their two imports (`contextmanager`, `SimpleNamespace`) placed mid-file at `:1183-1184` immediately above them, rather than inserted at the top.** That is deliberate and is the transferable part: a reviewer counted **39 live citations of the form `tests/factories.py:NNN` across 17 files outside the task's write scope**, including the widely-cited `:141` and `:148`, and a two-line insertion at the top would have silently shifted every one. A pure append leaves every pre-existing line number provably unchanged. **Appending to a widely-cited file is a citation-drift hazard, and a pure append with local imports is how to avoid it.** (b) **Three privilege helpers live in the test file, not in factories**, because they are Group-B-specific: `seed_moderator(s, user=None)` at `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py:83` (a `CommunityMember` row only), `make_site_admin(user)` at `:93` (a `Role` named literally `'Admin'` plus a `user_role` row -- see **D418** for why nothing else works), `make_instance_admin(user, instance)` at `:109` (an `InstanceRole` row on the composite PK `(instance_id, user_id)`, `app/models.py:167-168`). **None of the three overlaps another's disjunct**, which is what makes them usable as single-disjunct witnesses. (c) **None of the six Group B functions renders a template**, so Group A's rule about asserting `result.status_code == 200` (**D393**(c)) does not apply here: every one returns `user.id, post`, or `None` on the SRC_WEB arms of `lock_post`, `move_post`, `mod_remove_post` and `mod_restore_post`. A test written to Group A's rule cannot fail for the right reason. (d) **`Community.moderators()` (`app/models.py:716-722`) carries `.filter(CommunityMember.is_banned == False)`**, and `is_moderator()`/`is_owner()` at `:736-747` both read through it -- so a banned moderator is not a moderator for any gate in this module. The plan cited `:736-740` for `moderators()`; that range is `is_moderator()`, and an implementer following the re-derive rule caught it. (e) **`add_to_modlog` (`app/utils.py:3564`) COMMITS at `:3582`**, so a test asserting nothing was written must query the database rather than the session; it also **raises at `:3569`** for any action outside `ModLog.action_map`, so a mutation that swaps an action string to an unmapped one crashes rather than being observed | registered; binding on Groups C, D and E, which share the module, the two source arms and the same factories file | `tests/factories.py:1183-1234`; `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py:1-62` (the module docstring, which carries these facts in-tree) and `:83-140`; `app/models.py:167-168,716-747,778-779`; `app/utils.py:3564-3582`; Task 1's review, which produced the 39-citations-across-17-files count |

### 2. `s.author` is User id 1, and `User.is_admin()` makes id 1 an unconditional site admin -- D417

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D417 | `app/models.py:1259-1265`, `tests/factories.py:1204-1213`, `tests/conftest.py`'s per-test sequence reset | **A harness trap that makes a permission test pass while pinning nothing.** `User.is_admin()` opens `if self.id == 1: return True` -- **unconditionally, before any role lookup**. `seed_post_context` creates `author` before `voter` (`tests/factories.py:1206-1207`) and the conftest resets sequences after every test, so `author` deterministically lands on **id 1** and `voter` on id 2. **Therefore `s.author` is a site admin in every seeded context.** Any test using `s.author` as its "unprivileged actor" passes the gate through the `is_admin_or_staff()` disjunct and witnesses nothing -- and it looks exactly like a test that works. **Every unprivileged-actor test in this round uses `s.voter`**, and reviewers checked the fixture rather than the docstring in each of Tasks 4-9. This was a preflight ruling, then verified empirically with a throwaway scratch test rather than argued, and confirmed independently by a reviewer from source. The general shape: **a seeding order plus an id-keyed shortcut in production code can silently grant privilege to the actor a test chose precisely because it had none** | registered; binding on every later round that uses `seed_post_context`, and promoted to `tests/README.md` fact 216 | `app/models.py:1259-1265`; `tests/factories.py:1187-1213`; Task 3's empirical probe and Task 5's fixture audit (all six tests confirmed on `s.voter`); the same id-1 shortcut also decides `add_to_modlog`'s `action_type` at `app/utils.py:3570` |

### 3. `grant_permission` cannot make a site admin, because `is_admin()` and `is_staff()` check role NAMES -- D418

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D418 | `tests/factories.py:365` (`grant_permission(user, permission)`), `app/models.py:1259-1275` | **The plan as first written used `grant_permission(user, 'change instance settings')` to make a site admin in four tests, and it cannot work.** `User.is_admin()` (`:1259-1265`) and `User.is_staff()` (`:1268-1272`) iterate `self.roles` and compare `role.name` to the literals `'Admin'` and `'Staff'`; **they never look at the role's permissions**. `User.is_admin_or_staff()` at `:1274-1275` is their disjunction, and `Community.is_admin_or_staff(user)` at `:778-779` delegates to it. So a role carrying every permission in the system but named anything else is not an admin to any gate in `app/shared/post.py`. **The four tests would have exercised the unprivileged path while claiming to witness the admin disjunct of a permission gate -- and would have passed**, because at that point the round had not yet established **D417** and the actor would have been refused silently (see **D421**). Corrected before the plan was committed, by adding `make_site_admin(user)`, which inserts a `Role` named literally `'Admin'`. Verified safe for reuse: `User.roles` is `lazy='dynamic'`, so a raw insert is immediately visible, and the test config's NullCache neutralises `is_admin()`'s `@cache.memoize(timeout=30)` | registered and fixed in the plan before any code was written; the trap in production is unchanged and remains live for any future test | `app/models.py:1259-1275`; `tests/factories.py:365`; `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py:93`; promoted to `tests/README.md` fact 217 |

### 6. Two failure modes for one refusal, in one module, five functions apart -- D421

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D421 | `app/shared/post.py:1055-1056` and `:1097-1098` (raise) against `:941`, `:971`, `:1003` (fall through) | **Not a bug in either arm -- a contract divergence inside one module, now half-closed.** `mod_remove_post` and `mod_restore_post` spell their gate as a **negated early return** -- `if not post.community.is_moderator(user) and not user.is_admin_or_staff(): raise Exception('Does not have permission')` -- so a refusal is an exception on **both** source arms. `lock_post`, `move_post` and `sticky_post` spell theirs as a **positive wrapping `if`** with no `else`, so a refusal was silence on both arms. **The spelling of the gate, not any stated policy, decided what a refused caller observed.** PC2 (**D420**) closed the SRC_API half: all five now raise for a refused API call. **The SRC_WEB half is still divergent and deliberately so.** **CORRECTION, made by the round's final whole-round review and verified line by line before being written down: this entry previously said `mod_remove_post`'s web caller "sits inside a `try`, and the other three do not". THAT IS FALSE and was never true.** `post_delete` (`app/post/routes.py:1159-1190`) contains **no `try` and no `except`**, and `grep -n errorhandler` over `app/post/routes.py`, `app/post/__init__.py` and `app/__init__.py` returns **nothing**, so the `post` blueprint has no error handler either. What actually stands in front of `mod_remove_post`'s raise is a **route-level permission pre-check that is a different predicate from the shared gate**, at `app/post/routes.py:1164`: `post.user_id == current_user.id or community.is_moderator() or current_user.is_admin() or user_access('administer all communities', current_user.get_id())`. That is a **weaker** justification for the divergence than a `try`, and **two reachable unhandled-exception 500s follow from it. Both are PRE-EXISTING, neither was introduced by PC1 or PC2, and neither was fixed this round -- they are registered here for Group C or a later round with production scope over `app/post/routes.py` to own.** **(500-a)** `user_access` (`app/utils.py:1649-1658`) is a **permission-NAME** lookup against `role_permission`; `User.is_admin()`/`is_staff()` are **role-NAME** lookups (`tests/README.md` fact 217, **D418**). **The two predicates are orthogonal.** So an actor holding the permission `administer all communities` on a role NOT named `Admin` or `Staff`, who is not a moderator of the community and is not the post's author, passes `:1164`, is routed by `:1169`'s `if post.user_id != current_user.id` to `:1170`'s `mod_remove_post(..., SRC_WEB, None)`, fails `app/shared/post.py:1055`'s `is_moderator or is_admin_or_staff` gate, and gets an unhandled `Exception('Does not have permission')` -- a 500 on a normal moderator page. **(500-b)** `post_restore` (`app/post/routes.py:1193-1204`) has the same shape and this entry previously did not mention it at all. `:1197` admits `post.user_id == current_user.id`; `:1198` routes to `restore_post` only when `post.deleted_by == post.user_id`; otherwise `:1201` calls `mod_restore_post(..., SRC_WEB, None)`. **So an ordinary post AUTHOR whose post was removed by a MODERATOR** passes `:1197`, takes `:1198`'s false arm, reaches `:1201`, fails `app/shared/post.py:1097`'s gate and gets the same unhandled raise. That path is ordinary, not contrived. So the module today has **one contract for SRC_API and two for SRC_WEB**, and that is a smaller, sharper divergence than the one it started with rather than a closed question. `hide_post` has no gate at all, correctly: it writes per-user state through `user.mark_post_as_hidden`. **The three `test_an_unprivileged_web_*_still_returns_quietly` tests exist specifically to stop a later change "finishing the job"** by making the web arms raise too, and they assert the quiet return AND the absent side effects, so they cannot be satisfied by a raise. **A round that does take production scope should note that "finishing the job" on the three quiet verbs would ADD 500s of exactly the shape of (500-a)/(500-b) unless the route gates are aligned with the shared gates first; aligning the predicates is the real fix and it is a product decision, per D422** | registered; the SRC_API half FIXED by PC2, the SRC_WEB half live and pinned by three tests; the false `try` mechanism CORRECTED on the record; two reachable pre-existing 500s registered, NOT fixed | `app/shared/post.py:941,971,1003,1055-1056,1097-1098` at `5e2f5703`; `app/post/routes.py:1159-1190` (`post_delete`, gate at `:1164`, call at `:1170`, no `try` anywhere in the function) and `:1193-1204` (`post_restore`, gate at `:1197`, fork at `:1198`, call at `:1201`); `app/utils.py:1649-1658` (`user_access`); no `errorhandler` in `app/post/routes.py`, `app/post/__init__.py` or `app/__init__.py`; `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py`'s module docstring, "TWO FAILURE MODES, TOO, AND THE SPLIT IS BY SOURCE ARM" |

### 7. The permission gates diverge THREE ways, not two -- the spec understated it -- D422

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D422 | `app/shared/post.py:941`, `:971`, `:1003`, `:1055`, `:1097` and **`:387`**; `app/models.py:769-779`, `:1259-1282` | **Registered, deliberately not fixed. Note it is a different method from `User.is_instance_admin()` (`:1277-1282`), which keys on the **USER's** instance. **So P1 denies an actor P2 permits, P3 permits an owner the other two do not, and nothing in the source says which is intended.** **Not fixed**: choosing a predicate is a product decision unavailable from the source, and both directions are harmful if wrong -- unifying on P2 grants permission three functions currently withhold; unifying on P1 revokes a working path for remote-instance admins; and P3 sits in Group E, outside this round's scope. **The spec has been corrected in place with a marked CORRECTION block rather than silently rewritten**, following **D394**'s precedent. **Every operand of all five Group B gates is separately witnessed** -- twelve mutations, twelve distinct killing tests (**D426**) | registered, NOT fixed; the spec's two-way claim corrected on the record; P3 handed to Group E | `app/shared/post.py:387-388,941,971,1003,1055,1097` re-derived at `5e2f5703`; `app/models.py:736-747,769-779,1259-1282`; `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-11-coverage-post-b-35-design.md` (the corrected "two ways" section); P3 surfaced as a reviewer Minor on Task 7 that was a false positive about `:388` being unguarded and true about `:387` being a third predicate |

### 10. A later task's change can silently de-witness an earlier task's test -- D425

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D425 | `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py`'s `test_an_unprivileged_user_does_not_federate_a_sticky`, against `app/shared/post.py:1016-1021` | **The round's deepest finding. PC1 (D419) was untested from the moment PC2 (D420) landed, and PC1's own test asserted the opposite in its docstring.** The test makes its refused call through **SRC_API**. PC2 inserted `elif src == SRC_API: raise` at `:1020`, which fires **before** `:1016`'s federation block can be reached on that path. So the test's `assert calls == []` became **vacuous**: nothing can federate after the raise, whether the block sits inside `:1003`'s gate or outside it. The mutation pass proved it rather than inferring it -- **hoisting `:1016`-`:1019` back out of the gate, which is exactly PC1's regression, left all 56 tests green** (survivor P4). **Every gate in the process passed.** The test still ran, still asserted, still passed; Task 10 updated its docstring to describe the new behaviour and the new docstring claimed PC2 "only strengthens the guarantee this test pins", when PC2 had **removed the reachability that made it a witness at all**. The controller had even recorded the PC1/PC2 interaction at Task 10 -- noting that PC1's refusal test was one of five invalidated -- and still missed the consequence. **The reviewer's sharpened wording, which is the durable form: a change that inserts an EARLIER TERMINATOR on a path makes every downstream assertion on that path vacuous, and the task that updates the test is the least likely to notice, because it reasons about its own change rather than about reachability.** **Nothing in this campaign catches this except a mutation pass that re-mutates the EARLIER fix after the LATER one has landed** -- coverage cannot see it (the lines are still covered by other tests), a citation sweep cannot see it (the line numbers are right), and the test count does not move. Closed by `test_an_unprivileged_web_sticky_does_not_federate`: **SRC_WEB is the only arm that still reaches `:1016` after a refusal**, precisely because `:1020` deliberately does not match there (**D420**(ii)). A reviewer enumerated the code downstream of `:956`, `:987` and `:1020` on refused API paths and confirmed **no other test suffered the same** -- the class has exactly one instance in this round, and three of Task 10's other four updated tests are PC2's own killing witnesses and demonstrably live | registered as a defect class; the instance is CLOSED (new test) and the false docstring is corrected in-tree | `app/shared/post.py:1003-1023` at `5e2f5703`; mutation P4 (hoist) survived all 56 tests, and P4r kills with `assert ['sticky_post'] == []` after the new test; the corrected docstring carries this paragraph in-tree so the next reader of that test meets it; see **D398**, sub-project 34's coupled-production-changes finding, of which this is the sharper general case |

### 12. A mutation operator can be STRUCTURALLY VOID -- it crashes on dispatch, and the crash reads as a kill -- D427

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D427 | `app/shared/post.py:985-986`; `app/shared/tasks/__init__.py:66,68`; `app/shared/tasks/pages.py:373` | **A methodological finding, and the reason a recorded `K` was evidence of nothing.** The operator "swap the action string in a `task_selector(...)` call" was applied at `move_post:985` and recorded KILLED. The pasted failure was `TypeError: delete_post() got an unexpected keyword argument 'old_community_id'` -- **a Celery signature mismatch, not a test observing the federation key.** Re-derivation showed the operator cannot measure that site **at all**: `move_post(send_async, user_id, old_community_id, new_community_id, post_id)` (`app/shared/tasks/pages.py:373`) is the **only** one of the **40** entries in `task_selector`'s map (`app/shared/tasks/__init__.py:19-60`) taking `old_community_id`/`new_community_id`; the map is indexed with a **hard subscript** on both arms (`tasks[task_key].delay(...)` at `app/shared/tasks/__init__.py:66` and `tasks[task_key](...)` at `:68`); and **no task in the map accepts `**kwargs`**. So every key-only swap at `:985` either `KeyError`s on an unknown key or `TypeError`s on a known one, before any test can observe anything. **Recorded VOID rather than re-scored**, because "survived" would be as false as "killed". **The durable rule: "swap the action string" is a valid operator ONLY where a signature-compatible sibling exists, and the operator must CHECK that rather than assume it.** The general hazard is worse than a mis-scored row, because **a void operator produces a crash that reads as a kill, so the site scores as covered while being unmeasurable** -- and every later reader trusts the table | registered as a durable methodological fact; the site was then measured properly, which found **D429** | `app/shared/tasks/__init__.py:19-60` (the 40-entry map) and `:66,68` (both hard-subscript dispatch arms); `app/shared/tasks/pages.py:373`; `app/shared/tasks/locks.py:26`; the absence of `**kwargs` re-verified at `5e2f5703` by resolving all 40 map values to their `def` lines and grepping — zero matches |

### 13. A crash kill is not a kill -- the operative question, and what `-x` hides -- D428

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D428 | the whole 59-row mutation table (see **D426** for the table and for why 59 rows became 60 mutations); `./run_tests.sh ... -x` | **Thirteen of the 59 enumerated rows failed on a CRASH rather than an assertion, and exactly one of the thirteen was a false kill.** (**CORRECTION:** this entry previously said "thirteen of the 62 rows" and "the whole 62-row mutation table". 62 was never a row count -- the table enumerates 59 rows; see **D426**. Thirteen is right.) A false kill is **worse than a survivor**: a survivor honestly recorded is a finding someone acts on, while a false kill enters the table **as evidence that a site is covered when it is not**. Finding one therefore obliged an audit of every row of the same shape -- any row whose pasted failure is a `TypeError`, `AttributeError` or import error rather than an assertion. **The criterion offered was "is the crash the mutated line's own direct effect on the value it computes?", and the reviewer replaced it with a sharper one that goes in the register as the operative question: DOES A VIABLE NON-CRASHING VARIANT OF THE SAME FAULT SURVIVE?** That is better because it is a test rather than a judgement -- **D427**'s site fails it (the only viable variant survives; see **D429**) and the other twelve pass it. The twelve acquitted: six source forks crashing `AttributeError: 'NoneType' has no attribute ...` on the very binding the mutation changes; four return forks crashing `TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable NoneType object`, where **the unpacking statement IS the test's observation of the return contract**; three flash guards crashing `RuntimeError: Working outside of request context.` **Two of the three classes were re-verified BY RE-RUNNING rather than argued.** **DISCLOSURE, added by the round's final whole-round review: thirteen is the size of the AUDIT, not the size of the non-assertion-kill population. The twelve gate rows `G1-G12` also died on a non-assertion -- every one printed `Exception: Does not have permission` -- so up to twenty-five of the 59 rows are non-assertion kills and only thirteen were tabulated.** `G1-G12` were excluded deliberately and the exclusion is safe: the exception they raise is the **mutated predicate's own direct effect** -- dropping an operand from the gate is what sends control into the gate's own `raise` -- so each passes the operative question below with no viable non-crashing variant to check. **But a later round applying D428's rule must not read thirteen as the complete set of rows needing adjudication; the rule is "adjudicate every non-assertion kill", and the reason `G1-G12` needed no separate table is that a gate row's crash IS its assertion.** **Second finding, independent of the first: `-x` reports only the FIRST failing arm, so a crash kill can MASK an assertion kill elsewhere, and the summary table cannot show the difference.** Two rows were re-run with only the web tests selected to check the other half; for the flash-guard row the other half turned out to be an **outright assertion kill** (`assert 0 == 1` on the flash count) and the `RuntimeError` was merely what `-x` surfaced first. **A fork mutation has two arms and `-x` will always tell you about one of them** | registered as a durable methodological fact; the one false kill corrected and its site re-measured | the crash-kill audit in `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-11-coverage-post-b-35/task-11-report.md` (deleted with the round); re-runs on rows S1 and F1 with the 10 web tests selected, 3 of which call `lock_post`; see **D427** and **D429** |

Renamed to `test_the_web_arm_returns_none_when_restoring`. **The check is one line and belongs in every round's final gate:** `grep -oE "^def (test_[a-z_]+)" FILE | sort | uniq -d` -- empty output is the pass. ### 17. A production reorder moves the FIRST CRASH SITE, so a docstring's mechanism goes stale while its line numbers stay right -- D432

### 18. Replacing a test's oracle changes what the test proves, and "the finding is addressed" does not mean the replacement proves as much -- D433

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D433 | `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py`'s `test_the_api_arm_does_not_flash_when_locking` / `..._when_unlocking`, against `app/shared/post.py:949` and `:953` | **Three linked process findings from one test, fixed over two rounds.** (a) **The original test wrapped an SRC_API call in `web_ctx`** -- the only such occurrence in the suite, contradicting `tests/README.md` fact 206 **and its own docstring**. The code came verbatim from the plan and the implementer copied it without flagging the contradiction. (b) **The fix was not to unwrap the context but to REPLACE THE ORACLE.** Inside a request context `flash()` succeeds, so the test could only notice a deleted `SRC_WEB` guard by reading the flash queue afterwards. **With no context, `flash()` raises** -- Flask's `flash` writes to `session`, and `session` outside a request context raises -- **so a contextless SRC_API call becomes the oracle itself**: assert it does not raise. Vindicated by mutation: dropping a guard makes the contextless call raise `RuntimeError: Working outside of request context.` rather than silently succeeding. That is strictly stronger than what shipped, and it obeys the harness rule instead of excepting itself from it. (c) **The replacement then proved LESS than it claimed, and only a targeted question found it.** The rewritten test called with `locked=True`, so execution took `:948`'s true branch and **never reached the `else` at `:952-955` holding `:953`'s guard** -- yet the new docstring and the amended commit message both asserted both guards were intact and live-verified. `:953` was caught only incidentally, by two unlock tests that do not claim to. Closed by splitting into two tests, one per guard, with **per-guard mutation evidence**: dropping `:953` fails the unlock test while leaving the lock test unaffected. **The durable rule, and the question that found it: after a fix replaces an assertion, ask "does the new oracle pin one guard or both?" -- because "the finding is addressed" is fully compatible with "the replacement proves less than it says", and the standard review rubric does not ask it** | registered; all three addressed in commit `848f56b1` | `app/shared/post.py:948-955` at `5e2f5703`; `tests/README.md` fact 206; `grep -B3 "SRC_API"` returns zero `web_ctx` occurrences across all 18 SRC_API call sites in the file; per-guard isolation shown by a single `:953`-dropped mutant run against both tests |

### 20. Short-circuit evaluation is what makes two conjunct witnesses INDEPENDENT rather than overlapping -- D435

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D435 | `app/shared/post.py:1055` and `:1097` | **A hole found mid-round by an implementer's own mutation, and the reasoning that proves the fix is real.** Live mutation showed that dropping `:1055`'s **second** conjunct -- `not user.is_admin_or_staff()` -- still passed all 42 tests: **no test witnessed a non-moderator site admin being PERMITTED to remove a post**, so that conjunct was unpinned. There was an exact precedent in the same file (`lock_post`'s `test_a_site_admin_who_is_not_a_moderator_may_lock`, written in Task 4 for the same reason), so this was an omission rather than a decision, and it was closed immediately rather than deferred to the mutation pass four tasks later, when the context would have been gone. **The question that had to be answered, not assumed, was whether the FIRST conjunct had its own distinct witness**, because if both rested on the same test the finding was larger and applied equally to `:1097`. It does: **because `:1055` is `not A and not B`, a moderator actor makes `not A` False and Python NEVER EVALUATES `not B`.** So `test_a_moderator_removes_a_post` genuinely witnesses the first conjunct **alone**, and the new `test_a_site_admin_who_is_not_a_moderator_may_remove_a_post` the second. **Short-circuit semantics are what make the pair independent, and they are also what let a single test look like it covers a compound gate when it has only ever evaluated half of it.** Carrying the finding forward worked: `mod_restore_post:1097` shares the spelling, and the next task closed the same gap **before** it shipped rather than after. All four conjuncts confirmed by the mutation pass with four distinct killing tests (G9-G12, **D426**) | registered; both gaps CLOSED | `app/shared/post.py:1055,1097` at `5e2f5703`; dropping `:1055`'s second conjunct took 43 passed to 42 with exactly the new test failing on `Exception: Does not have permission`; commits `de60971d` and `5a589e1a` |

### 21. Predicted test counts and hand-copied citations are unreliable; pytest's own output and a re-derivation are not -- D436

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D436 | the round's plan and task briefs (`.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-11-coverage-post-b-35/`, deleted with the round) | **Not a defect in the code -- a measured property of plan-authored figures, recorded because the mitigation is cheap and it worked every time.** **The plan's predicted test count was wrong FIVE times in eleven tasks** (predicted 27/30/40/46/"two tests will break" against actual 29/32/42/50/five). Every one was caught by a standing constraint -- **test counts come from pytest's own collection output, never from the plan** -- and every implementer noted the discrepancy rather than silently reconciling. **The plan's line citations were wrong too**, in the same proportion: `Community.moderators()` cited at `app/models.py:736-740` when that range is `is_moderator()` and the real function is `:716-722`; the whole Task 11 brief's line numbers stale by up to +6 after PC2; a brief's `:1071` that was `:1077`. Each was caught by the companion constraint -- **every line number a task cites must be RE-DERIVED with numbered `awk`/`grep -n` output against the working tree, never copied from the brief.** **The finding is not that the controller made errors; it is that two mechanical constraints converted every one of them into a noted discrepancy instead of a shipped defect, and that they are the constraints worth keeping when everything else about a round is negotiable.** The corollary for counts specifically: **a test count that is merely "close" hides a duplicate-name shadowing (D431) perfectly**, so the two constraints are not independent. **A THIRD process gap, added by the round's final whole-round review because it is otherwise unrecorded and a later reader would misread its residue as deliberate:** Task 3's review was shown a list of imports in `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py` that nothing yet used, and **cleared them as deliberate forward-provisioning for Tasks 4-10** rather than asking for their removal. That was the right call at the time. **Nothing re-ran the check once Tasks 4-10 were done**, and three of them -- `SimpleNamespace`, `Post` and `make_user` -- were never used by any task and are still imported and unused at round close. **The rule: a review that clears a defect BECAUSE a later task will consume it creates an obligation on the LAST task, and if no task is given that obligation the clearance silently becomes a permanent leftover.** They are harmless, they are not a mistake by any individual task, and a later round with scope over the file should simply delete them | registered as a process finding; both counting constraints held for all eleven tasks; the deferred-clearance gap did not | `tests/test_shared_post_moderation.py` (65 collected, 65 `^def test_`); `app/models.py:716-722` vs `:736-740`; the eight-to-eleven recorded instances lived in the round's `progress.md`, deleted at close |

### 11. A crash kill answers "is this line reached", never "is this line's effect asserted" -- D447

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D447 | `app/shared/post.py:799` (`restore_post`) against `:823` (`report_post`) | **Process finding, general lesson.** Replacing `restore_post:799`'s `authorise_api_user(auth, id_match=post.user_id)` with `user_id = post.user_id` -- no authorisation at all -- passed ALL 46 tests then in the file (mutation #40, **D446**). Every pre-existing SRC_API test in this file used `bearer(s.author)`; none ever passed a non-author token. The suite had already recorded `:797`'s source-fork inversion (mutation #9) as KILLED, all five of its failures crashes on `current_user`/`incorrect_login` -- and that crash kill answered "is `:797`'s branch reached," not "does anything downstream of it get checked." **The general lesson: a crash kill is evidence the mutated line was REACHED, never evidence that the mutated line's EFFECT was asserted** -- those are different questions, and the fork-inversion crash at `:797` being a legitimate kill said nothing about whether `:799`'s own authorisation logic was ever exercised for its actual purpose. **The identical mutation died instantly in `report_post`, for a reason specific to what that suite happened to assert, not to any difference between the two functions**: `report_post`'s tests call with `bearer(s.voter)` and assert `reporter_id == s.voter.id`; the voter is never the author, so a mutant deriving the reporter from `post.author` diverges from an already-asserted value on the very next line. The asymmetry between the two functions' mutation results is a property of what each suite happened to assert (author-only tokens in one, a non-author token in the other), not a property of the functions themselves. | closed (`:799`); registered as a process lesson | `task-10-report.md` "Fix round 1" MAJOR section (mutation #40's survival and closure, mutation #41's immediate kill, side by side) |

### 15. Four distinct ways a test can fail to witness what it names -- a checklist for later rounds -- D451

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|

### 1. Why `make_post` stood at 0.0% through 36 sub-projects -- three blockers, each with its mechanism -- D454

Every `seed_post_context`-shaped local author is refused at `make_post:187` with `Exception('You are not permitted to make posts in this community')` -- a message naming a PERMISSION problem, giving no hint that the actual cause is a missing key. (2) `g.site` is never populated for a harness call: `make_post:219` is `community.last_active = g.site.last_active = utcnow()`, and `can_create_post` has its own `g.site` fallback at `:2508-2509` (`if not hasattr(g, 'site'): g.site = db.session.query(Site).get(1)`) -- but that fallback sits on the REMOTE-user `else` branch, which a local author never reaches. In production `g.site` is set by the `before_request` hook (`app/request_hooks.py:79`, the `@app.before_request` registered at `app/__init__.py:366`, populating `g.site` at `:95` for every request except `/inbox` and `/static/`); this harness dispatches no request for the SRC_API arm at all, and even the SRC_WEB arm's `web_ctx` only pushes a request context, not a real WSGI dispatch, so `before_request` never runs either way -- `g.site` must be supplied explicitly by the test fixture. (3) `notify_about_post` (imported at `:17`, called at `:239`) fires on the ordinary path: `:238`'s guard is `if post.status == POST_STATUS_PUBLISHED:`, which is the column default, and `tests/conftest.py:106` sets `task_always_eager=True`, so any Celery body inside it runs inline and synchronously rather than being silently swallowed by a queue nothing drains -- a naive first call pays for whatever that body does.
