### 2. `make_post` DUPLICATES `edit_post` in FOUR PLACES -- one finding, not four -- D455

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D455 | `app/shared/post.py:168-169`/`:173-179` against `:254`/`:256`,`:318`,`:321-327`; `:190-195` against `:565-569`; `:197-204` against `:461-468` | **Not a defect -- `make_post:231` passes `from_scratch=True` to `edit_post`, so all four duplicate ranges below always run on every call, and `make_post:183`'s own comment ("instead, make_post shares code with edit_post") states an intent the code only HALF-implements: the `:231` delegation is the sharing; these four blocks are the part that duplicates instead.** (a) **Title**, `:168` (SRC_API, bare `input['title']`) / `:173` (SRC_WEB, `.strip()`ped) against `edit_post:254` (`.strip()`ped) / `:318` (`.strip()`ped) -- recomputed by `edit_post`, then unconditionally overwritten onto the Post at `edit_post:395` (`post.title = title`). **CORRECTED AFTER THE FINAL WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW: the original text here said `make_post`'s own title is "visible nowhere in the finished row". That is WRONG, and it is wrong in the direction that makes a live line look dead.** `post.title` is indeed overwritten, but `make_post:224` calls `post.generate_ap_id(community)` ELEVEN LINES ABOVE the delegation, and that method slugifies the title (`app/models.py:2561`, `slug = slugify(self.title, max_length=...)`) into BOTH `post.ap_id` and `post.slug` (`:2563-2564`). `edit_post` never regenerates either. So `make_post`'s own title survives permanently in the post's public identity and URL, and `:224` is neither dead nor redundant -- it is the one place a duplicated value has a lasting effect. **How the error was made, because the shape recurs:** the analysis established that the title is recomputed downstream, concluded from that it was dead, and stopped reading at `:395` without looking at what ran between `:173` and `:231`. Showing a value is overwritten proves only that the LAST write wins, never that no read happened in between. The round's own mutation pass then skipped `:224` entirely, because the pass was scoped by the arc table and `:224` is a statement with no branch -- so nothing caught it until the final review read the function top to bottom. `:224` is now mutated and asserted: deleting it leaves `post.ap_id` as the 10-character `gibberish()` from `:207`, which tests on both arms now detect. (b) **Url**, `:169`/`:174-179` against `edit_post:256`/`:321-327` -- also recomputed; `make_post`'s local `url` never reaches the `Post` at all, since `:206-207`'s constructor call takes only `title` and `language_id` (`Post(user_id=..., community_id=..., instance_id=..., from_bot=..., posted_at=..., ap_id=..., title=title, language_id=language_id)`) with no `url=` keyword. (c) **Domain check**, `:190-195` against `:565-569` -- the guarded raise itself (`:194-195` / `:568-569`) is byte-identical text at identical indentation (`if domain.banned or domain.name.endswith('.pages.dev'): raise Exception(domain.name + ' is blocked by admin')`); only the OUTER guard's condition differs (`:190` bare `if url:` vs `:565` `if url and (from_scratch or url_changed):`). (d) **Extension check**, `:197-204` against `:461-468` -- **byte-identical including the comment** (`# check if this is an allowed type of file`), confirmed line-for-line. **The duplication is not merely redundant -- the domain and extension checks buy TIMING, at a real cost the other two ranges do not.** `make_post`'s copies refuse BEFORE `:206` creates anything; `edit_post`'s copies refuse AFTER `:209`/`:228` have already committed a Post and a PostVote, which `:233-235`'s `except` block must then explicitly delete. The title and url duplicates buy nothing at all -- their own values are thrown away downstream (title overwritten, url never used) -- so of the four, (c) and (d) buy timing, (a)'s title is read once at `:224` for the permanent `ap_id`/`slug` before being overwritten, and only (b)'s url is genuine waste -- computed, used solely to drive `:192`'s domain lookup, and never stored. | not a defect, registered (duplication, not a bug) | `app/shared/post.py:168-169,173-179,183,190-207,231,254,256,318,321-327,395,461-468,565-569` read this round; `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-12-coverage-post-d-37/task-2-report.md`, `task-3-report.md` |

### 4. THE `:165` AUTHORISATION HOLE -- THE SECOND CONSECUTIVE ROUND THE SAME MUTATION FOUND A REAL HOLE -- D457

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D457 | `app/shared/post.py:165` | **Registered as a general rule, cross-referencing D446(c)/D447 rather than repeating the lesson as a new instance.** Replacing `user = authorise_api_user(auth, return_type='model')` with a query that skips authorisation entirely (`user = User.query.order_by(User.id).first()`) SURVIVED all 29 tests in this file on first application. This is the SECOND CONSECUTIVE sub-project the identical mutation shape finds a real hole: sub-project 36's `restore_post:799` (`authorise_api_user(auth, id_match=post.user_id)` -> `post.user_id`, no authorisation) survived all 46 tests then in that file (**D446(c)**, general lesson **D447**). Both times, for the IDENTICAL reason: **every test authenticates as the permitted actor, so the suite asserts that the authorised path was TAKEN and nothing about authorisation having HAPPENED.** `s.author` is both the bearer-token holder in every `test_shared_post_make.py` test AND the first (in most, the only) row in the `User` table, so "return the first user" and "authorise the bearer" are indistinguishable against every existing fixture. Closed by `test_an_api_call_is_authorised_against_its_own_bearer_token`: a second, UNKEYED `intruder` user is created after `s.author` and given its own bearer token; real code identifies `intruder` via the token and `can_create_post` then refuses for a missing `private_key` (D454's blocker 1); the mutated code ignores the token and substitutes the keyed, first-row author instead, and the post would succeed. Re-mutated: fails this one test, 1/32. **The rule, stated generally so a third round does not have to rediscover it**: any test suite whose only authenticated actor is also the fixture's structurally-privileged default (first row, sole keyed user, etc.) cannot distinguish "authorisation ran" from "authorisation was skipped and a plausible default was substituted" -- a dedicated non-default, unprivileged, second identity is required to test authorisation AT ALL, not merely to test its refusal path. | closed; registered as a cross-referenced general rule (no new instance-lesson number) | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-12-coverage-post-d-37/task-6-report.md` (mutation M1, `:165`, and its closure); **D446(c)** and **D447** (sub-project 36's `restore_post:799` occurrence, cited rather than re-derived) |

### 5. The `try`/`except` at `:230-236` has NO branch arc -- D458

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D458 | `app/shared/post.py:230-236` | **Process finding, general lesson, not a defect.** coverage.py does not model `except` handlers as branches -- the `try:`/`except Exception as e:` at `:230`/`:232` contributes no arc to the branch count at all, so `:233` (`db.session.delete(vote)`), `:234` (`db.session.delete(post)`), `:235` (`db.session.commit()`) and `:236` (`raise e`) are four statements COUNTED in the statement total but INVISIBLE to the arc count -- a function can reach 26/26 arcs, as `make_post` now does, while its own exception handler has never been reached by anything. It was reached and tested here (`test_a_failing_edit_post_rolls_back_the_post_and_the_vote`, monkeypatching `post_module.edit_post` to raise; `test_a_failing_edit_post_re_raises_the_original_exception`, asserting the SAME exception object propagates), and mutation-verified (`:234`'s delete and `:236`'s `raise e` -> `pass` both KILLED by these two tests) -- but nothing in the arc-coverage number itself would have revealed their absence had they not been. **General lesson for every future round in this module or any other: full arc coverage of a function says nothing about its exception handlers.** A `try`/`except` block must be checked for tests by name, never inferred as covered from a 100% branch figure. | not a defect; general lesson | `app/shared/post.py:230-236` read this round; `tests/test_shared_post_make.py:908-964` (`test_a_failing_edit_post_rolls_back_the_post_and_the_vote`, `test_a_failing_edit_post_re_raises_the_original_exception`); `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-12-coverage-post-d-37/task-5-report.md` |

### 7. A void mutation is worse than a survivor -- D460

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D460 | `app/shared/post.py:226` | **Process finding, general lesson (an instance of fact 215's rule, applied to this round).** Deleting `:226`'s `vote = PostVote(user_id=user.id, post_id=post.id, author_id=user.id, effect=1)` outright leaves the name `vote` undefined at `:233`'s `db.session.delete(vote)`, which every path through the `except` block executes -- the result is an immediate `NameError: name 'vote' is not defined` cascading through 18 of this file's tests. Taken at face value, 18 failing tests reads as an overwhelming, convincing kill; it is not one, by fact 215's own test ("is the crash the test observing the thing the mutation changed?") -- a `NameError` from a missing local name is a Python-scoping accident, not evidence that any test noticed the PostVote row itself was never created. The viable non-crashing variant of the SAME fault -- keep `vote` bound to something, so nothing crashes, but stop a real `PostVote` row from being created -- was constructed and run separately (`vote = post`, which binds the name and lets `:227`'s `db.session.add(vote)` proceed harmlessly against an already-tracked object, without inserting a second `PostVote` row). That variant IS killed, by `test_creating_a_post_seeds_its_author_upvote`'s direct query (`votes = db.session.query(PostVote).filter_by(post_id=post.id).all(); assert len(votes) == 1`), so the underlying fault is genuinely covered despite the literal deletion's crash being uninformative. **The general lesson: a void mutation is worse than a survivor, because a survivor is a finding someone still has to act on, while a void crash-kill is scored as evidence the site is covered when it has proven nothing about the fault at all** -- 17 convincing-looking failures (this round's analogue of sub-project 35's single false kill, fact 215) is a bigger false signal than one honest survivor would have been. | closed (fault genuinely covered via the non-crashing variant); void crash discounted per fact 215 | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-12-coverage-post-d-37/task-6-report.md` (mutation #21/#21b, the 18-test `NameError` cascade and the `vote = post` non-crashing re-run); `tests/test_shared_post_make.py:859-880` (`test_creating_a_post_seeds_its_author_upvote`); `tests/README.md` fact 215 |

### 10. `make_post`'s rollback does not roll back -- the post counts survive a failed create -- D463

| id | where | what | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D463 | `app/shared/post.py:218`, `:220`, `:228`, `:233-236` | **A REAL DEFECT, found by the final whole-branch review after seven tasks and eight reviews had read the same `except` block.** `:218` does `community.post_count += 1` and `:220` does `user.post_count += 1`. `:228` commits them. If `edit_post` then raises at `:231`, the handler at `:233-235` deletes the `PostVote` and the `Post` and commits -- **and never decrements either counter.** So every `make_post` that fails inside `edit_post` permanently inflates both the community's and the author's post count, by one, for a post that does not exist. The same block leaves `:219`'s `community.last_active`, `:221`'s `user.last_seen` and `:222`'s `user.ip_address` un-reverted too, though those are activity timestamps whose wrongness is self-correcting; the counts are not -- they are displayed, and `:215` feeds `ranking_scaled` off `community.scale_by()`, which reads `post_count`. **NOT FIXED THIS ROUND**, and the restraint is deliberate: the fix is to move the counter increments below the delegation, or to decrement them in the handler, and reordering a commit boundary is a production change well outside a coverage round's remit. It is registered so the next person to touch this function inherits it. **Why nobody caught it:** Task 5 wrote two tests for this handler and mutated it twice, and both tests assert what the handler DELETES -- `Post.count() == 0`, `PostVote.count() == 0`. Neither asks what it LEAVES BEHIND. A rollback test that only checks the rows that vanished cannot see a row that should have changed back and did not. The general form is worth carrying: **when testing a compensating action, assert the full prior state is restored, not merely that the thing created is gone.** | **open, registered, not fixed** | `app/shared/post.py:206-236` read top to bottom at `4cdfdfc0`; `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-12-coverage-post-d-37/final-review.md` MAJOR 1; `app/models.py:866` (`Community.scale_by`) for the ranking dependency |

### 2. A PRODUCTION DEFECT: the original upload file is never unlinked when a format is configured -- ONE site, not three (corrected) -- D465

| id | where | what | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D465 | `app/shared/post.py:487,527,531,563`; `app/activitypub/util.py:1864-1872,1893` (medium) and `:1911-1919,1941` (thumbnail) | **A REAL DEFECT, found because a test asserted a file count and got two.** `edit_post:487` saves the original upload to `<name><original_ext>`. THE ORIGINAL TEXT BELOW CLAIMED THREE SITES. THERE IS ONE.** The `make_image_sizes_async` sites do NOT leak, and the reason is the precondition rather than the shape: at `:1868` the `medium_image` being saved is an IN-MEMORY object, derived by `Image.open` on the caller's file and thumbnailed at `:1862`, and it is saved exactly once, at `:1872`, to whatever `final_place` then holds. There is no earlier `.save()` to the pre-rewrite path, so rewriting the variable orphans nothing that function created. `:1915` is the same story for the thumbnail. Only `edit_post:527` has a genuine prior write behind it -- `:487` -- which is what makes it a leak.

**How the error was made, because it is this campaign's most persistent shape.** The duplication between `edit_post:524-531` and these two sites is real and is registered as D466: same `kwargs` dict, same format and quality gates, same `os.path.splitext` rewrite, same `optimize=True` save. From that resemblance the controller inferred the defect travelled with it, and wrote 'three sites' without checking whether a prior save existed at the other two. **Shape similarity is not behavioural equivalence**; the defect here is not the rewrite, it is the rewrite AFTER an earlier write to the old path, and only one of the three has that. The next round inherits one fix target, not three. The original three-site text is kept below so the inference and its correction stay visible.

ORIGINAL TEXT, WRONG: **The identical shape exists at two more sites in `make_image_sizes_async`** (`app/activitypub/util.py:1733`, reached from `edit_post` via `make_image_sizes` at `:614`/`:616`): `:1868` rewrites `final_place` for the medium image and `:1915` rewrites `final_place_thumbnail` for the thumbnail, neither preceded by an unlink of the pre-rewrite path; each function's own S3 branch (`:1893`, `:1941`) unlinks only the NEW path, exactly mirroring `edit_post:563`. The original text then concluded, WRONGLY, that the defect fires at THREE sites per upload that both (a) configures a non-default `MEDIA_IMAGE_FORMAT`/`medium_image_format`/`thumbnail_image_format` and (b) produces a medium/thumbnail size -- every such upload leaks more than once. **NOT FIXED THIS ROUND** -- deliberate restraint, the remedy (unlink the pre-rewrite path, or reuse it in place) is a production change outside a coverage round's remit. | **open, registered, not fixed** | `app/shared/post.py:485-531,563` (`awk` in `task-4-report.md` and `task-5-report.md`); `app/activitypub/util.py:1864-1872,1893,1911-1919,1941` (`awk` in `task-5-report.md` fix-round-1); `tests/test_shared_post_upload.py` (`test_media_image_format_avif_imports_pillow_avif_a_second_time`, `test_a_configured_format_rewrites_the_saved_extension`) |

### 4. `:503` mutates `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` process-wide and never restores it -- D467

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D467 | `app/shared/post.py:503` | **`Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = 89478485` is a module-level PIL class attribute, not scoped to the current request or thread.** **Corrected after the final review: `89478485` is Pillow's OWN default**, so the assignment does not widen the ceiling on a stock install and the hazard is narrower than this entry first implied. What it does is CLOBBER any narrowed ceiling a deployment or an earlier test set -- a site that lowered the limit deliberately has it silently restored to default by the first upload, and a test that narrows it is poisoned for the rest of the process. Once any upload reaches this line, the process-wide decompression-bomb ceiling changes for every subsequent `PIL.Image.open` call for the rest of the process's life -- there is no matching restore anywhere in `edit_post` or elsewhere in the module. The mutation pass's own `503` row (`89478485`->`9`) produced a real, legitimate crash-kill (`DecompressionBombError`, 24 tests) precisely because the line does what it says -- confirming the line is reached and load-bearing, not that the missing-restore is safe. Tests in this suite avoid being poisoned by ordering only because they never rely on a specific `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` value; a future test asserting a DecompressionBombError from a large-but-legitimate image could pass or fail depending on what upload test ran earlier in the same process. NOT FIXED -- a global PIL setting change is outside a coverage round's remit; registered so the next person who adds an image-size-dependent test inherits the hazard. | open, registered, not fixed | `app/shared/post.py:503` (`task-1-report.md`, `task-6-report.md` citations); `task-7-report.md` mutation row `503` (`DecompressionBombError`, 24 failures, "legitimate -- this is the mechanism working as designed") |

### 1. The pixelfed host match diverges between `:404` and `:619`, and the scheme-less disjunct is REACHABLE -- D478

| id | where | what | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D478 | `app/shared/post.py:403-404` and `:619` | **Two pixelfed classifiers in one function disagree about what a pixelfed url looks like, and the difference is not cosmetic.** `:404` is `if post.url.startswith('https://pixelfed.social/') or post.url.startswith('https://pixelfed.uno/'):` -- scheme AND trailing slash on both disjuncts. `:619` is `elif url.startswith('https://pixelfed.social') or url.startswith('pixelfed.uno'):` -- **no trailing slash on the first, and no scheme at all on the second.** So `pixelfed.uno/p/bob/2`, submitted without a scheme, is typed `POST_TYPE_IMAGE` by `:619` and is NOT matched by `:404`; and `https://pixelfed.socialite.example/x` matches `:619`'s first disjunct but not `:404`'s. **THE SCHEME-LESS DISJUNCT IS REACHABLE, probed rather than argued.** For a scheme-less url with no registered route, `httpx` raises `httpx.UnsupportedProtocol`; that class **IS** an `httpx.HTTPError` (MRO measured in the container: `UnsupportedProtocol -> TransportError -> RequestError -> HTTPError`), so `mime_type_using_head`'s handler at `app/utils.py:345` catches it and returns `''`, `is_image_url` falls through to extension sniffing, finds no image extension in `pixelfed.uno/p/1`, and returns `False`. `:601` is therefore not taken and control reaches `:619`. Measured output: `startswith 'https://pixelfed.uno/' -> False`, `startswith 'pixelfed.uno' -> True`, `is_image_url -> False`, `UnsupportedProtocol is HTTPError -> True`. **AND THE TWO SITES READ DIFFERENT VARIABLES AT DIFFERENT POINTS IN THE FUNCTION.** `:403`/`:404` read `post.url` -- the value ALREADY ON THE ROW, before this edit's url is applied. `:619` reads the local `url` -- the value BEING SUBMITTED. A post whose stored url is scheme-less keeps whatever type `:404` failed to assign, while a submission of the same string gets `POST_TYPE_IMAGE`. **REGISTERED, NOT FIXED.** `:619`'s disjunct is reachable, so this is not dead code that can be deleted without thought, and which of the two patterns is correct -- whether pixelfed urls should be accepted without a scheme at all, and whether the trailing slash is load-bearing against lookalike hosts -- is a product question a coverage round has no standing to answer. What is new here is the ID-VERSUS-NAME divergence and what it does to this suite's fixtures.** `Site.admins()` filters on `user_role.c.role_id == ROLE_ADMIN`, and `app/constants.py:81` is `ROLE_ADMIN = 4` -- a ROLE ID. `User.is_admin()` iterates `self.roles` and tests `role.name == 'Admin'` -- a ROLE NAME. ### 7. `wc -l` IS NOT A MUTATION TRIPWIRE. `git diff --quiet -- app/` is -- D484

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D484 | the campaign's own hygiene check, applied to a mutation pass | **The campaign's standing line-count check is structurally blind to exactly the edit shape a mutation run produces, and this round proved it by leaving a live mutant in production code across two turn boundaries.** Every mutation applied in this round's pass is a **single-line replacement** -- `sed`-style substitution of one expression for another on one line. The line count is therefore INVARIANT under it: `wc -l app/shared/post.py` read `1193`, the expected value, for the whole of a ~26-minute window during which `app/shared/post.py` carried a live `:654` mutant while the implementer ended turns waiting on a background run. Nothing in the hygiene protocol could have flagged it. **`git diff --quiet -- app/ && echo CLEAN` is the load-bearing check** -- it is sensitive to any change at all, including a one-character one, and it is cheap. `wc -l` remains a useful SECOND signal (it catches a bungled multi-line restore, a truncation, a stray paste) and is **not a substitute**. Nothing in the tree needed repairing -- the sweep script's own restore step ran and the controller independently verified CLEAN -- so this is registered for the protocol, not for the damage. The rule now carried in the code, in `TestGenericOpengraphArm`'s class docstring beside the mutation table where the next person running mutants will be standing: restore from a pristine copy immediately after each run, and gate on `git diff --quiet -- app/` before stopping, reporting or committing. | registered; the check is now stated in the test file, not only in a report | `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-12-coverage-post-e2-39/task-7-report.md` §12; `tests/test_shared_post_url.py` (`TestGenericOpengraphArm` docstring) |

### 12. AN "ONLY OCCURRENCE" ABSOLUTE IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE GREP PATTERN THAT ESTABLISHED IT -- D489

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D489 | `tests/test_shared_post_url.py:643` (the raw-SQL write) vs a grep written for ORM attribute assignment | **A docstring asserted that one line was the only place in the suite that set `post.image_id` to a dangling value, and the grep that established it could not see the counterexample sitting in the same file.** The counterexample is `db.session.execute(text('UPDATE post SET image_id = 999999 WHERE id = :pid'), ...)` -- **raw SQL**, which a pattern written for ORM attribute assignment (`\.image_id\s*=`) does not match in any useful form. The raw-SQL form exists precisely because the ORM form cannot work here: `post.image_id = 999999; commit()` raises `ForeignKeyViolation` before the code under test is reached, so the test disables the constraint path by writing through SQL instead. **The instrument for an "only occurrence" claim is a grep PLUS A READ, and the grep is only as good as its pattern.** The specific trap: the alternative spelling of a database write (raw SQL, `bulk_update_mappings`, `Table.update()`, a fixture factory, a migration) is invisible to a pattern derived from the spelling you happen to be looking at -- and it is most likely to exist exactly where the ordinary spelling fails, which is where the interesting test lives. The round's framing was softened from "re-tested" to "re-checked" on this finding. **Generalise it to every absolute in a docstring: an "only", a "never", a "nothing else" is a claim about a SEARCH, and the search's pattern belongs in the citation.** | registered; the absolute was softened rather than re-established | `tests/test_shared_post_url.py:643`, `:651-652`; `.superpowers/sdd/2026-09-12-coverage-post-e2-39/progress.md` (the ruling on row 49) |

### 1. `restore_reply` does not mirror `delete_reply` -- two counters are decremented and never restored -- D496

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D496 | `app/shared/reply.py:251-255` vs `:279-281` | **A REAL DEFECT, registered not fixed, and PINNED BY A TEST THAT ASSERTS THE WRONG NUMBERS ON PURPOSE.** `delete_reply` decrements four counters -- `reply.post.reply_count` (`:252`), `reply.post.reply_count_cross_posted` (`:253`) and `reply.community.post_reply_count` (`:254`), all three inside `if not reply.author.bot:` (`:251`), plus `reply.author.post_reply_count` (`:255`) outside it. `restore_reply` increments **two**: `reply.post.reply_count` (`:280`, inside its own `if not reply.author.bot:` at `:279`) and `reply.author.post_reply_count` (`:281`). The strings `reply_count_cross_posted` and `community.post_reply_count` do not appear anywhere in `restore_reply`'s body. **A delete-then-restore cycle therefore leaves both counters one lower than it found them, and every further cycle loses one more.** The asymmetry is confined to the bot-guarded block: `:255` and `:281` mirror each other exactly, which is why a test pinning this must read `post.reply_count`, `post.reply_count_cross_posted` and `community.post_reply_count` and must NOT read `author.post_reply_count`, which would witness nothing. **Same shape as D463** (`make_post`'s failure handler incrementing two counters at `app/shared/post.py:218`/`:220` and never decrementing them on the rollback path) and **the local, non-federated form of D200**, whose federated half is `app/activitypub/util.py:2237-2298`; D200's cell already names this pair and calls it "the sharper form of the finding", but at reading level only -- this round is the first to execute it. Not fixed for D200's reasons, which have not changed: correcting a counter changes numbers users already see, the historical drift is unmeasurable from the rows that survive, and the federated pair would have to move in the same commit for the fix to mean anything | **FIXED in sub-project 42 task 7** -- `restore_reply`, `mod_remove_reply` and `mod_restore_reply` each gained `reply.post.reply_count_cross_posted` and `reply.community.post_reply_count` inside their existing `if not reply.author.bot:` guard, six statements in all, so all four functions now move the same four counters. THE DIRECTION WAS SETTLED BY `app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py`, which recomputes `community.post_reply_count` as `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM post_reply WHERE deleted is false and community_id = :community_id`: the column means the number of non-deleted replies, so a delete must decrement it and a restore must increment it, and `delete_reply` was the one function already correct. `reply_count_cross_posted` is derived from `reply_count` at `app/models.py:3099-3108`, so the two step together. The three tests that pinned the old behaviour were inverted in the same commit, each renamed because its old name was itself a claim; every one of the six new statements is killed by exactly one test, measured line-scoped. THE FEDERATED TWIN MOVED IN THE SAME TASK, under Ruling 17: `restore_post_or_comment`'s `PostReply` branch in `app/activitypub/util.py` carried the identical defect, and fixing the local half alone would have created the one-twin repair D520 registers as invisible. Both halves are now symmetric with their own delete. IT DID: sub-project 42 task 7 inverted that test and renamed it `..._a_delete_restore_cycle_returns_all_three_counters_to_level` |

### 2. A REACHABLE PRODUCTION 500 in both `delete_reply` and `restore_reply`, from a one-element `path` -- and the `path` column has FIVE writers, not four -- D497

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D497 | `app/shared/reply.py:256-258` and `:282-284`; `app/cli.py:664-670`, `:694`, `:715`; `app/api/alpha/views.py:669-687`, `:734-735`; `app/cli.py:1929`, `:1934` | **FIXED on branch `blentz`, after the coverage round closed -- see D517.** **A REACHABLE PRODUCTION 500, registered not fixed, NOT pinned by a test and deliberately so.** `:256-258` executes `update post_reply set child_count = child_count - 1 where id in :parents` with `{'parents': tuple(reply.path[:-1])}`; `:282-284` is the same statement with one character changed (`- 1` to `+ 1`). **A one-element `path` makes `reply.path[:-1]` an EMPTY tuple, psycopg2 renders `where id in ()`, and it raises** -- measured in the container against the live test database (sqlalchemy 2.0.52, `postgresql+psycopg2`) with `:257`'s own statement text: `(1, 2)` and `(1,)` both run and return no rows, `()` raises `ProgrammingError: (psycopg2.errors.SyntaxError) syntax error at or near ")"`. The `if reply.path:` guards at `:256`/`:282` do not help -- a one-element list is truthy. **The one-element path is reachable in production.** `@app.cli.command("lemmy-import")` (`app/cli.py:275`) builds `piefed_path` at `:664-670` from `path_parts[1:-1]` -- ANCESTORS ONLY, the reply's own id excluded, `'0'` filtered out by `:667` and unmapped ancestors by `:669` -- and writes it at `:694` and `:715`. For a first-level nested comment whose Lemmy ltree path is `0.<parent>.<self>` AND whose parent was mapped, `path_parts[1:-1]` is `['<parent>']`, so `path == [parent_id]` and both statements raise. **The scope is every imported reply that ends up with EXACTLY ONE mapped ancestor, which is broader than the first-level case and was first stated too narrowly here.** A top-level comment (`0.<self>`) yields `[]` and a first-level one whose parent is unmapped also yields `[]`, and both are falsy and merely skip the update -- but a DEEPER comment also raises when exactly one of its ancestors is mapped: for `0.A.B.<self>`, `path_parts[1:-1]` is `['A', 'B']` and `:669`'s `if piefed_ancestor_id:` drops whichever of A or B is absent from `lemmy_to_piefed_comment`, leaving one element. The original wording said the scope was "exactly" the mapped-parent first-level case; that UNDERSTATES the reach and is corrected here rather than silently replaced. **So on any instance that has run `flask lemmy-import`, the author of an imported first-level reply with a mapped parent can neither delete nor restore it.** **It does not self-heal.** `calculate_path` (`app/api/alpha/views.py:669-687`) would rewrite a broken row into the right convention, but its only call site is `:735`, guarded at `:734` by `if not reply.path:` -- and a one-element path is TRUTHY, so the repair never fires on exactly the rows that need it. **The remedy exists and is the FIFTH writer**: `flask populate_post_reply_for_api` (`app/cli.py:1906`) rebuilds every path from the `parent_id` chain unconditionally, raw SQL at `:1929`, committed at `:1934`. **Any statement of this defect that names the 500 without naming that command is worth less than one that names both.** Not pinned by a test because reaching it needs a row shaped by the cli importer, which no factory in `tests/factories.py` produces and which a unit test of `delete_reply` has no business simulating. **WHY IT IS NOT FIXED, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO THE BLANKET NO-PRODUCTION-CHANGE POLICY, because this is the only live defect in the round whose disposition would otherwise rest on that policy alone.** Unlike D499, D500 and D501 this entry carries NO behavioural trade-off -- the crash is unambiguous and a guard changes nothing for a correctly-shaped row -- so "it is a product decision" is not the reason here and must not be read as one. The reason is SCOPE: a real fix is not a guard at `:256`/`:282` but a correction of the convention divergence, and that means moving D498's nine `tuple(path[:-1])` sites together, plus deciding whether the importer or the readers are wrong. A guard at two of the nine sites leaves the other seven silently miscounting and makes the codebase harder to reason about, not easier. That is beyond a coverage round, and it is what makes register-not-fix correct for D497 rather than the policy. **THE METHOD NOTE IS THE DURABLE HALF: there are FIVE writers of `PostReply.path`, and the fifth is raw SQL and is structurally invisible to an attribute grep.** The first enumeration in this round used `grep -rn "\.path\b" --include=*.py app/` filtered by `grep -E "\.path\s*=\|path=\|\.path\["`, found four, and called itself complete. `app/cli.py:1929` DOES appear in the unfiltered grep -- it contains `reply_path.path` -- and the hand filter discarded it, because `SET path =` has a space before the `=` and no dot before `path`. The enumeration that holds is two methods that fail differently: an AST walk over attribute assignments and `path=` keywords (finds 1-4, cannot reach raw SQL by construction), plus an AST walk over string constants containing both `post_reply` and `path` filtered for `update`/`insert` (finds 5). Cross-references **D489**, the same shape one round earlier | **not fixed, registered; REACHABLE, not latent; not pinned** | all nine cited spans re-derived with numbered output at `5543f6ca`. The five writers: (1) `app/models.py:3053-3059`, the ActivityPub/web creator -- top-level `[0, reply.id]`, nested `in_reply_to.path[:] + [reply.id]`, always >= 2, corroborated independently by `:3060`'s `reply.root_id = reply.path[1]` which would IndexError on anything shorter; (2) `app/cli.py:694` and `:715`, the importer, the only writer that can emit one element; (3) `app/api/alpha/views.py:686` via `calculate_path`, always >= 2, cleared; (4) `app/post/util.py:79` in `create_real_reply` (`:53`), whose own comment at `:54` says "Create a PostReply instance (not persisted to DB)" and whose file contains no `db.session.add`, no `flush` and no `commit` at all (a grep for all three over `app/post/util.py` returns nothing) -- the only non-persisting writer, cleared; the test file's docstring used to put that comment one line late at `:55` and was corrected to `:54` in the round's final fix wave, so the citation is no longer divergent; (5) `app/cli.py:1929`, a recursive CTE with base `ARRAY[0, id]` and step `rp.path \|\| pr.id`, always >= 2, cleared, and the remedy. The psycopg2 raise was EXECUTED, not read. `tests/test_shared_reply_interactions.py`'s `TestDeleteReply` class docstring carries the probe in full and `TestRestoreReply`'s points at it |

### 3. The persisting `path` writers disagree on the convention, so `path[:-1]` means different things depending on who wrote the row -- D498

Under `'reversal'` both first conjuncts are false, so **neither `can_upvote` nor `can_downvote` is consulted at all** and control reaches `:30`, `:33` and `reply.vote()` with no permission check. A community-banned voter, or a bot (refused by `can_upvote` at `app/utils.py:2481` and by `can_downvote` at `:2437`), can send `score: 0` and undo their existing vote. **The narrowing is part of the finding and must travel with it**: a reversal reaches a vote only when one already exists, because `PostReply.vote` remaps it at `app/models.py:3316` only `if existing_vote` and `:3321` then asserts the direction is `'upvote'` or `'downvote'`. So the gates are bypassed for UNDOING a vote, not for casting one. **THREE EXTENSIONS, all of them found by the round's review rather than by the original finding, and the entry is incomplete without them.** (i) **The emoji channel.** The gate-free call forwards `emoji` too: `post_reply_like` reads `data['emoji']` at `app/api/alpha/utils/reply.py:434` and passes it at `:444`, and the remapped reversal lands on `app/models.py:3325-3331` -- an early `return None` that rewrites `existing_vote.emoji` and commits.
```
app/activitypub/routes.py:2438:                votes_cast_today(user.id) <= current_app.config['VOTE_QUOTA']:
app/activitypub/routes.py:2459:                votes_cast_today(user.id) <= current_app.config['VOTE_QUOTA']:
app/shared/post.py:53:    if votes_cast_today(user.id) > current_app.config['VOTE_QUOTA']:
app/shared/reply.py:33:    if votes_cast_today(user.id) > current_app.config['VOTE_QUOTA']:
app/user/routes.py:127:        vote_quota_used = votes_cast_today(user.id) / current_app.config['VOTE_QUOTA']
```

**FOUR of them enforce the boundary.** `:33` and `:53` spell it `> N` as a REFUSAL; `app/activitypub/routes.py:2438` and `:2459` spell it `<= N` as a PERMISSION, inside `process_upvote` and `process_downvote`, each guarding a direct `liked.vote()` call on the federation inbox path. `> N` refusing and `<= N` permitting are the SAME boundary written two ways, so all four agree and **all four carry the same off-by-one**; a fix that moves only the two `>` sites leaves federated votes on the old boundary. The fifth, `app/user/routes.py:127`, is a division for a display percentage and enforces nothing. So this is a CONSISTENT off-by-one across FOUR enforcement sites, not a divergence. Every other twin finding in this module (D499, D500(ii), D406) is the two copies DISAGREEING; this one is the two copies agreeing on the same wrong boundary. That is a different defect shape and a different fix: a divergence is repaired by making one side match the other, and there is no correct side here to copy from -- all four must change together, and changing a subset alone manufactures the divergence. Not fixed because tightening a quota changes behaviour users already depend on. **THE METHOD NOTE IS WORTH MORE THAN THE OPERATOR, AND IT IS D497'S OWN, REPEATING INSIDE THE ENTRY THAT CITES IT:** a filtered grep that finds N and is then described as "exactly N" is an enumeration only over the paths it was given. This entry's original two-site claim was run by the controller by hand, credited in this very column as mechanical, and still wrong -- being run mechanically makes a search reproducible, not complete. **Re-derive an inherited premise with a SECOND METHOD THAT FAILS DIFFERENTLY, never a second grep of the same shape.** Two environment facts belong with it: the interactive `grep` here is a `ugrep` wrapper carrying `--ignore-files`, which silently skips anything a `.gitignore` excludes (`/usr/bin/grep` does not), and the same sweep that caught this one also found the round's `:555-561` route span surviving in four places in the spent plan | not fixed, registered; PINNED | `app/shared/reply.py:33` and `app/shared/post.py:53` read with numbered output at `5543f6ca`; `app/activitypub/routes.py:2434-2462` read with numbered output at `e4d1e18e`. The original two-site grep was run by the controller mechanically rather than left to this entry to assert, **and was under-inclusive anyway** -- the correction above is the full-tree re-derivation. Pinned by `TestVoteForReplyGuardsAndReturns::test_a_voter_exactly_at_the_vote_quota_is_still_allowed_through`, which sets `VOTE_QUOTA` to **0** against a `votes_cast_today` of 0 and asserts the vote LANDS (`up_votes == 1` and a `PostReplyVote` row) -- 0 is not strictly greater than 0, so `:33` is false and N = 0 permits one vote. The refusal side is `test_a_user_over_the_vote_quota_is_refused_with_429`, which sets `VOTE_QUOTA` to **-1**. **Note the method, which differs from `tests/README.md` fact 209's:** both tests move the BOUNDARY with `monkeypatch.setitem(app.config, 'VOTE_QUOTA', ...)` rather than moving the COUNT by writing the Redis key, which is safe on the session-scoped `app` fixture because monkeypatch restores it at teardown, and which makes the boundary pair cost no Redis teardown at all. `_clear_votes_cast` is still mandatory in the boundary test, because a vote completes there, and is correctly absent from the 429 test, where none does |

### 12. 29 security-scanner false positives across the campaign, and the rule that settles them -- D507

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D507 | the campaign's security-scanner reports; `app/shared/reply.py` during task 7's mutation window | **A process finding with one durable rule.** Twenty-nine security-scanner reports have fired across this campaign and every one was a false positive; five of them fired during sub-project 40's task 7, inside the window in which mutated production code was sitting in the working tree. Each was verified against `git show HEAD:<file>` rather than against the finding text or the tree, HEAD was correct every time, and no mutant ever reached a commit. **The rule: DURING A MUTATION WINDOW, HEAD IS THE ARTIFACT, NOT THE TREE.** A scanner, a reviewer, or a second agent reading the working tree during a mutation pass is reading deliberately broken code and will report it as a defect; the only question worth answering is what `git show HEAD:` says. This also states the limit of the scanners' value on this campaign in the other direction: **the same five scanner runs that found twenty-nine non-defects did not find D500, a live permission bypass in the file they were scanning.** A mutation operator found it. Cross-references **D484**, which established that `git diff --quiet -- app/` and not `wc -l` is the mutation tripwire | process finding, registered | the 29 are the campaign's own count across its reports; the 5 in task 7's window were each re-verified against `git show HEAD:` at the time |

### 13. Sweep the ACCOUNT, not just the artifact -- D508

| # | site | defect | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D508 | the round's reporting discipline | **A silently-fixed defect is invisible to the register.** When a round fixes something in passing -- a docstring corrected, a claim withdrawn, a count reconciled -- the artifact ends up right and the ACCOUNT of how it got there ends up missing, so the register records a state rather than a correction and the next round cannot tell a fact that was always true from one that was wrong for four tasks. The rule: at the end of a round, sweep the account as well as the artifact, and register what CHANGED, not only what IS. Sub-project 40 produced three instances in one round -- the retracted `:48` equivalence claim, the withdrawn "the docstring now matches" verification, and the `:275`/`:247` mislabel -- and in each case the fixed artifact carried no trace of the error | process finding, registered | the round's task 7 report, its two fix rounds and their reviews |

### 14. Re-derive an inherited premise with a SECOND METHOD THAT FAILS DIFFERENTLY -- D509

### 19. THE BRANCH WENT BACK AND FIXED TWO OF ITS OWN REGISTERED DEFECTS -- D517

The coverage round that found D497, D498 and D500 registered all three rather
than repairing them, on the standing reasoning that changing production
behaviour is a product decision a coverage round has no standing to make.
**That reasoning was overruled by the repository's owner, who asked for both
defects fixed.** This entry records what was done, because a register whose
"open" entries are silently closed elsewhere is worse than no register: the
campaign's own process finding 1 is *sweep the account, not just the artifact*
-- a silently-fixed defect is invisible to the register.

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D517 | `app/cli.py:664-682`; the nine `tuple(path[:-1])` guards; `app/shared/reply.py:26-39`; `app/shared/post.py:39-50`; `app/models.py:2742-2747`, `:3326-3331` | **FOUR CHANGES, TEST-DRIVEN, EACH WITH A FAILING TEST PASTED BEFORE THE FIX.** **(1) D497/D498's root cause, in the importer.** `app/cli.py` built `piefed_path` from the mapped ancestors ALONE -- no leading `0` sentinel, no reply id -- so a first-level nested comment got a ONE-ELEMENT path, `tuple(path[:-1])` became the EMPTY tuple, psycopg2 rendered `where id in ()` and Postgres raised. The array is now `[0] + piefed_ancestors + [row.id]`, matching `app/models.py:3053-3060`'s convention exactly: top-level `[0, id]` at depth 0, one level down `[0, root, id]` at depth 1. `depth` is computed from `piefed_ancestors` and `root_id` by the existing code, so **neither changes**; the edit is confined to `path`. **(2) The same defect's defence, at all nine sites.** Every one carried the byte-identical guard `if X.path:`; each is now `if X.path and len(X.path) > 1:`, which makes rows ALREADY WRITTEN by an earlier import non-fatal. A path with no ancestors has nothing to decrement, so skipping is the correct outcome, not a workaround. **(3) D500's bypass, in both twins at once.** `'reversal'` names no permission of its own, so gating it on a direction literal is impossible; the new arm RESOLVES THE EXISTING VOTE and requires the permission that would have cast it -- `can_upvote` for an `effect` above zero, `can_downvote` for one below. **`app/shared/post.py` got the identical arm in the same change**, because a fix landing in one twin alone would have manufactured exactly the mirrored-pair divergence this file registers as a defect class. **(4) The `-O` amplification.** `app/models.py:2742` and `:3326` were `assert vote_direction == 'upvote' or ...`. Asserts vanish under `python -O`, and in `PostReply.vote` that assert is what stops a reversal with no existing vote from reaching the else-branch and casting a NEW downvote past the caller's gates. Both are now explicit `raise ValueError`. **THE CHOSEN DISPOSITION HAS A COST AND IT IS STATED HERE RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER: a user the community bans AFTER they voted can no longer withdraw those votes.** Gating on the matching permission was chosen deliberately over allowing withdrawal outright; the alternative was rejected, not overlooked. | **FIXED**; D497, D498 and D500 closed. ### 10. A LINE CAN BE MUTATED, KILLED, AND STILL BE UNGUARDED IN EVERY OTHER RESPECT -- D529

| D529 | the round's own mutation pass | **THE NARROWING IS THE FINDING, NOT THE EIGHT MUTANTS.** The pass first reported 12 continuation lines where 20 exist, excluding the `add_to_modlog` argument lines silently -- not as a judgement that they were cosmetic, but as an unexamined narrowing, and the report then presented the narrowed figure AS the space. All 8 of the excluded `add_to_modlog` lines survived. **AND THE REPORTED FIGURES WERE THEMSELVES WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, WHICH SUB-PROJECT 41's FINAL FIX WAVE CORRECTED HERE AND IN THE TEST FILE'S DOCSTRING**: the "12 continuation lines" were 11 applied, so **nine** of the 20 went unmutated rather than eight -- `:572`, `targets=targets_data)`, the last line of `choose_answer`'s `Notification(...)` call, is not an `add_to_modlog` line and so fell outside the pattern that found the other eight, and unlike them it DIES against the notification test; and the "151 mutants" were **150 of the 159 plus one supernumerary**, `A426b`, a second mutant on statement line `:426`. The two errors offset, which is why the 138/21 stage figure was right anyway and why nothing downstream caught either. **THAT IS THE SHARPEST VERSION OF THIS ENTRY'S OWN RULE: a reconciling total is not evidence that its addends are right**, and a narrowed denominator can be wrong in the reported count as well as in its scope. **Six more were hidden the same way and were not continuation lines at all**: `target_user` and `reason` share `:437`, `:473` and `:506` with the action literal, whose mutant died -- and a dead mutant on a line makes the whole line LOOK interrogated. ### 16. INDENTATION IS LOAD-BEARING EVIDENCE, AND AN `awk` FIELD ASSIGNMENT DESTROYS IT -- D536

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D536 | the measurement-block checklist | **A near-miss in Task 9, recorded because it would have produced a confidently wrong register entry -- and the first version of THIS entry misnamed the culprit, which is recorded too, because naming the wrong tool is the damaging half.** Re-deriving D522 meant counting which counter statements sit inside `if not reply.author.bot:`. The pipeline in use rendered all four at the same apparent depth, so `delete_reply` read as moving four counters inside the guard and `mod_remove_reply` two, against the controller's inherited three and one. The inherited figure is right: `:269` and `:429` are dedented and outside the guard. **THE CULPRIT IS NOT `cat -n`.** `sed -n 'A,Bp' file \| cat -n` preserves every column -- `cat -A` on its output shows `     1^I    if not reply.author.bot:` and `     2^I        reply.post.reply_count -= 1`, four spaces against eight, intact. **What destroys the indentation is the downstream `awk '{n=$1+OFFSET; $1=""; printf ...}'`.** In awk, **assigning to ANY field rebuilds `$0` from the fields joined by a single `OFS`**, so every run of leading and interior whitespace collapses to one space. The offset arithmetic is what triggers it; the numbering tool is innocent. **The finding stands and the remedy changes.** `cat -n` is safe -- keep it. `awk 'NR>=A && NR<=B {printf "%d\|%s\n", NR, $0}'` is safe, because it prints `$0` without ever assigning to a field. Any awk that writes to `$1` or rebuilds `$0` is not, whatever it is piped to. **And the checklist gains a question, which is the transferable part**: (c) "does any OTHER line in the same paste contradict it" cannot fire when the rendering removed the contradicting evidence before you read it. So **(d) -- does this rendering preserve everything the claim depends on?** For any claim about control flow, scope or block membership in an indentation-significant language, the answer is no unless the pipeline preserves columns. | **process finding, register-bound; proposed addition to the measurement-block checklist** | The mechanism was established by running `sed -n '265,269p' app/shared/reply.py \| cat -n \| cat -A` (columns intact) against the same input through the field-assigning awk (columns gone), at `cee27b84`. D522's and D523's figures are stated from the column-preserving form |

### 2. THE COUNTER REPAIR LANDED, AND TWO RESIDUALS SURVIVE IT -- D543, D544

**D523, D522, D496 and D200 are all marked FIXED in their own cells above**
(sub-projects 40 and 41 and, for D200, sub-project 12). The evidence that
settled the DIRECTION is the same for every one of them and is recorded here
once: **`app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:314-316` recomputes
`community.post_reply_count` as
`SELECT COUNT(*) as c FROM post_reply WHERE deleted is false and community_id
= :community_id`**, run daily by `update_community_stats`
(`app/shared/tasks/maintenance.py:284`, dispatched from `app/cli.py:848`,
`:873` and `:925`). **The column means "the number of non-deleted replies."** A
delete must therefore decrement it and a restore must increment it, and of the
four functions in the family `delete_reply` was the one already correct -- so
the three that moved neither extra counter were wrong, and the repair adds
rather than removes. `post.reply_count_cross_posted` is DERIVED:
`app/models.py:3099-3108` recomputes it as `sum(Post.reply_count)` across the
cross-post set, or as `post.reply_count` when there is no set, so decrementing
it by one alongside `reply_count` preserves the invariant instead of guessing
at it. **D200's "the local pair would have to move in the same commit for the
fix to mean anything" was a condition the entry set on itself, and Task 7's fix
round met it**: six lines in `app/shared/reply.py` and two in
`app/activitypub/util.py`, one commit apart and both on the branch, so neither
half shipped as the one-twin repair **D520** registers as invisible to every
instrument this campaign runs.

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|

What IS established by reading is the divergence itself: two mirrored delete paths, one floor-guarded and one not, over a column a third code path recomputes. **Establishing or refuting reachability is the open work, and it is cheaper than it looks** -- the round-trip cases are all lossless since the repair, so only unrestored deletes and mixed sequences need examining. Task 7 declined to mirror the floor guard onto the restore increments, and was right to: the guard protects against going below zero, an increment has no floor to protect, and mirroring it would skip the increment in exactly the case where the delete took the column from 1 to 0 -- the commonest instance of the defect the repair exists for. **WIDENED BY SUB-PROJECT 42's FINAL REVIEW: THE GUARD HAS A SECOND EFFECT THIS ENTRY DID NOT SEE, AND ON THAT LIMB REACHABILITY IS NOT UNESTABLISHED -- IT IS ESTABLISHED, AND THIS ROUND QUADRUPLED THE EXPOSURE.** `if to_delete.post.reply_count_cross_posted:` is a TRUTHINESS test, so it guards against `None` exactly as much as against `0`. `migrations/versions/6814385881d3_cross_posted_reply_count.py:22` is the only migration that touches the column and it adds it `nullable=True` with **no `server_default` and no backfill `UPDATE`**; `app/models.py:1723`'s `default=0` is INSERT-time only. **So every `post` row predating that migration that has not had a reply created through `PostReply.new` since carries `NULL`**, and an unguarded `+=`/`-=` on it raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +=: 'NoneType' and 'int'`. ### 3. A KNOWN TRAP, A BUILT TOOL, A PROVEN HELPER -- AND THREE TESTS THAT SHIPPED WITHOUT IT -- D540, D541

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D540 | `tests/test_shared_reply_make.py`'s `TestEditReply`; `app/models.py:1259-1261`; `tests/conftest.py:131` | **THE ROUND'S MOST SERIOUS FINDING, AND IT INDICTS WORK THAT HAD ALREADY PASSED REVIEW TWICE.** Probe P01 replaced `reply.community.is_moderator(user)` with the constant `False` at BOTH `edit_reply:224` and `:239` simultaneously -- moderator status made invisible to the entire function -- and **all 38 tests passed**. Cause: `_seed_for_reply` mints `author` first, `tests/conftest.py:131`'s teardown resets every sequence to 1 after every test, and `User.is_admin` opens `if self.id == 1: return True`. Three `TestEditReply` tests omitted the `_burn_a_seed()` call that offsets the sequence, so their actor was id 1, an admin outright, and every `make_moderator()` call in them was **decorative**. One of the three stated in its own docstring that it proved `:223` gates `:224`; it could not, because `:224` would not have refused its user even if reached. **P02 IS THE CONTROL AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THIS A FINDING ABOUT THREE TESTS RATHER THAN ABOUT THE FIXTURE**: the identical substitution against `make_reply:177`, whose actor is `s.actor` at id 2, dies immediately. **THE PROCESS FAILURE IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART. ### 3. `unfollow_user` DECREMENTS COUNTERS THAT `follow_user` NEVER INCREMENTED -- D557

### 4. TWO QUERY-SHAPE DIVERGENCES, IN SIBLING FUNCTIONS OF ONE MODULE -- D558, D559

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D558 | `app/shared/user.py:33-34` against `:35`; `app/constants.py:80-81` | **A one-row read standing in for a set membership test.** `:33-34` execute `SELECT role_id FROM "user_role" WHERE user_id = :person_id` and take `.scalar()`, which returns the FIRST row's first column and discards the rest; `:35` then asks `if role == ROLE_ADMIN or role == ROLE_STAFF:`. **`user_role` is a many-to-many association table** -- a user may hold several roles -- so for a multi-role user the guard is answered by whichever row the planner happened to return first. A user holding an admin role plus any other can therefore be blocked, or not, depending on row order, with no ordering clause anywhere to make it deterministic. The correct shape is a membership test (`WHERE user_id = :person_id AND role_id IN (3, 4)` with `.first() is not None`, or the `IN` pushed into an `EXISTS`). Note this is also a THIRD spelling of "is this user privileged" in a campaign that has already registered two -- **D295**/**D442**/**D481** cover `Site.admins()` keying on role ID against `User.is_admin()` keying on role NAME; this one keys on a raw role ID read out of the association table directly, bypassing both. | **open, registered, not fixed** | Read at source in Task 10 |
| D559 | `app/shared/user.py:91` against `:151`, `:216`, `:219`, `:237`, `:284` | **`.one()` where every sibling in the module uses `.get()`.** `subscribe_user:91` is `person = db.session.query(User).filter_by(id=person_id, banned=False).one()`, which raises `sqlalchemy.exc.NoResultFound` -- an uncaught 500 -- for a `person_id` that does not exist OR that exists and is banned. `ban_user`, `unban_user`, `follow_user` and `unfollow_user` all reach their target with `db.session.query(User).get(...)`, which returns `None` and fails later and differently. **The divergence matters most on the banned limb**, because that is not a missing row: subscribing to a user who was banned between page render and form submission is an ordinary race, and this function answers it with a traceback. Direct sibling of **D506**, the same `.one()`-versus-404 divergence at `delete_reply:247` and `restore_reply:275` one module over -- **second sighting of that class, and the first one outside `app/shared/reply.py`.** | **open, registered, not fixed** | Read at source in Task 10 |

### 2. THE ROUND'S ONE PRODUCTION CHANGE: FOUR BAN STATES, ONE REFUSAL, AND A REFUSAL THAT CREATED THE STATE THAT FELL THROUGH -- D576

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D576 | `app/shared/auth.py:57-75`, fixed at `d8e870a2` | **FIXED. A BANNED USER WAS REFUSED ONCE AND ADMITTED ON EVERY ATTEMPT AFTERWARDS FROM THE SAME ADDRESS.** `:57` is `if user.id != 1 and (user.banned or user_ip_banned() or user_cookie_banned()):` -- a three-way disjunction that admits four distinct states to the ban block. The refusal (`:66-73` the web arm's flash, banned-tracking cookie and redirect; `:74-75` the API arm's `raise Exception('incorrect_login')`) was nested inside `:59`'s `if user.banned and not user_ip_banned():`, which exists only to **detect a banned user arriving from a new IP address** and add an `IpBan` row for it. So the refusal fired only on `:59`'s condition, not on `:57`'s. The four states `:57` admits, `(banned, ip_banned, cookie_banned)`: **row 1 `(True, False, *)` -- `:59` true, a new `IpBan` is inserted and committed, and the user IS refused.** **Row 2 `(True, True, *)` -- `:59` false, falls straight through to `:77`, `login_user(user, remember=True)`, admitted with a JWT on the API arm.** **Row 3 `(False, True, *)` -- an IP-banned user who is not account-banned: `:59` false, admitted.** **Row 4 `(False, False, True)` -- a cookie-banned user: `:59` false, admitted.** Three of four ban states were not refusals at all. **The serious part is that row one PRODUCES row two**: refusing a banned user is precisely the act that bans their IP, so their second attempt from that address arrives already IP-banned, matches row two instead of row one, and is admitted. The ban held for exactly one request. **The fix is a dedent of `:66-75` by one level**, so the refusal hangs off `:57` directly and `:59` keeps only the IpBan insert -- ten lines, no logic added, no line deleted. **Three tests were written FIRST asserting the defective behaviour** (`..._admits_a_banned_user_whose_ip_is_already_banned`, `..._admits_an_ip_banned_user_who_is_not_banned`, `..._admits_a_cookie_banned_user`, each carrying a self-verifying assertion inside its `_ban_state` patch block so a silently-failing monkeypatch could not make them vacuous), then **inverted to `refuses_`** when the dedent landed; `test_log_user_in_web_refuses_a_banned_user_row_one` is the control and passed unchanged on both sides of the fix. **The fix is load-bearing rather than decorative, and that was proved by execution, not asserted**: the mutation pass re-nested `:66-75` inside `:59` (MAN1) and exactly those three inverted pins failed, 3 failed / 123 passed, while the row-one control kept passing -- which is what a control for row one should do. | **FIXED `d8e870a2`; three pins inverted; re-nest mutation killed** | Task 2's four ban-state pins, Task 4's dedent and inversion, MAN1 in the mutation pass |

### 3. TWO TAXONOMY CORRECTIONS -- A CAUSE THAT DOES NOT EXIST, AND A SHAPE THAT IS NOT CATALOGUED -- D577, D578

These are the round's most consequential documentation findings, and neither is
cosmetic: a wrong cause number in a committed artifact propagated through two
sub-projects, and an uncatalogued shape is the reason two separate tasks reached
for the wrong number independently.

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D577 | `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_reply.py:1584`; `tests/README.md` fact 75; this round's spec and `global-constraints.md`, corrected at `8f8402c7` | **`tests/README.md` FACT 75 HAS NO CAUSE 4(c).** Item 4, "Tautology", has exactly two shapes, (a) and (b); the full catalogue is 1, 2, 3, 4(a), 4(b), 5, 6, 7, 8. The shape the label was reached for -- an unreachable `try`/`except` whose body can never run because the callee inside the `try` has no raising path for the argument shape the call site can produce -- **is cause 8, "Unreachable handler"**, added by sub-project 19 for exactly that purpose. **The wrong label originates at `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_reply.py:1584`, a committed artifact of sub-project 20, which mis-cited the very cause sub-project 19 had just added, one sub-project earlier, in the same campaign.** Sub-project 44's spec and `global-constraints.md` inherited it verbatim and were corrected mid-round at `8f8402c7`. **AMENDED AT THE ROUND'S FINAL REVIEW: `:1584` IS STILL WRONG, AND IT IS NOT THE ONLY RESIDUAL -- THIS ENTRY ASSERTED IN BOLD THAT IT WAS.** A repo-wide `/usr/bin/grep -rn "4(c)" docs/ tests/` finds **THREE** tracked sites the round did not account for, not one. **(1) `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_reply.py:1584`** -- the origin, still wrong, still owed the proposed fix below. **(2) `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-14-auth-repair-and-three-module-close-44.md:21` and `:1300`** -- **this round's own plan**, which inherited the label from the round's spec and was missed when the spec and `global-constraints.md` were corrected at `8f8402c7`, because that correction was applied to the two files it was reported against rather than to everything the label had propagated to. **Both plan lines are now FIXED**, each carrying an explicit note that it originally cited 4(c) and that the cause that stands is 8. **(3) `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-25-coverage-campaign-findings.md:7189`** -- pre-existing narrative prose from the sub-project that introduced the error, reading *"fact 75's cause 4(c) now has a pattern rather than a one-off"*. **Deliberately NOT edited: it is another round's record, and rewriting a prior round's entry text is not this round's to do.** A reader who lands on `:7189` should read it as naming **cause 8**; this entry is the correction of record for it. **The sharpened lesson: a claim that a bad citation has exactly one remaining site is itself a COUNT, and a count is a claim -- derive it with `grep` before writing it in bold.** The original note follows. **THE SOURCE CITATION AT `:1584` IS STILL WRONG.** It was deliberately left alone: correcting a committed test file's comment is not a spec amendment, and this round's production budget was one change. **PROPOSED FIX, owed to whoever next touches that file: change the cited cause from "4(c)" to "8" at `tests/test_shared_tasks_send_reply.py:1584`, leaving the surrounding argument untouched** -- the substance was right in all three places and only the number was wrong, which is exactly why it survived two reviews. A reader who checks the argument and not the number sees nothing amiss. The general rule is registered as README fact 251: **a cause number handed to you in a brief is a claim like any other -- open fact 75 and read the item before citing it** -- with its corollary, that having learned 4(c) does not exist you must not now force-fit cause 8 either, since cause 8 is scoped to a `try`/`except` and a bare `if <cond>: raise` is not cause 8 however unreachable it is (D587). | **open in the source file, registered with a proposed fix; the spec and constraints are FIXED at `8f8402c7`** | Fact 75 read in full at source by two independent tasks, both of which reported the absence of 4(c) |
| D578 | `app/shared/auth.py:54`, `:74`, `:111` against `:21-39`; `tests/README.md` fact 75 cause 4(b) | **A SHAPE FACT 75 DOES NOT CATALOGUE: AN INVARIANT THAT MAKES A CONDITION A *TAUTOLOGY* AND STRANDS ITS *FALSE* ARM.** `app/shared/auth.py`'s three residual dead branches `[[54,57],[74,77],[111,-18]]` are the **mirror image** of cause 4(b), not an instance of it. 4(b)'s literal text is *"The condition is falsified by an invariant established BEFORE the guard runs -- by a caller, or by an enclosing guard -- so its **True** branch is dead code."* Here the invariant does the opposite: `:21-39` is an exhaustive `if src == SRC_WEB / elif src == SRC_API / else: return None`, and `src` is a parameter that is **never reassigned anywhere in the body**, so every line after `:39` runs with `src` provably in `{SRC_WEB, SRC_API}`. Each later `elif src == SRC_API:` is therefore reached only when its paired `if src == SRC_WEB:` was false, which makes it **always true when reached** -- and it is the **False arm** (the fall-through that `[54,57]`, `[74,77]` and `[111,-18]` denote) that is dead, not a True branch. Filing it under 4(b) as written would be precisely the mis-shelving fact 75 warns against, and **the first draft of Task 3's ruling did exactly that, quoting 4(b) with a bracketed "[non-matching]" substituted for the source's literal "True"** -- a bent quotation that concealed the polarity mismatch. That was caught in review and corrected before it shipped; it is the first of this round's two citation corrections. **This is NOT sub-project 43's D564 mistake.** A third `src` value genuinely can be passed -- `test_log_user_in_refuses_an_unknown_source` passes one -- and the proof is that it is intercepted and returned at `:39`, never reaching `:46`, `:66` or `:111`. Both the "no input reaches it" and "no test reaches it" questions are answered, and they are answered the same way. **PROPOSED FIX: register this shape in fact 75 itself, either as a new sub-shape under cause 4 alongside (a) and (b), or as an explicit note extending 4(b) to its mirror image** -- so the next reader who meets a tautology-with-a-dead-False-arm does not re-derive it, and does not reach for 4(b), for cause 8, or for a number that does not exist. It is recorded in the meantime as README fact 252. **Do not file it as 4(b) and do not file it as cause 8.** No test is written for the three branches. | **open, registered with a proposed taxonomy amendment; the round's own mis-citation of 4(b) is CORRECTED** | `src` re-read at source, the `:21-39` exhaustiveness proved over all three of its own branches, and the SRC_PUB test as the positive control |

### 4. PRODUCTION DEFECTS FOUND BY READING OR BY TESTING, REGISTERED NOT FIXED -- D579, D580, D581, D582, D583, D584

The `if` is false, control reaches `:84`, and **every real HEIC upload dies on `raise Exception('filetype not allowed')` after being decoded successfully.** The extension is advertised as allowed and cannot be used. **The distinction that makes this registerable rather than a hypothesis is that `repr(img.format)` was OBSERVED in the container** -- a real HEIF buffer built with `pillow_heif.from_pillow(...).save(buf, format='HEIF')`, opened, and printed: `'HEIF'`. ### 10. A ROW-ORDER WEAKNESS IN A MODULE ALREADY AT FLOOR 100 -- D593

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D593 | `tests/test_shared_user_blocks.py:274-292` against `app/shared/user.py:74`; contrast `tests/test_shared_domain.py:147-163` | **A TEST WHOSE DISCRIMINATION DEPENDS ON WHICH ROW AN UNORDERED `.first()` HAPPENS TO RETURN, IN SHIPPED WORK.** `test_unblock_another_user_leaves_someone_elses_block_alone` exists to catch a mutant that drops `blocker_id=user_id` from `app/shared/user.py:74`'s `filter_by(blocker_id=user_id, blocked_id=person_id).first()`, and its docstring says so. But it seeds **the subject's own block row at `:283` BEFORE the bystander's at `:284`**, and `:74` has no `ORDER BY`. Under the narrowed filter the query matches both rows and `.first()` returns whichever the planner hands back -- for a small table, ordinarily the first-inserted, which is the subject's own row. **The mutant then deletes exactly the row the test expects to be gone, `remaining == {(bystander.id, s.target.id)}` still holds, and the test passes while asserting nothing.** Seeding the bystander first inverts that: `.first()` returns the bystander's row, the mutant deletes it, and the assertion fails as intended. `app/shared/user.py` is at **floor 100**, so this is a weakness in work this campaign has already shipped and ratcheted -- not a gap in something unfinished. **The sibling written THIS round does it the other way round deliberately and says so in its docstring**: `tests/test_shared_domain.py:154-156` seeds the bystander's `DomainBlock` first, and `:147-149` explains that a mutant narrowed to `domain_id` alone would find the bystander's row first and delete it. Same family as this campaign's standing rule against ordered assertions over rows a query planner returned, arriving from the other side: **here the SEEDING order, not the assertion order, is what the evidence rests on, and unlike an ordered assertion it fails silently in the safe-looking direction.** **RECIPE: swap `:283` and `:284` so the bystander's row is inserted first, and add the docstring sentence that says why** -- one line moved, no new fixture, and the assertion at `:290-292` is already a set comparison and needs no change. Worth a sweep: any test that relies on `.first()` to pick a row out of a set the mutant widens has this shape. | **open, registered with recipe, not fixed** | `:274-292` and `app/shared/user.py:74` read at source; the domain sibling's deliberate inverse |

## Sub-project 44, final review: one production finding registered -- D594

The whole-branch review of sub-project 44 turned up one finding that is about
production code rather than about the record, surfaced while checking D586's
Evidence line. It is registered, not fixed: this round's production budget was
the one dedent at `d8e870a2`, and it is spent.

| ID | Where | What | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D594 | `app/models.py:1586-1591` against `:1566` and `:1504-1507`; `app/shared/user.py:175-176` (M53, D586) | **`purge_content`'s THIRD LEG IS DEAD CODE, AND THE CONSEQUENCE IS THAT PURGING A USER NEVER FLUSHES THEIR UPLOADED IMAGES FROM THE CDN.** `purge_content` calls `self.delete_dependencies()` at `:1566`. That function, at `:1504-1507`, runs `db.session.query(File).join(user_file).filter(user_file.c.user_id == self.id).all()` and, for every row, calls `file.delete_from_disk(purge_cdn=False)` and then `DELETE FROM "user_file" WHERE file_id = :file_id` -- **every** `user_file` row for the user, unconditionally. `purge_content:1586` then re-runs the **identical** query, `File.query.join(user_file).filter(user_file.c.user_id == self.id).all()`, against a join table from which those rows have just been removed, so it **always** gets `[]` and the loop body at `:1587-1591` never executes. Both loops were read at source. **Two consequences, both real and neither hypothetical. (a) The `File` ROWS ORPHAN.** `:1504-1507` deletes the `user_file` link and the file on disk but **never** `db.session.delete(file)`; the only code that would have deleted the `File` row is `:1590`, which never runs. A purged user's uploaded `File` rows therefore survive in the database with no `user_file` link and no owner. **(b) THE CDN IS NEVER PURGED FOR A USER'S UPLOADS.** The dead `:1588` is `file.delete_from_disk(purge_cdn=flush)` -- it honours `purge_content`'s `flush` argument, which `app/shared/user.py:176` passes as `flush=flush_cdn`, the operator's explicit choice. The call that actually runs is `:1506`'s `delete_from_disk(purge_cdn=False)`, hard-coded. **So a moderator who bans-and-purges with CDN flush requested gets the local files removed and the CDN copies left in place**, for exactly the class of images -- user uploads -- the flush is most obviously for. The `Post`-joined leg at `:1562-1564` does honour `flush`; only the `user_file` leg does not. **THIS DOES NOT CHANGE M53's EQUIVALENCE VERDICT (D586), AND IT IS PART OF WHY THE MUTANT SURVIVES.** M53 replaces `app/shared/user.py:175`'s `to_ban.delete_dependencies()` with `pass`. On the unmutated arm `:175` empties `user_file` and `:1566`'s repeat finds nothing; on the mutated arm `:1566` empties it. **Either way `:1586` is reached with the join already empty**, so the dead leg is dead on both arms and cannot distinguish them -- the ruling stands unchanged, and the dead code is one of the reasons it does. **NOT FIXED: registered only.** The round's single production change is spent, and this is a behavioural fix to a purge path, not a test or a comment. **PROPOSED FIX, for whoever takes it**: delete `:1586-1591` and pass `purge_cdn` through to `app/models.py:1506` (i.e. give `delete_dependencies` a `purge_cdn` parameter defaulted to `False` and have `purge_content:1566` pass `flush`), adding the missing `db.session.delete(file)` at `:1507` -- so the rows are deleted once, by the code that actually runs, with the caller's flush honoured. **It needs a test that asserts the `File` row is gone after a purge and that `delete_from_disk` was called with `purge_cdn=True` when `flush=True`; there is no such test today, which is how a whole loop stayed dead.** | **OPEN PRODUCTION DEFECT, registered not fixed; D586's verdict UNCHANGED, D586's Evidence line CORRECTED** | Both loops (`app/models.py:1504-1507` and `:1586-1591`) read at source; `:1566`'s call site read at source; `app/shared/user.py:176`'s `flush=flush_cdn` read at source |

## Sub-project 45: `app/shared/site.py` and `app/shared/community.py` Group A -- two refusals that flashed and fell through, and a mutation headline scoped rather than rounded up

**The round in one line: two guards flashed a refusal message and then fell
through into the code the refusal existed to prevent, in the third
consecutive round to ship exactly that shape; both are fixed, `site.py`
closes at 100 for the campaign's 26th floor, `community.py`'s first of four
function groups closes with no floor because three groups remain, and a
27-mutation pass killed all 27 -- reported here as "27 of 27 decision-point
and guard-deletion mutants killed," not as "zero survivors," because one
whole class of mutation (seven unconditional `cache.delete_memoized` calls)
was deliberately not attempted.**

**BOTH FIXES ARE THE SAME SHAPE AS EACH OTHER AND AS TWO EARLIER ROUNDS'
FIXES, AND THAT PATTERN IS ITSELF REGISTERED (D597).** `app/shared/site.py:19`
flashed `'You cannot block the local instance.'` and fell through to the
block-creation code with no `return`; `app/shared/community.py:60` used
`not cm.is_owner or not cm.is_moderator` where the De Morgan-correct guard
is `and`, so a plain moderator (`is_moderator=True, is_owner=False`) satisfied
the flipped condition and left freely instead of being refused. Neither
defect required an unreachable line, a crash, or a missing test file to
survive: every line involved executed on every run, and the gap was that no
test asserted the *outcome* the refusal was supposed to prevent -- an
`InstanceBlock` row not created, a `CommunityMember` row not deleted. That is
this round's whole lesson, and it recurs from sub-project 43 (`if SRC_WEB:`)
and sub-project 44 (the mis-nested ban refusal, D576).

### 1. THE ROUND'S TWO PRODUCTION CHANGES: TWO REFUSALS THAT FLASHED AND FELL THROUGH -- D595, D596

Coverage tooling has nothing to say about any of them: a covered line and a covered branch are not evidence that the code *does what its message claims*. **The single mechanical remedy that catches all three, stated once for the register**: a test of a refusal must assert the state the refusal exists to prevent -- a row not created, a row not deleted, a session not logged in -- never merely that a message was flashed or an exception's text matched. This is the discipline `global-constraints.md` calls out as "the rule this round turns on," and it is registered here as a recurring pattern rather than three unrelated coincidences, because a fourth round meeting the same shape should recognise it as a class, not rediscover it as a lucky read of the source.
